name: Adults
theme: A guided course for adults: the faith made plain, and what to do with it

units.title: Knowing God
units.eq: Is it reasonable to believe, and who is the God Christians believe in?

lessons.title: The question of God
lessons.idea: Almost every culture asks where the world came from and what it is for. The Church holds that reason can reach God as the source of all things, and that this natural knowledge is a doorway to what God has revealed, not a substitute for it.
lessons.question: What experiences (wonder, loss, love, guilt) have made you ask whether God is real?
lessons.activity: Write the two strongest reasons you have heard for belief and for unbelief. Swap with a partner and answer each in a sentence, without arguing, only clarifying. Then name which reason you find most moving, and why.
teach: Reason can know that God exists: “by the natural light of human reason” (CCC 36; Romans 1:19–20; Vatican I). The Church claims this as a possibility open to every person, not a proof that forces belief, and she does not claim reason alone reaches the Trinity or the Gospel.

The classical paths start from the world (motion, cause, contingency, order; Aquinas’ five ways, CCC 34) and from the person (conscience, the longing for truth, goodness and beauty; CCC 33). Each leads to the conclusion that there is a source of all that is, which “all call God.”

Honest limits: these are arguments for a first cause, not the God who calls us by name. Revelation completes what reason begins (CCC 50–53). Faith is not against reason but “goes beyond” it (CCC 156–159).
Take objections seriously: the problem of evil, the success of science, religious diversity and the hiddenness of God. A good answer names the strongest version of the objection before replying.
talk: Where does your own desire for something “more” show up?
Which objections to belief do you find hardest, and why?
What would it take to move from “I think there might be a God” to trusting him?
quiz: What does the Church teach about reason and God?|Only faith can know God and reason is useless|Reason can say nothing about God|Reason can reach God as the source of all things, though faith goes further|God can only be known by feeling|2|CCC 36 teaches that God can be known with certainty by reason from creation.

Which is the better description of faith?|Obedience to rules|Believing without any reason|A free and reasonable trust in God who reveals himself|A feeling of certainty|2|Faith is a personal adherence to God and assent to his truth (CCC 150, 154-155).

Is doubt always a sign of unbelief?|No, it can be a step toward deeper faith if it keeps asking|Yes, always|Only for the uneducated|Only in teenagers|0|Doubt held with honesty and prayer can lead to a stronger faith.
lessons.life: This week, spend ten quiet minutes outside without your phone. Notice what you see, then thank the Creator or, if you are unsure, simply say: “If you are there, show me.”
lessons.saint: C. S. Lewis: an Oxford atheist who called himself the most reluctant convert in England. (Not a Catholic, but a witness many Catholics read.)
misc: “Arguments for God are meant to force belief.”
lessons.mem: “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” (Augustine)
lessons.hook: Ask the group to write, privately, the question about God they would most like answered. Collect them anonymously and read two aloud.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to state, in two sentences, one reason reason can point to God and one limit of that reasoning.

script.open: Welcome the group, and ask each person to answer in one sentence: “What is a question about God that you have not been able to put down?” Write them on a board or sheet without comment. Say, “Tonight we are not here to settle these. We are here to see whether the question is a door.”
teach: Say: “The Catechism begins its whole treatment of faith with a surprising claim: ‘The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God.’ (CCC 27) It continues: ‘Man is by nature and vocation a religious being. Coming from God, going toward God, man lives a fully human life only if he freely lives by his bond with God.’ Almost every culture in history has had prayer, sacrifice and some account of the divine. The Church doesn’t treat this as proof, but as a pointer. Hunger points to food; thirst to water; the desire for God, perhaps, to God. Lewis argued this in Mere Christianity: ‘If I find in myself a desire which no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.’”

Say: “The Church also teaches that reason can know God. CCC 31-35 names the ways: the world (its order, beauty, contingency), and the human person (conscience, longing for truth and happiness, openness to the infinite). First Vatican Council: God ‘can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.’ Aquinas’s five ways and others are arguments, not coercion. They show faith is reasonable. They aren’t the same as faith. Faith is a gift and a free response to a God who reveals himself. And the Church admits the obstacles (CCC 29): ‘the rebellion against evil in the world, religious ignorance or indifference, the cares and riches of this world, the scandal of bad example on the part of believers.’ Many people leave not because the arguments fail, but because of wounds.”

Say: “Doubt and seeking. The Church does not treat honest questions as sin. The father in Mark 9:24 prays, ‘I believe; help my unbelief!’ Augustine’s Confessions is a prayer from a restless heart. A seeker’s task is to be honest: follow the evidence where it leads, keep asking, notice what you are afraid of, and be willing to pray, even tentatively: ‘God, if you are there…’ Jesus promised: ‘Seek and you will find.’ (Matthew 7:7) Lewis’s conversion shows how God works through friends, books, longing and hard thinking all together. If you believe already, the task is to understand why, and to give an account to others (1 Peter 3:15). If you don’t, the invitation is to keep the question open.”
ask: What does the Catechism claim about the desire for God? (It is written in the human heart because we are made by God and for God.)
Name two kinds of evidence the Church points to for God. (The created world and the human person: conscience, longing for truth and happiness.)
Is honest doubt a sin? (No; the Church welcomes honest seeking.)
practice: In pairs, each person names a moment they felt a longing that nothing in the world satisfied. Listen without fixing.
Individually, write down your strongest reason to doubt and your strongest reason to hope. Swap with a partner, who writes a one-sentence honest response to each.
Together, read Psalm 63:1-8 slowly.
Each person writes a two-line prayer, however tentative: “God, if you are there…” or “God, you are here, and…”
script.close: Close with silence for a minute, then the Our Father together. Sign of the Cross. Invite everyone to read the first chapter of Book 1 of Augustine’s Confessions or the first part of Mere Christianity before next time.

tryit: Write down the strongest reason you have doubted God.
Write the strongest reason you have hoped.
Trade with a partner and respond honestly, without fixing.
lessons.saintStory:
Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast in 1898. His mother died of cancer when he was nine, after he had prayed for her recovery, and he began to drift from faith. By his mid-teens he was an atheist. He fought in the First World War, was wounded, and then became a brilliant student and a fellow at Oxford, and a rationalist who thought religion was a beautiful but false myth.
But he kept being ambushed by what he called Joy: a piercing longing, set off by a line of poetry or a northern landscape, that nothing in the world satisfied. And his best friends at Oxford, including J. R. R. Tolkien, were Christians. In 1929, he later wrote, “I gave in, and admitted that God was God, and knelt and prayed: perhaps, that night, the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.” That was belief in God. Belief in Christ came in September 1931, after a late-night conversation with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson on a walk at Magdalen College, in which Tolkien argued that the Christian story was a myth that had really happened. A few days later, riding to the zoo in a motorcycle sidecar, Lewis realized that he believed.
He became an Anglican, and the author of Mere Christianity, The Screwtape Letters and the Chronicles of Narnia. He died on November 22, 1963.

lessons.title: One God in three Persons
lessons.idea: Christians believe in one God who is a communion of three Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is not a puzzle to solve but the heart of the faith: God is love, and love is shared.
lessons.question: Why does it matter that God is one and also a communion of Persons?
lessons.activity: Take the usual analogies (shamrock, water, sun) and name exactly where each one fails, using the errors of Arius, Sabellius and tritheism as a guide. Then write one sentence about the Trinity that is true and does not fall into any of those errors.
teach: The Trinity is a mystery in the strict sense: a truth we could not know unless God revealed it (CCC 237). It is not a contradiction. We say one God (one divine nature) in three Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), really distinct, equal and eternal (CCC 253–256).

The Church’s language came from the New Testament’s witness (Matthew 28:19; John 1:1–14; 2 Corinthians 13:13) and was fixed at Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381) and later councils to exclude errors: Arius (the Son is a creature), Sabellius or modalism (one God wearing three masks), and tritheism (three gods).

“God is love” (1 John 4:8). If God were a single solitary Person, love would be something God does only after creating. In the Trinity, love is eternal: the Father gives himself wholly to the Son, the Son returns it, and that love is the Holy Spirit (CCC 221).

Every analogy limps (shamrock, water, sun). Use them to name where they fail: the shamrock suggests parts, water suggests modes. The right response to the mystery is worship and the Sign of the Cross, a creed in a gesture (CCC 232–237).
talk: If God is love by nature, what does the Trinity say about why anything exists?
How does knowing God as Father change prayer?
Which Person of the Trinity do you find easiest to pray to? Hardest?
quiz: What does the Church mean by “mystery” when it speaks of the Trinity?|Something nonsensical|A story|A truth we could not know unless God revealed it|A secret for priests|2|CCC 237: the Trinity is the central mystery of faith.
Which description is an error?|The Spirit proceeds from the Father|The Son is begotten of the Father|Three Persons in one God|One God, three masks worn in turn|3|That error is called modalism.
What makes the Persons distinct?|Their power|Their names only|Their relations to one another|Their age|2|The Father, Son and Spirit are distinguished by their relations (CCC 254).
lessons.life: Pray the Sign of the Cross slowly this week, once each morning, thinking of each Person as you say the name.
lessons.saint: Andrei Rublev: a Russian monk who painted three angels at a table as a window on the Trinity.
misc: “The Father is God, the Son is half-God.”
lessons.mem: “Go and make disciples… baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Ask the group to draw the Trinity in 30 seconds, then compare drawings. Which pictures help? Which mislead?
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain why the Trinity is not three gods and not one God in three masks.

script.open: Place an image of Rublev’s Trinity where all can see (printed or on a screen). Say nothing for two minutes. Then ask, “What do you notice first? What draws your eye?” Take answers without correcting.
teach: Say: “The Trinity is the central mystery of the Christian faith: one God in three Persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Catechism: ‘The Trinity is One. We do not confess three Gods, but one God in three persons, the ‘consubstantial Trinity.’ The divine persons do not share the one divinity among themselves but each of them is God whole and entire.’ (CCC 253) Three statements must be held together: God is one; each Person is fully God; the Persons are really distinct, as the Father begets, the Son is begotten, and the Spirit proceeds. A mystery is not a contradiction: it is a truth too rich for us to grasp fully. We can know it only because God revealed it.”

Say: “Where does it come from? The Old Testament speaks of God’s oneness (Deuteronomy 6:4) and hints at plurality (Genesis 1:26; the three visitors of Genesis 18). In the New Testament, the Trinity is revealed in Jesus. At his baptism, the Father speaks, the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove (Matthew 3:16-17). Jesus commands baptism ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ (Matthew 28:19) Paul’s blessing: ‘The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.’ (2 Corinthians 13:14) John 1:1: ‘the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’ The Church spent centuries finding language, at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). Words like ‘person’ and ‘substance’ were tools to protect the truth.”

Say: “Why does it matter? Because of what it says about God: God is not a lonely monad but a communion of love. ‘God is love’ (1 John 4:8) means that from all eternity the Father loves the Son in the Spirit. Creation and salvation flow from that love: the Father sends the Son, and they send the Spirit. We are made in the image of this communion; our lives are meant to be relationships of self-gift. Prayer is participation in the Trinity: we pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Every Sign of the Cross is a creed. Rublev’s icon: the table has an open place, which invites us into the life of God. St. Patrick’s shamrock is a familiar teaching image, but analogies fall short; the Church avoids the heresies of modalism (one God in three masks) and tritheism (three gods).”
ask: State the Trinity in one sentence. (One God in three divine Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.)
Where in the New Testament is the Trinity most visible? (The baptism of Jesus; the baptismal formula in Matthew 28:19.)
Why does the Trinity matter for how we live? (God is a communion of love, and we are made in his image.)
practice: Sit in silence before the icon for five minutes. Then write three things you noticed and one question.
In pairs, explain to each other what you think each Person of the Trinity does (the Father, the Son, the Spirit), and where you find it hard.
Together, pray the Sign of the Cross slowly, naming each Person.
Individually, write a two-sentence answer to a friend who asks, “Isn’t the Trinity just three gods?”
script.close: Pray the Glory Be slowly and then the Sign of the Cross. Invite the group to make the Sign of the Cross thoughtfully once a day this week, naming the Persons.

tryit: Look at the Rublev icon for five silent minutes.
Write what you notice.
Say which truth about the Trinity it shows.
lessons.saintStory:
Andrei Rublev was a monk and icon painter, born around 1360 in Russia, in a time of war and the Mongol domination. He lived at monasteries in Moscow, and worked with the famous painter Theophanes the Greek. He was gentle and quiet, a man of prayer.
Around 1411, he was asked to paint an icon in honor of St. Sergius of Radonezh, who had founded the Trinity Monastery. He chose the scene from Genesis 18, where Abraham welcomes three mysterious visitors at Mamre, whom the Church Fathers saw as a sign of the Trinity. Rublev painted three angels around a table, their heads inclined toward one another, a cup at the center. The circle formed by their bodies draws the viewer in, and there is an open place at the table.
The icon became the most famous in Russia. Rublev died around 1428. The Russian Orthodox Church canonized him in 1988. The icon shows the Trinity not as a puzzle but as a communion of love, with room for us.

lessons.title: Jesus: who do you say he is?
lessons.idea: Jesus is the Son of God made man. He is not merely a great teacher: he claims to forgive sins, to be Lord of the Sabbath and one with the Father, and he rose from the dead. The question he asks, “Who do you say that I am?”, is put to every generation.
lessons.question: Who do you actually think Jesus is, and where did that come from?
lessons.activity: Read Mark 2:1–12 aloud. List every claim the passage makes about who Jesus is, directly or indirectly, and what reaction each claim causes. Decide what you would have had to believe about him to be offended, and what to believe to be amazed.
teach: The Church confesses that Jesus is true God and true man: one divine Person with two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation (Chalcedon, 451; CCC 464–469). He has a human body, soul, mind and will.

The Gospels show claims that go beyond a teacher: forgiving sins (Mark 2:5–7), lordship over the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The Jewish listeners understood what he claimed (John 10:33).

C. S. Lewis’ trilemma (liar, lunatic or Lord) is useful but incomplete; a fair account also considers legend and the reliability of the sources (see Session 2.1). The best case rests on the Gospels, the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15) and the faith of the first community, not on a single argument.

Titles carry meaning: Messiah (anointed king), Son of God, Son of Man (Daniel 7), Lord (the divine name in the Greek Old Testament) (CCC 436–451). Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27–30) is the hinge of the Gospels.
talk: Why do people often want Jesus to be only a teacher?
What changes in your life if he is only a good man? What changes if he is Lord?
Which title (Messiah, Son of God, Lord) speaks to you most right now?
quiz: What did the Council of Chalcedon teach?|Jesus became God at his baptism|Jesus had a divine mind in a human body|Jesus is one Person in two natures, divine and human|Jesus only seemed to be human|2|CCC 467.
Which Gospel passage shows Jesus claiming to forgive sins?|Mark 8:27|John 21|Luke 2:1|Mark 2:1-12|3|Only God can forgive sins, which is why the scribes object.
What does “incarnation” mean?|Man became divine|God speaks through a prophet|Christ had no body|God became man|3|CCC 461.
lessons.life: Read one chapter of Mark this week in one sitting, as if you had never read it, asking one question: what does this tell me about who he is?
lessons.saint: Martha of Bethany: the busy sister who confessed, before Lazarus rose, that Jesus is the Christ.
misc: “Jesus is just a great moral teacher.”
lessons.mem: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If a friend asked who Jesus is, what would you say in one sentence?” Collect answers, then read Mark 8:27–30.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to list two claims Jesus makes about himself and what follows if they are true.

script.open: Give each person an index card. Ask them to write, anonymously, one sentence beginning, “Jesus is…” Collect, shuffle and read them aloud one by one, without comment. Notice the range together.
teach: Say: “Jesus asked his disciples at Caesarea Philippi, ‘Who do men say that the Son of man is?’ and then, ‘But who do you say that I am?’ (Matthew 16:13-15) The whole Christian faith turns on the second question. The Church answers in the Creed: Jesus is the eternal Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, truly God and truly man, who died and rose to save us. The Gospels preserve what Jesus said and did that provoked this question: he taught with authority; forgave sins; healed; claimed to be Lord of the Sabbath; said, ‘Before Abraham was, I am’; accepted worship from Thomas, ‘My Lord and my God’; and was killed for claiming to be the Son of God.’”

Say: “C. S. Lewis posed the argument well: ‘I am trying here to prevent anyone saying the really foolish thing that people often say about Him: ‘I’m ready to accept Jesus as a great moral teacher, but I don’t accept His claim to be God.’ That is the one thing we must not say. A man who was merely a man and said the sort of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher. He would either be a lunatic—on a level with the man who says he is a poached egg—or else he would be the Devil of Hell. You must make your choice.’ Critics say Lewis ignores the option that the stories are legend. But the Gospels were written within decades by people who knew eyewitnesses, and the early Church’s worship of Jesus was very early (Philippians 2:6-11). The Resurrection is the decisive evidence.”

Say: “Jesus is not just an idea; he is a person who asks, ‘Do you believe this?’ The Church’s faith is a personal trust. The Catechism (CCC 426): ‘At the heart of catechesis we find, in essence, a Person, the Person of Jesus of Nazareth.’ How do we come to know him? Reading the Gospels (the best way is to read one slowly), the sacraments, prayer, the community of believers, and acts of service (Matthew 25). Martha confessed her faith before she saw the miracle. Our answer to Jesus’ question may be partial and still growing. The invitation of this course is to take the question seriously and to let him answer it in us. Peter’s response (‘You are the Christ’) is a gift of the Father (Matthew 16:17). Pray for that gift.”
ask: What is the central question of the Gospels? (“Who do you say that I am?”)
What did Martha confess? (That Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.)
What is Lewis’s argument in short? (Jesus can’t be merely a good teacher; he was either Lord, a liar or a lunatic.)
practice: Read John 11:17-27 aloud, slowly, in turns.
Write your own answer to the question, “Who do you say that I am?” in three sentences, as honest as you can.
In pairs, share one sentence from your answer, and what it costs you to say it.
Choose one Gospel passage to read this week, and write down which question of Jesus you will bring to it.
script.close: Close by praying together Martha’s words slowly: “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to read Mark’s Gospel, a chapter a day.

tryit: Write your own answer to “Who do you say that I am?”
Say what it costs you to say it.
Say where it shows up in your week.
lessons.saintStory:
Martha lived in Bethany, near Jerusalem, with her sister Mary and brother Lazarus. Jesus often stayed in their house. Luke records the famous scene: Martha was “distracted with much serving,” and complained to Jesus that Mary had left her to serve alone. Jesus said, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; one thing is needful. Mary has chosen the good portion.” Martha is often remembered for this mild rebuke.
But John tells a deeper story. When Lazarus fell ill, the sisters sent word to Jesus, who delayed. By the time he arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days. Martha went out to meet him, and said, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Jesus said, “Your brother will rise again,” and then, “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” He asked, “Do you believe this?”
She answered, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, he who is coming into the world.” This confession echoes Peter’s. Shortly after, Jesus raised Lazarus. Martha served at the supper afterward. The Church honors her on July 29.

units.title: Can I trust the Bible and the Church?
units.eq: How does God speak, and who speaks for him today?

lessons.title: How the Bible came to be
lessons.idea: The Bible is a library of 73 books written over about a thousand years. Catholics believe God is its author and that human authors wrote in their own style and time. The Church recognized which books belong and reads them as one story that leads to Christ.
lessons.question: What do you assume about the Bible, and where did you get that idea?
lessons.activity: Compare the healing of the paralytic in Mark 2:1–12 and Luke 5:17–26. List what the two share and what differs, and say what each author seems to want you to notice. Then read the same story in Matthew 9:1–8 and ask what the differences teach about how the Gospels were written.
teach: The Bible is a library of 73 books (46 Old Testament, 27 New) written over about a thousand years in many forms: history, law, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, gospel, letter, apocalypse. God is the author and human writers were “true authors” who used their own powers (CCC 105–107).

Inspiration means Scripture teaches “without error the truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation” (CCC 107; Dei Verbum 11). That does not make every verse a lesson in science or modern history. Ask what the author intended, given the form and the time (CCC 109–110).

Three rules for reading (CCC 112–114): attend to the unity of the whole Bible, read it within the living Tradition of the Church, and keep the coherence of the faith in view (the analogy of faith). Add the four senses: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical (CCC 115–117).

The canon: the Church, in the fourth century (Hippo 393, Carthage 397; confirmed by Pope Innocent I), recognized which books were inspired. Catholics and Orthodox keep seven Old Testament books (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees) that were in the Greek Bible of the early Church; many Protestants omit them.
talk: What is the difference between asking “did this happen?” and “what is this passage teaching?”
Why does it matter that the Church read the Bible before it was written down in one book?
What part of Scripture have you never read? What is stopping you?
quiz: Who is the author of Scripture, according to the Church?|God, who inspired the human authors|Only human beings|Nobody knows|The Church councils|0|CCC 105-106.
How many books are in the Catholic Bible?|66|73|100|81|1|46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New (CCC 120).

Which is NOT one of the Church’s three criteria for interpreting Scripture?|Each person’s private feeling alone|The living Tradition of the Church|The analogy of faith|The unity of the whole of Scripture|0|CCC 112-114.
lessons.life: Read the Mass readings each day this week using the Readings page and write one sentence on what stood out.
lessons.saint: Paula of Rome: a widow who learned Hebrew in middle age and helped Jerome translate the Bible.
misc: “The Church invented the Bible to control people.”
lessons.mem: “All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable.” (2 Timothy 3:16)
lessons.hook: Show a hand-copied page and a printed page. Ask how we can trust that an ancient text has been passed on well.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain inspiration, the canon and one way to read a hard passage well.

script.open: Ask: “How do you think the Bible got into the book you hold? Who wrote it? Who decided what was in it? Who translated it?” Let people share what they know and what they have heard. Write the questions that come up on a board.
teach: Say: “The Bible is not one book but a library of 73 books (46 Old Testament, 27 New) written over about 1,000 years, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, by many human authors, with God as the principal author (2 Timothy 3:16; Dei Verbum 11). The Old Testament took shape over centuries, from oral tradition, court records, prophetic oracles, songs, laws. The New Testament was written in the first century, between about AD 50 and 100: Paul’s letters first (1 Thessalonians around AD 50), then the Gospels (Mark around 65-70; Matthew and Luke around 80-85; John around 90-100). The Gospels came from the preaching and memories of eyewitnesses, shaped for particular churches.”

Say: “The canon, the list of inspired books, was recognized by the Church over time. By around AD 200 the four Gospels and most of Paul’s letters were widely used. Athanasius’s Easter letter in 367 lists the 27 books we have; the Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) approved it. Why those books? The Church looked for apostolic origin, orthodoxy of teaching, and use in the liturgy. The Old Testament canon: the Church used the Greek Septuagint, which included the books Protestants call apocrypha (the deuterocanonical books: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1-2 Maccabees, parts of Daniel and Esther). Luther dropped them in the 16th century. Trent defined the canon in 1546. Other early writings, like the Gospel of Thomas, were rejected because they were later, not apostolic, and taught ideas contrary to the apostolic faith.”

Say: “How reliable is the text? We have no original manuscripts, but we have an enormous number of copies: over 5,800 Greek New Testament manuscripts, some from the second century (the John Rylands fragment, c. 125), and many early translations. The vast majority of variations are minor, like spelling. Textual scholarship allows us to be highly confident of what the authors wrote. The Old Testament: the Dead Sea Scrolls (found 1947) confirmed the accuracy of the Hebrew text over a thousand years. Translations: Jerome’s Vulgate was the standard for a thousand years; English translations like the Douay-Rheims, RSV-CE, NABRE, and ESV-CE. Reading the Bible well: with the Church, in context, with attention to literary form, and in prayer. Paula’s story shows that women and men have always given their lives to bring the Scriptures to the people.”
ask: How many books are in the Catholic Bible? (73: 46 Old Testament and 27 New.)
Who recognized the canon? (The Church, over centuries, at councils like Hippo, Carthage and Trent.)
How reliable is the New Testament text? (Very: thousands of manuscripts, some from the second century.)
practice: Draw a timeline from Abraham to AD 400. Mark when each part of the Bible was written and when the canon was recognized.
In pairs, trace how your own Bible reached you: translator, publisher, bookstore, giver. Name the chain.
Compare a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible’s table of contents and mark the differences.
Each person makes one commitment: a daily time and place to read a short passage this week.
script.close: Pray the prayer before reading Scripture: “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” Sign of the Cross. Ask each person to bring a Bible next time, and note which translation they use.

tryit: Trace how the Bible came to you.
Name the people between you and the original.
Say one thing you will do to read it better.
lessons.saintStory:
Paula was born in 347 into a noble Roman family. She married a senator and had five children. When her husband died in 379, she gave herself to prayer and charity. In 382, she hosted at her house a visiting group of bishops, including Jerome, a learned monk who was working for Pope Damasus.
Paula and her daughter Eustochium became his students. They studied Scripture with him, even learning Hebrew, which was unusual for Roman women. After Damasus died, Jerome was driven from Rome, and in 385 he sailed for the Holy Land. Paula and Eustochium followed him, leaving behind her other children. In Bethlehem, they founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women, near the Church of the Nativity, with a guesthouse for pilgrims. Paula spent her fortune on the poor.
She worked alongside Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, the Vulgate. He dedicated many of his Bible commentaries to Paula and Eustochium, and said Paula pressed him to keep going. She died in 404. Jerome wrote her biography.

lessons.title: Tradition and the teaching authority
lessons.idea: Jesus did not write a book; he formed a community and sent it. The apostles handed on what they had received in preaching and worship before the New Testament was complete. Catholics believe Christ keeps the Church faithful in teaching through the pope and bishops.
lessons.question: Why do you think many people trust a book more than a community, or the reverse?
lessons.activity: Read 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 2 Timothy 2:2, and trace the chain of teaching they describe from Paul to Timothy to others. Draw it as a diagram, then label where Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium appear. Write one sentence on what would go wrong if any one were removed.
teach: Jesus did not write a book; he formed a community and sent it (Matthew 28:19–20). The apostles handed on what they received by preaching and worship before and alongside the New Testament (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 2 Timothy 2:2). This living handing-on is Tradition (CCC 75–79).

Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine source and form one deposit of faith (CCC 80–82). Tradition is not a second book of extra teachings; it is the Church’s living memory of the Gospel in her teaching, worship and life, and it is how the Church knows what Scripture means and which books belong.

The Magisterium, the bishops with the Pope, interprets the Word of God authentically. It is not above the Word but serves it, teaching “only what has been handed on” (CCC 85–87). The Spirit’s promise (John 16:12–13) is that the Church will be guided into all truth.

Infallibility is narrow: the Pope teaching definitively as pastor of all on faith or morals, or the bishops with him doing the same, are preserved from error (CCC 889–892). It does not make every statement of a pope infallible, nor does it mean the Pope is sinless. Doctrine develops (deepens) without contradicting what came before.
talk: What do you gain from a Church that teaches with authority? What do you find hard?
What is the difference between Tradition and traditions (customs)?
How does the idea of apostolic succession answer the question “who decides?”
quiz: What is the “deposit of faith”?|The truth of revelation entrusted to the Church|The Church’s buildings|Money kept in a bank|A list of rules|0|CCC 84.
Infallibility means the pope…|Never sins|Can invent new doctrine|Is right about science|Cannot err when defining a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church|3|CCC 891.
What is apostolic succession?|Bishops receiving authority in unbroken line from the apostles|Popes choosing their heirs|Using the same Bible|Priests wearing the same vestments|0|CCC 861-862.
lessons.life: Choose one teaching of the Church you find hard. Read the Catechism paragraph on it and, before you decide, read the reasons the Church gives.
lessons.saint: Hegesippus: a second-century traveler who checked the churches’ teaching against Rome’s.
lessons.mem: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught.” (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do you know what your grandparents were like if you never met them?” Link to oral and written handing-on.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe how Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together.

script.open: Write three beliefs on the board, such as the Trinity, the Eucharist, and Sunday Mass. Ask the group, “Where did you first hear each one? Who vouched for it?” Take a few examples.
teach: Say: “Catholic teaching on revelation: God revealed himself fully in Jesus Christ. This revelation is handed on in two ways, Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, which ‘flow from the same divine wellspring’ and make up a single deposit of faith (DV 9-10). The Church’s teaching authority, the Magisterium, interprets this deposit. It doesn’t add new revelation but guards, explains and applies it. The Catechism: ‘The task of interpreting the Word of God authentically has been entrusted solely to the Magisterium of the Church, that is, to the Pope and to the bishops in communion with him.’ (CCC 85) Why? Because Jesus promised to be with the Church until the end, and the Spirit would guide her ‘into all the truth.’ (John 16:13)”

Say: “Tradition is not mere old customs. The Greek paradosis means ‘handing on.’ Paul: ‘I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received.’ (1 Corinthians 15:3) ‘Hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter.’ (2 Thessalonians 2:15) The apostles taught by preaching, by example, by liturgy; some of this was written down in the New Testament, and some was handed on in the Church’s life: creeds, worship, the canon of Scripture itself. Tradition is the living memory of the Church, guided by the Spirit. The test: continuity with the apostles (Vincent of Lérins: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all). Tradition allows development, like an acorn to an oak, but never contradiction.”

Say: “Why not Scripture alone? Because the Bible doesn’t say that it alone is the authority; because someone must say which books belong; because Scripture needs interpretation, and sincere Christians disagree; and because the early Church lived by the apostolic teaching before the New Testament was finished. Protestant Christians honor Scripture deeply; the difference is about how its meaning is guarded. The Magisterium has levels: dogmas (infallible); definitive doctrines; authoritative non-definitive teaching requiring religious assent; prudential judgments. The laity are not passive: the whole Church has a sense of the faith (sensus fidei). It is reasonable to wonder, ‘Why should I trust this?’ The answer: Christ’s promise, and the evidence of two thousand years of continuity. For you: ask, study, and also trust.”
ask: What are the two ways revelation is handed on? (Scripture and Tradition.)
What is the Magisterium? (The Pope and bishops in communion with him, who interpret the deposit of faith.)
What test did Hegesippus use? (Continuity of teaching with the apostles in the churches.)
practice: Each person lists three beliefs they hold and writes where they learned them (parent, teacher, Scripture, experience).
Take one belief and trace it back: who taught the one who taught you? How far can you get? Where does the Church vouch for it?
In pairs, explain the difference between Tradition and traditions.
Write a two-sentence answer to the question: “Why trust the Church’s teaching?”
script.close: Pray the Nicene Creed together slowly. Sign of the Cross. Ask the group to read CCC 74-100 this week and underline one line that surprised them.

tryit: List three beliefs you hold and where you learned them.
Trace each back as far as you can.
Say who vouches for them.
lessons.saintStory:
Hegesippus was a Christian of Jewish background who lived in the second century. He was concerned about growing confusion: various teachers were spreading secret doctrines and claiming to be the true Christianity. In about 155, he decided to find out for himself what the churches taught. He traveled from the East to Rome, visiting many cities and bishops along the way, including Corinth, where he stayed for some time.
He found, he reported, that in every church he visited, they taught the same thing: “In every succession and in every city, the teaching is in accordance with the Law and the Prophets and the Lord.” When he reached Rome, he made a list of the bishops in succession, from the apostles to the present. He wrote five books of Memoirs, now lost except for quotations preserved by the historian Eusebius.
His journey is a snapshot of how early Christians knew they had the true faith: not by private revelation, but by the continuity of teaching in the churches founded by the apostles.

lessons.title: Why the Church? Why not just Jesus?
lessons.idea: Many say, “I like Jesus but not the Church.” The Church teaches that Christ founded a visible community and that he is present in it, the Body of Christ. The Church is made of sinners and saints, and her sins are real; but she is also where we receive the sacraments and hear the Gospel.
lessons.question: What hurt, scandal or disappointment has shaped how you think about the Church?
lessons.activity: Read Acts 2:42–47 and list the four things the first believers “devoted themselves to.” For each one, write whether your life already includes it, and one small step to add it. Then write a candid sentence about what bothers you most about the Church and one thing she has given you.
teach: Christ founded a visible community: he chose the Twelve, gave Peter the keys (Matthew 16:18–19), instituted the Eucharist and sent the apostles with authority to teach, baptize and forgive sins (Matthew 28:19; John 20:21–23; CCC 551–553, 765).

The Church is both holy and made of sinners (CCC 827). She is holy in her Head and in her means of grace, and always in need of purification. The scandals are real; the saints show the same Church can also produce astonishing holiness.

The Church is described as the Body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 1:22–23), the People of God, and the Temple of the Spirit (CCC 781–801). “I like Jesus but not the Church” misses that Jesus chose to be present to us through a body: Word, sacraments and a community.
Acts 2:42–47 shows the pattern: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers. A fair test of whether you are part of the Church is whether you have those four.
talk: What is the difference between the Church’s teaching and the failings of her members?
What would you miss if the Church were not there?
What community of faith do you actually belong to right now?
quiz: What are the four marks of the Church?|One, holy, catholic, apostolic|Rome, Paris, Jerusalem, Antioch|Old, big, rich, strict|Faith, hope, love, mercy|0|CCC 811.
Is the Church free of sin?|Her members sin, though she is holy in Christ and her sacraments|No one is holy|Yes, all members are sinless|Only the clergy sin|0|CCC 827.
What did the first Christians devote themselves to?|Silence|Debate|Teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers|Wealth and travel|2|Acts 2:42.
lessons.life: Go to Mass this week, even one weekday, and arrive early. Pray for the person who first taught you about God.
lessons.saint: Venerable Mary Ward: a woman who loved the Church so much that she kept obeying while it jailed her.
lessons.mem: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” (Matthew 18:20)
lessons.hook: Poll: “Have you ever said ‘I like Jesus but not the Church’? What makes you say it?” Listen without defending.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to give two reasons the Church is more than an institution and one honest struggle.

script.open: Say: “Be honest. Name something about the Church that frustrates or hurts you.” Go around, and write each answer on a sheet. Receive them without defending. After everyone has spoken, say, “Now name one thing that you would be poorer without.”
teach: Say: “‘I like Jesus but not the Church’ is a very common view, and it deserves a serious answer. First, the Church is not an optional add-on. Jesus founded a community: he called twelve, gave Peter the keys, sent them to baptize and teach, and said he would be with them. Paul says the Church is the Body of Christ: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ (Acts 9:4) Jesus identifies himself with his people. You can’t be a Christian alone: Baptism incorporates you into a body. St. Cyprian: ‘He cannot have God for his Father who has not the Church for his mother.’”

Say: “What does the Church give that we can’t give ourselves? The Word of God (the Bible comes from her); the sacraments (Baptism, Eucharist, Confession); the truth, guarded and handed on; community and mission; the saints; correction when we go astray. Without a community, faith tends to become private opinion. Without sacraments, we can’t receive the bread of life. We don’t invent Christianity; we receive it. And the Church is for the world, running hospitals, schools, charities. The Church feeds the poor in more places than any other organization.”

Say: “But the Church is also full of sinners, and her history includes serious failures: corruption, abuse, wars, cover-ups, injustice. The Church doesn’t deny it. The Catechism (CCC 827): ‘The Church, embracing sinners in her own bosom, is at once holy and always in need of purification.’ Her holiness comes from Christ. Jesus knew his Church would include weeds and wheat (Matthew 13:24-30), a net with good and bad fish (13:47-50). He chose Judas. Catherine of Siena and Mary Ward show how to respond: neither leave nor pretend. Stay, speak the truth with love, work for reform from within, and keep your own life holy. Pope Francis described the Church as a ‘field hospital’: not for the perfect but the wounded. A key question: Is the problem the Church or specific people in the Church? Both can need healing. And if you have been hurt, the Church should hear you.”
ask: Did Jesus found a Church? (Yes: the Twelve, the keys to Peter, the commission to baptize and teach.)
What does the Church give that we can’t give ourselves? (The Bible, sacraments, guarded teaching, community, saints.)
How can the Church be holy and sinful? (Her holiness is Christ’s; her members are sinners.)
practice: In pairs, each person shares their honest frustration with the Church and what they would lose without her.
On a sheet, list five gifts the Church has given you, even indirectly.
Write one thing you would change and one thing you will do toward it, such as praying, serving or speaking to your pastor.
Share one commitment with the group.
script.close: Pray for the Church: “Lord, purify your Church and make her holy, beginning with me.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to read about one saint who reformed the Church.

tryit: List what bothers you about the Church.
List what you would lose without it.
Say what you owe and what you would change.
lessons.saintStory:
Mary Ward was born in 1585 in Yorkshire, England, in a Catholic family during the time when Catholicism was illegal. She grew up hearing of martyrs and hiding priests. At fifteen, she felt a call to the religious life, and crossed to Flanders, where she became a lay sister among the Poor Clares. Soon she felt God wanted something else: a community of women, living without enclosure, who would teach girls and serve the Church actively in the world, as the Jesuits did.
In 1609 she began her Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary, with schools for girls in Saint-Omer and elsewhere. The idea of women religious teaching and traveling freely was unacceptable to many bishops. Critics attacked her, and in 1631 Pope Urban VIII suppressed her institute. She was arrested by the Inquisition and imprisoned in a convent in Munich, as a “heretic, schismatic and rebel to Holy Church.”
She wrote, from her sickbed, to the pope, protesting her loyalty. She was released, and spent the rest of her life quietly in England, dying in Yorkshire in 1645. Her work survived, and the Institute was approved in 1877. She was declared Venerable in 2009. Her legacy shows what it means to love the Church even when she is wrong.

units.title: Prayer: learning to talk with God
units.eq: How do I pray when it feels empty?

lessons.title: What prayer is and why it is hard
lessons.idea: Prayer is the raising of the mind and heart to God. It is a relationship, not a performance. Dryness, distraction and doubt are normal, and the saints describe them too. The way through is to keep showing up with honesty.
lessons.question: What gets in the way of your prayer: time, boredom, doubt, guilt, noise?
lessons.activity: Try ten minutes of silent prayer with no phone. After, write one honest sentence about what happened, even if it is “I was bored.” Then choose one practice from the lesson (a psalm, the Jesus Prayer, a Gospel scene) and commit to it for one week.
teach: Prayer is “the raising of one’s mind and heart to God” (CCC 2559). It is a relationship: God thirsts for us first (CCC 2560), and prayer is our answer. The Psalms and the Our Father are the Church’s school of prayer (CCC 2585–2589, 2759–2761).

Dryness, distraction and doubt are normal and not a sign of failure (CCC 2726–2733). Distraction is not sin; it becomes a problem only when we cling to it. Acedia, a kind of spiritual laziness, is the great enemy of persevering prayer (CCC 2733).

Practical help: choose a time and place; start with a short, fixed amount (ten minutes); use Scripture, a psalm or the Jesus Prayer to hold your attention; keep a note of what you notice. Jesus’ own advice: pray in secret and without piling up words (Matthew 6:5–8).

The Church names five forms (blessing/adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise) and three expressions (vocal, meditation, contemplation) (CCC 2626–2643, 2700–2724). Most beginners need only start with one.
talk: When have you felt closest to God in prayer? What was different?
What would you say to God if you were completely honest?
How is prayer different from meditating or clearing your mind?
quiz: What is prayer?|A way to get what we want|The raising of the mind and heart to God|A technique to relax|Reciting words|1|CCC 2559.
Which is one of the five forms of prayer?|Rituals|Thanksgiving|Argument|Silence only|1|CCC 2626-2643.
What should you do when prayer feels dry?|Skip it|Keep praying, keep it simple, and be honest|Pray longer words|Give up until you feel it|1|CCC 2729.
lessons.life: Set an alarm for a daily five-minute prayer for seven days. Same time, same place, same short routine.
lessons.saint: Brother Lawrence: a wounded soldier turned monastery cook who learned to pray among the pots and pans.
misc: “If prayer feels dry, God is absent.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, teach us to pray.” (Luke 11:1)
lessons.hook: Set a ten-second silence. Ask: “What was your mind doing?” Name the experience of distraction.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name one obstacle in their prayer and one remedy they will try.

script.open: Say: “Be honest: how is your prayer life right now? One word.” Go around the group (answers like ‘dry,’ ‘nonexistent,’ ‘rushed,’ ‘good’). Say, “We’ll talk about why prayer is hard, and what helps.”
teach: Say: “The Catechism defines prayer as ‘the raising of one’s mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God.’ (CCC 2559) It’s a relationship with a Person who loves us, who comes to meet us: ‘Prayer is the encounter of God’s thirst with ours.’ (CCC 2560, quoting Augustine) Even the desire to pray is a gift. So the first step is to receive: God is already seeking you. Prayer isn’t performance or technique, though it has methods. It involves vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation. It involves petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise and adoration. And it includes silence and listening.”

Say: “Why is it hard? CCC 2726-2728 and common experience: Distractions: our minds wander. Dryness: we feel nothing. Doubt: ‘Is anyone there?’ Busyness: no time. Boredom or acedia: spiritual laziness. Discouragement: ‘I’m not good at this.’ Pride or perfectionism: wanting results. Wrong expectations: wanting consolation instead of God. Brother Lawrence had these too; he said that for the first ten years he suffered much. The Church’s guidance: persevere. Prayer is a battle (CCC 2725), and a gift. Fidelity matters more than feeling. Start small: five minutes a day is better than an hour once a month. Choose a time and place. Use a simple structure: begin with the Sign of the Cross, a prayer to the Spirit, read a short Scripture passage, speak in your own words, be silent, end with the Our Father.”

Say: “The practice of the presence of God: offer ordinary tasks to God, remember him briefly through the day (a short phrase like ‘Jesus, I trust in you’), and turn back gently when you forget. Thérèse called prayer ‘a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven.’ Jesus’ own teaching: go to your room and shut the door (Matthew 6:6), don’t babble (6:7), pray the Our Father, ask persistently (Luke 11:5-13), and pray always (Luke 18:1). Pray with others and alone. Use the Church’s prayers. Not feeling anything doesn’t mean prayer isn’t working. Many saints have gone through long dryness. Look at fruits over time: more patience, love, honesty. If you struggle, talk to a priest or a spiritual director.”
ask: How does the Catechism define prayer? (Raising the mind and heart to God; the encounter of God’s thirst with ours.)
Name two obstacles to prayer. (Distraction, dryness, busyness, doubt.)
What is the practice of the presence of God? (Remembering God throughout the day and offering ordinary tasks to him.)
practice: Try three minutes of silent prayer together after reading Psalm 23 slowly. Then each person writes one sentence: what happened?
In pairs, share your biggest obstacle and one thing that has helped.
Write a simple rule: when, where and how long you will pray this week.
Choose a short phrase to repeat during the day, such as ‘Jesus, I trust in you.’
script.close: Close with a minute of silence, then the Our Father slowly. Sign of the Cross. Invite each person to text or tell a partner at the end of the week how it went.

tryit: Try three minutes of silent prayer.
Note what happens.
Write one realistic practice for this week.
lessons.saintStory:
Nicolas Herman was born in 1614 in Lorraine, France. As a young man he joined the army, and in the Thirty Years’ War he was badly wounded and left with a permanent limp. He worked as a footman. At eighteen, he had an experience while looking at a bare tree in winter, thinking of how it would leaf in spring: a deep awareness of God’s providence, which never left him.
In 1640 he entered the Discalced Carmelite monastery in Paris as a lay brother, taking the name Lawrence of the Resurrection. He was assigned to the kitchen, which he hated at first, then to repair sandals. He spent over forty years in ordinary work. He found that he could be in the presence of God while peeling vegetables, as much as at the chapel. He wrote: “The time of business does not with me differ from the time of prayer; and in the noise and clatter of my kitchen… I possess God in as great tranquility as if I were upon my knees at the blessed sacrament.”
He didn’t write a book; his conversations and letters were collected after he died in 1691 as The Practice of the Presence of God. Many people over three centuries have found them helpful.

lessons.title: Praying with Scripture: lectio divina
lessons.idea: Lectio divina is a slow, prayerful reading of a short passage in four movements: read (lectio), reflect (meditatio), respond (oratio), rest (contemplatio). It lets God’s word become a conversation.
lessons.question: Which passage of Scripture has ever “spoken” to you?
lessons.activity: Practice lectio divina on Luke 24:13–35 together, or alone. After each step, write a few words. Share one thing from the oratio step (your response to God). Plan three more mornings this week using the next day’s Mass reading.
teach: Lectio divina is the Church’s ancient way of praying with Scripture: read (lectio), reflect (meditatio), respond (oratio), rest (contemplatio), and then act (actio) (CCC 2705–2708). It comes from the Fathers and monasteries (Origen, Ambrose, Benedict), and Dei Verbum 25 urges all the faithful to it.

The key is slowness: read a short passage aloud, stop at the word or phrase that stands out, ask what God is saying to you through it, answer him in your own words, then be still. You are not trying to finish a text but to meet a Person.

Scripture is the place God speaks: “the word of God is living and active” (Hebrews 4:12; Psalm 119:105). The Emmaus story (Luke 24:13–35) shows the pattern: Jesus explains the Scriptures and the disciples’ hearts burn within them; they recognize him in the breaking of bread.

Keep it ordered: pray with the Church’s readings (the Mass of the day is a good source), read with the Church’s mind (see Session 2.1), and test your insights with a wise guide. Prayer with Scripture is meant to lead to Christ and to love of neighbor.
talk: What phrase stood out to you? Why do you think?
How is this different from studying the passage?
How could you do this with the Mass readings each morning?
quiz: What are the four steps of lectio divina?|Study, memorize, quote, teach|Read, reflect, respond, rest|Ask, seek, knock, wait|Sing, kneel, stand, sit|1|The traditional movements.
Whom did Jesus walk with on the road to Emmaus?|Mary and Joseph|Two disciples|The apostles|Peter alone|1|Luke 24:13.
Why pray with Scripture?|To impress others|To hear God’s word as addressed to me|To avoid thinking|To replace the Mass|1|CCC 2653.
lessons.life: Pray with the Sunday Gospel before Mass this week: read it Monday, linger on one line each day.
lessons.saint: Guigo II the Carthusian: a monk who set down the four steps of sacred reading.
lessons.mem: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” (Psalm 119:105)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 23 first fast, then slowly with pauses. Ask what changed.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe the four movements of lectio divina and share one word that stood out.

script.open: Hand out a short passage (Luke 5:1-11 or Psalm 131). Say: “Read this as you would read an email.” Allow one minute. Ask, “What did you retain?” Then say, “Now we will read it as a letter from someone who loves us.”
teach: Say: “Lectio divina, ‘divine reading,’ is an ancient way of praying with Scripture. Dei Verbum 25: ‘Prayer should accompany the reading of Sacred Scripture, so that God and man may talk together.’ Benedict XVI, in 2005, said that if lectio divina is promoted effectively, ‘it will bring to the Church—I am convinced of it—a new spiritual springtime.’ The method follows Guigo. Lectio: read slowly, preferably aloud, twice. Notice words, images and actions. Meditatio: ask what it says; ponder a word or phrase; connect it to your life. Mary ‘kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.’ Oratio: respond to God in your own words—praise, thanks, sorrow, petition. Contemplatio: rest quietly in God’s presence, beyond words. Some add actio: resolve to act on what you received.”

Say: “Why this way? Scripture isn’t just information; it’s God speaking. ‘The word of God is living and active.’ (Hebrews 4:12) Lectio treats the text as a person to meet. It engages the mind and the heart. It slows us down in a fast culture. It also protects us: reading in the Church’s context, with attention to the Catechism and the Church’s teaching, avoids private distortions. The Church’s liturgy is the other great school: the Mass readings. Pairing both: read the Sunday Gospel in advance, using lectio. Also: Ambrose and Augustine; Augustine’s own conversion started when he heard ‘Take and read.’ A good choice of passages: Gospel scenes, Psalms, the letters of Paul in small pieces. Avoid reading randomly or hunting for guidance in verses. Start with a Gospel: Mark or Luke.”

Say: “Practical tips. Choose a regular time, 10 to 20 minutes. Find a quiet place. Begin with a prayer to the Holy Spirit. Use a good Catholic Bible with notes. Keep a journal. Don’t aim for insights every time; fidelity matters. Distractions: gently return to the text. Dryness: stay with the words. If a phrase strikes you, stay on it. Share with others: lectio can be done in groups (the Benedictine form): read the passage three times, each time share a word, an image and an invitation. In the Ignatian form, you imagine yourself in the scene. Over time, the habit of lectio shapes your thinking. Mary treasured the Word. Let it become the way you pray.”
ask: What are the four steps of lectio divina? (Read, meditate, pray, contemplate.)
What does Dei Verbum 25 say about prayer and Scripture? (Prayer should accompany reading so that God and man may talk together.)
How does reading in the Church protect us? (It guards against private distortion.)
practice: Choose Luke 5:1-11. Read it aloud slowly twice. Let each person name a word or phrase that stands out.
Silent meditation, five minutes: write what the passage says to you.
Write a short prayer in response, then rest in silence for two minutes.
Share one insight aloud in pairs and choose a passage for daily lectio this week.
script.close: Pray the Our Father slowly. Sign of the Cross. Invite everyone to practice lectio with the coming Sunday’s Gospel.

tryit: Practice the four steps on one passage.
Write what you noticed at each step.
Choose a passage for the week.
lessons.saintStory:
Guigo II was a Carthusian monk who became prior of the Grande Chartreuse, in the French Alps, around 1174, and died around 1188. The Carthusians lived in solitude, silence and prayer, reading and copying books. He wrote a short letter to a fellow monk named Gervase, known as the Scala Claustralium, “The Ladder of Monks.”
He described the spiritual life as a four-rung ladder: reading (lectio), meditation (meditatio), prayer (oratio) and contemplation (contemplatio). He compared them to eating. Reading is like putting food in the mouth, meditation chews it, prayer tastes it, and contemplation is the sweetness that nourishes. “Reading without meditation is arid; meditation without reading is liable to error; prayer without meditation is lukewarm; meditation without prayer is unfruitful; prayer with devotion leads to contemplation, but to obtain contemplation without prayer would be rare.”
His letter turned a long tradition of monastic reading into a clear method that has been used ever since, and which Pope Benedict XVI recommended to the whole Church.

lessons.title: The Mass as prayer
lessons.idea: The Mass is the Church’s greatest prayer. In it Christ’s sacrifice on the cross is made present and we receive him. Praying the Mass means more than watching: it means offering your life with Christ.
lessons.question: What do you usually think about during Mass? What would you like to think about?
lessons.activity: Go through the Order of Mass using Mass mode in the app. At each part, name one thing you could offer to God (a worry, a person, a gift, a failure). Pick the part you most often tune out and plan one way to be present for it next Sunday.
teach: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life” (CCC 1324). At Mass, Christ’s one sacrifice on the Cross is made present and we are united to it (CCC 1362–1367); we also receive him as food (John 6:51–58). Praying the Mass means offering ourselves with Christ, not only attending.

The shape follows Emmaus: gathering, Liturgy of the Word, Liturgy of the Eucharist, sending (CCC 1346–1355). At each step you can offer something: sorrow at the penitential act, attention to the readings, your week at the offertory, your needs at the Prayer of the Faithful, thanksgiving after Communion.

Full, conscious, active participation (Sacrosanctum Concilium 14) is first interior: listening, responding, singing, kneeling, silence. Preparation (reading the Sunday readings in advance, Confession if needed, the fast of one hour) and thanksgiving matter (CCC 1385–1387).
On dry days the Mass still works: it is Christ’s action, not our mood (ex opere operato, CCC 1128), though our faith and attention open us to its fruit.
talk: What do you find hard about Mass? What helps?
How would you explain to a friend why Catholics go every week?
What is something you could offer to God at the offertory?
quiz: The Eucharist is…|A symbol of unity|A meal like others|The source and summit of Christian life|Only a memorial|2|CCC 1324.
The two main parts of the Mass are…|Offering and sermon|The Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist|Entrance and dismissal|Songs and prayers|1|CCC 1346.
What is “active participation”?|Singing loudly|Offering oneself with Christ in prayer and attention|Holding hands|Doing lots of tasks|1|CCC 1368.
lessons.life: Attend Mass once during the week and use Mass mode. Afterwards write the one line you want to carry into the day.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a teenager from Milan who called the Eucharist his highway to heaven.
misc: “I get nothing out of it, so it’s pointless.”
lessons.mem: “Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you bring to Mass besides yourself?” Invite one thing to offer this Sunday.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name the parts of the Mass and one way to participate more fully.

script.open: Invite the group to arrive five minutes early to a Mass this week as an experiment, or show a short video clip of a Mass beginning. Ask them to notice what they feel in the first five minutes. Share the impressions.
teach: Say: “The Catechism: ‘The Eucharist is ‘the source and summit of the Christian life.’’ (CCC 1324) In the Mass, Christ’s sacrifice on Calvary is made present, and we are united to it. The Mass has two main parts: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist, framed by Introductory and Concluding Rites. We can think of four movements: Gathering (we come as a community, confess our sins, sing, pray the Collect); Listening (readings, psalm, Gospel, homily, creed, prayers of the faithful); Offering and Consecration (gifts brought, the Eucharistic Prayer: thanks, memorial, Spirit, consecration, intercessions, doxology); Communion and Sending (Our Father, sign of peace, Lamb of God, reception of Christ, thanksgiving, blessing and dismissal).”

Say: “Participation: Vatican II urged ‘full, conscious and active participation.’ (SC 14) This doesn’t mean a lot of activity but an interior engagement: listening, singing, responding, offering. At the offertory, offer yourself: your week, your work, your struggles, with the bread and wine. At the consecration, adore. At Communion, receive. Then give thanks. A helpful rhythm: before Mass (arrive a few minutes early, read the Sunday readings, ask for a particular grace), during Mass (be present), after (silent thanksgiving, then live it out). Common obstacles: distraction, routine, unfamiliarity, poor music or preaching. Tips: sit near the front; follow along with the missal; pray the responses; bring an intention; receive reverently.”

Say: “Why bother on Sunday? The Church teaches that Catholics are obliged to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days (CCC 2180-2183) because it is the center of our relationship with God, and because we are a body. This is not an arbitrary rule but a response to love. Deliberately missing is grave; illness or serious obstacle excuses. In the Eucharist, we receive Christ and are united with the Church. The Eucharist transforms us and sends us. ‘Ite, missa est.’ Carlo’s secret was very simple: he went to Mass, adored, and let it shape him. He said, ‘All people are born as originals but many die as photocopies.’ Don’t let routine kill the wonder. Try daily Mass or Eucharistic adoration sometime. Receive worthily: in a state of grace, after a one-hour fast. If you’ve been away from the sacraments, come back through Confession.”
ask: What are the four movements of the Mass? (Gathering, listening, offering and consecration, communion and sending.)
What does full, conscious, active participation mean? (An interior engagement: listening, responding, offering.)
Why is Sunday Mass obligatory? (It is the center of our relationship with God and the Church.)
practice: Use a missal or Mass outline. Walk through the four movements, and write at each what you will offer.
In pairs, share what helps you pay attention, and what distracts you.
Plan your preparation for next Sunday: read the readings in advance, arrive early, bring an intention.
Write a short thanksgiving prayer for after Communion.
script.close: Pray the Anima Christi together. Sign of the Cross. Invite the group to attend one extra Mass or a holy hour this month.

tryit: Walk through the Mass in four movements.
Say what you offer at each.
Plan to prepare for next Sunday.
lessons.saintStory:
Carlo Acutis was born in London in 1991 and grew up in Milan. He was an ordinary teenager who loved computers, soccer, video games and his dog. His family was not particularly devout, but he asked at seven to receive First Communion. From then on, he went to Mass every day, and prayed the Rosary and made Eucharistic adoration. He said, “The Eucharist is my highway to heaven.”
He taught himself computer coding and created a website cataloguing Eucharistic miracles around the world, which has since been exhibited in many countries. He helped the homeless, was kind to classmates who were left out, and used his Sunday allowance for others.
In October 2006, at fifteen, he was diagnosed with acute leukemia. He offered his suffering for the pope and the Church. He died on October 12, 2006. He was beatified in 2020 and canonized in 2025. He is called the first millennial saint, and he shows that the Mass can be the center of a young person’s life.

units.title: Sin, mercy and Confession
units.eq: How do I deal with guilt and failure?

lessons.title: Sin: what it is and what it does
lessons.idea: Sin is an offense against God and a wound to ourselves and others. The Church distinguishes mortal sin (which breaks our friendship with God) from venial sin (which weakens it). Naming sin honestly is the first step toward mercy.
lessons.question: Why is it hard to speak honestly about sin?
lessons.activity: Read Psalm 51 slowly. Underline each action David asks of God (wash, cleanse, create, restore). Write what you would ask for in your own words. Then list three effects of sin (on God, self, others) and one way mercy answers each.
teach: Sin is an offense against God and a wound to ourselves and others (CCC 1849–1851). It is not only breaking rules; it is a failure of love and a lie about who we are. Scripture is honest about it: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

The Church distinguishes mortal sin, which breaks our friendship with God, from venial sin, which wounds it. Mortal sin needs three conditions together: grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1855–1862). Many people worry too much or too little; Confession is the place to sort it out.

Romans 7:15–25 describes the divided heart: “I do not do what I want.” Paul does not despair: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ.” Concupiscence, the inclination to sin that remains after Baptism, is a struggle and not itself a sin (CCC 1264).

Psalm 51 is the model prayer after sin: honest naming (“I know my transgressions”), a plea for mercy and a clean heart, and a promise to teach others. God does not stop at forgiving; he renews (“create in me a clean heart”).
talk: How is guilt different from shame?
Why do you think the Church names specific sins instead of only talking in general?
What is the difference between a mistake and a sin?
quiz: Which is NOT a condition for mortal sin?|Full knowledge|Being caught|Grave matter|Deliberate consent|1|CCC 1857.
Venial sin…|Weakens charity but does not destroy it|Is not really sin|Cuts off grace entirely|Cannot be forgiven|0|CCC 1855.
What is conscience?|Habit|A feeling|The Church’s rules|A judgment of reason that tells us the moral quality of an act|3|CCC 1778.
lessons.life: Spend ten minutes in an examination of conscience this week using the app’s Examination page. Write nothing down; simply notice.
lessons.saint: Augustine at sixteen: the pear tree that taught him what sin is for.
misc: “I am too bad to be forgiven.”
lessons.mem: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” (1 John 1:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do people mean when they say ‘that’s not a big deal’? When is that true and false?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to define mortal and venial sin and explain the three conditions for mortal sin.

script.open: Ask: “What is the difference between making a mistake, hurting someone by accident, and sinning?” Take answers. Then, “Why do you think a sixteen-year-old would steal fruit he didn’t even want?” Let the group suggest reasons.
teach: Say: “Sin is ‘an offense against reason, truth and right conscience; it is a failure in genuine love for God and neighbor’ (CCC 1849). It’s first of all about a relationship: ‘Against you, you only, have I sinned.’ (Psalm 51:4) Sin harms our relationship with God, with others and ourselves. It isn’t just breaking rules, but misdirected love. The Church distinguishes original sin (the wounded condition we inherit from the first sin; Baptism removes its guilt but leaves concupiscence, the inclination to sin), and personal sin. Personal sins can be mortal or venial. Mortal sin has three conditions: grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent. It destroys charity in the heart and separates us from God’s grace. Venial sin wounds charity but doesn’t destroy it.”

Say: “What does sin do? It enslaves: ‘Everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin.’ (John 8:34) Repeated sins form habits, called vices, and the capital sins: pride, greed, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth. Sin damages others and creates ‘structures of sin’ in society. It also leaves shame and hiding: Adam and Eve hid after eating the fruit. It makes us blind to our own faults. The deadliest thing is when we stop seeing sin at all. John Paul II said the loss of the sense of sin is the sin of our age. Our culture tends to explain away sin as psychology, society, genetics, or says that ‘there are no moral rules.’ It’s true that many factors affect our freedom (upbringing, addiction, trauma), and the Church recognizes that these can reduce culpability. But it doesn’t eliminate responsibility; to deny sin also denies freedom and dignity.”

Say: “Why talk about sin, then? Because the Gospel begins with it: ‘Repent, and believe in the gospel.’ (Mark 1:15) Naming the problem is the first step to the cure. Sin is not the last word: ‘Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.’ (Romans 5:20) The Church says: God’s mercy is greater than all sin; no sin is beyond forgiveness except refusing forgiveness. Honesty about sin is not self-hatred but truth. We ask: What am I really seeking in this? Augustine found the answer: ‘Thou hast made us for thyself.’ Every sin is a misdirected search for a good that only God satisfies. The antidote is honesty, repentance, and returning to the Father (Luke 15). A healthy examination of conscience is not scrupulosity; it’s a habit of looking at our life in God’s light.”
ask: How does the Catechism define sin? (An offense against reason, truth and right conscience; a failure of love for God and neighbor.)
What are the three conditions for a mortal sin? (Grave matter, full knowledge, deliberate consent.)
What is Augustine’s point in the pear story? (Sin can be loved for itself; it’s a twisted search for freedom.)
practice: Write briefly about a time you did something you knew was wrong, and ask: What was I really seeking? Share only what you choose to.
In pairs, discuss why we hide sin and what helps us tell the truth.
Read Psalm 51:1-12 slowly and underline the lines that speak to you.
Write a one-line prayer of honesty to God.
script.close: Pray Psalm 51:10-12 together. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to do a short examination of conscience nightly this week.

tryit: Write about a time you did something wrong for no good reason.
Name what you were really after.
Say where you needed mercy.
lessons.saintStory:
In Book Two of his Confessions, Augustine recalls a night when he was sixteen. He and a gang of friends went to steal pears from a neighbor’s tree. They weren’t hungry; they had better pears at home. They took a few bites, and threw most of them to the pigs. “It was foul, and I loved it. I loved my own undoing. I loved my error—not that for which I erred, but the error itself.”
He analyzed it for pages. Why would he do something so pointless? He realized that on his own, he wouldn’t have done it; it was the company, the thrill of belonging, the desire to do wrong simply because it was forbidden. It showed him that sin is not just breaking a rule but loving something disordered, a twisted imitation of freedom.
Augustine wrote his Confessions as a prayer to God, years later, after his conversion. He used the story not to excuse himself but to confess it. It is an honest look at how sin works. He wrote, “Thou hast made us for thyself, and our heart is restless until it rests in thee.” The Confessions are the first Western autobiography.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Confession
lessons.idea: In Confession Christ forgives sins through the priest. The sacrament has four parts: contrition, confession, penance and absolution. It is a meeting with mercy, not a courtroom.
lessons.question: What is your biggest worry about going to Confession?
lessons.activity: Learn the steps of Confession and practice them aloud (not your real sins). Read the parable of the Prodigal Son and notice who runs. Then write a short examination of conscience based on the Ten Commandments, and decide a date for your next Confession.
teach: Christ gave the apostles power to forgive sins on Easter evening (John 20:21–23), and the Church exercises it through bishops and priests acting in the person of Christ (CCC 1441–1445, 1461). The sacrament goes by several names: Penance, Reconciliation, Confession, Conversion.

The parts: contrition (sorrow, with the intent to sin no more), confession (naming sins, grave ones in kind and number), satisfaction (penance), and absolution (CCC 1450–1460, 1480). Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect from fear or shame, and is still enough for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

The seal is absolute: a priest may never reveal anything heard in Confession (CCC 1467). Mortal sin must be confessed before receiving Communion, and everyone who has reached the age of reason must confess grave sin at least once a year (CCC 1457, 2042).

The parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) shows the Father who runs. The sacrament gives more than a feeling: forgiveness of sin, restored grace, peace, and strength to resist (CCC 1468–1470). If it has been years, just say so: “It has been a long time.” The priest will help.
talk: Why did Jesus give the power to forgive sins to men?
What do you think the father in the Prodigal Son parable says about God?
What would make it easier for you to go?
quiz: What are the four parts of Confession?|Contrition, confession, penance, absolution|Confession, counseling, therapy, forgiveness|Prayer, fasting, almsgiving, silence|Sorrow, regret, shame, hope|0|CCC 1450-1460.
Who can forgive sins in the sacrament?|A deacon|A bishop only|A priest, in the person of Christ|Any believer|2|CCC 1461.
The seal of confession means…|The priest may never reveal what was confessed|The sacrament is private|The priest may share it with the bishop|The penitent cannot speak|0|CCC 1467.
lessons.life: Schedule a Confession this week. If it has been years, say so; the priest will help you.
lessons.saint: John Nepomuk: a Bohemian priest who, according to tradition, died rather than break the seal of confession.
lessons.mem: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” (John 20:23)
lessons.hook: Read the Prodigal Son. Ask: “Who runs? Who waits? What does the father say?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to list the four parts of Confession and answer “Why a priest?”

script.open: Say: “Be honest: when did you last go to Confession? What do you remember about it? What gets in the way?” Give the group a moment of silence, then invite a few answers, without judgment. Some may say they have never been or feel afraid.
teach: Say: “Reconciliation is the sacrament in which Christ forgives the sins committed after Baptism through the ministry of the Church. Its roots: John 20:21-23, where the risen Jesus breathes on the apostles and says, ‘If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven.’ Also Matthew 18:18 and 2 Corinthians 5:18-20. The early Church practiced it, first in public and later privately. The Council of Trent (1551) taught that Christ instituted the sacrament. Why confess to a priest?
