Because Christ gave this power to the apostles and their successors; because sin harms the Church too; because naming sin aloud breaks its power; and because we need to hear forgiveness spoken. The priest acts in persona Christi.”

Say: “The rite. The penitent prepares by an examination of conscience (use the Ten Commandments, the Beatitudes, or a guide). In the confessional: Sign of the Cross; ‘Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been ___ since my last confession.’ Confess your sins clearly, simply, with number and kind of mortal sins; the priest may offer counsel; he gives a penance (a prayer or act); you say an Act of Contrition; the priest gives absolution: ‘I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ Then thanksgiving and do your penance. Required elements: contrition (sorrow, with the intention to amend), confession, satisfaction. Imperfect contrition (fear of punishment) is enough for the sacrament. The seal of confession is absolute: the priest can never reveal what he hears, and the penalty for breaking it is automatic excommunication. Face-to-face or behind a screen are both options.”

Say: “Common fears. ‘I’ve forgotten how.’ Tell the priest; he’ll guide you. ‘My sins are too bad.’ No sin is beyond God’s mercy. ‘The priest will judge me.’ Priests hear confessions regularly and are there to help. ‘I’ll just confess to God.’ You can and should pray, but Christ gave us this sacrament for certainty of forgiveness. ‘I keep confessing the same sins.’ That’s common; it’s part of the process, and a sign you’re fighting. Frequency: the Church requires confession of mortal sins at least once a year, and before Communion if in mortal sin; frequent confession (monthly) is recommended even for venial sins for growth. Effects: reconciliation with God and the Church, peace of conscience, spiritual strength, restoring grace. The Church also offers sacramental seal for everyone, and John Nepomuk’s story signals how serious it is. Pope Francis: ‘Confession is not a torture chamber but the place of mercy.’”
ask: Who has the power to forgive sins in the sacrament? (Christ, through the priest.)
What are the acts of the penitent? (Contrition, confession, satisfaction.)
What is the seal of confession? (The priest may never reveal anything heard in confession.)
practice: Use a guide to write a private examination of conscience.
In pairs, walk through the rite aloud, taking turns as penitent and priest, with a generic script.
Memorize or read the Act of Contrition.
Decide when you will go, and put it on your calendar.
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition together. Sign of the Cross. Offer to go together to Confession, or share the parish confession times.

tryit: Walk through the rite of Confession.
Write an honest examination of conscience.
Plan when you will go.
lessons.saintStory:
John of Nepomuk was born around 1345 in Bohemia. He studied law, became a priest and served as vicar general of the archdiocese of Prague. He was a skilled administrator and a popular preacher. King Wenceslaus IV was a violent, unstable ruler who quarreled with the archbishop over church property and appointments.
A later tradition said that John was the confessor of the queen, and that the jealous king demanded that he reveal what she had told him in confession. John refused. He was arrested, tortured, and thrown from the Charles Bridge into the Vltava River on March 20, 1393. Historians think the real cause was the quarrel over a church appointment, but the tradition of the seal grew strong and he was canonized in 1729.
Whatever the historical details, John became the patron saint of confessors and of bridges. His statue stands on many bridges in Europe. Priests have indeed died rather than reveal confessions, and the Church’s law is absolute: the seal can never be broken.

lessons.title: Receiving mercy and giving it
lessons.idea: Forgiveness is not only something we receive; it is something we are asked to give. Jesus ties the two together in the Our Father. Mercy changes how we treat those who have wronged us.
lessons.question: Who is hardest for you to forgive?
lessons.activity: Write an unsent letter to someone you need to forgive (or to ask forgiveness from). Pray over it. Decide whether to send, to speak, or to leave it with God for now. Then choose one work of mercy to perform this week and do it.
teach: Forgiveness is a gift we receive and a gift we are asked to give: “forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us” (Matthew 6:12–15; CCC 2838–2845). Jesus ties them together and the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35) makes the point sharply.

Forgiving does not mean excusing, forgetting or staying in an unsafe situation (CCC 2843–2845). It means letting go of the claim to repay hurt with hurt, wishing the other well and, where possible, being open to reconciliation. Justice and safety remain important; some wounds need time, counsel and sometimes professional help.

Mercy is more than a feeling: the works of mercy (CCC 2447) are corporal (feeding, clothing, visiting) and spiritual (instructing, counseling, forgiving, bearing wrongs patiently, praying). “Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

The Church’s own history shows both the need and the practice: John Paul II’s apology for sins of the Church’s children in 2000, the witness of Maria Goretti and Maximilian Kolbe, and the forgiveness of Pope John Paul II toward his attacker.
talk: What is the difference between forgiving and trusting again?
Why does Jesus say we are forgiven as we forgive?
Which work of mercy could you do this week?
quiz: What does the Our Father say about forgiveness?|Forgive and forget|Forgive us when we ask|Forgive us as we forgive others|Forgive only the good|2|Matthew 6:12.
Which is a corporal work of mercy?|Visit the sick|Instruct the ignorant|Counsel the doubtful|Pray for the dead|0|CCC 2447.
Forgiveness means…|Letting go of resentment and wishing the other well|Never speaking of it|Pretending nothing happened|Being weak|0|CCC 2843.
lessons.life: Do one work of mercy this week that costs you something: time, money or comfort.
lessons.saint: Corrie ten Boom: a Dutch watchmaker’s daughter who hid Jews, survived Ravensbrück, and later forgave a guard. (A Reformed Christian, honored by Christians of all traditions.)
lessons.mem: “Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.” (Our Father)
lessons.hook: Ask silently: “Who is hardest to forgive?” Hold the question; do not share.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain what forgiveness is not and one step toward it.

script.open: Say: “Forgiveness is easy to talk about and hard to do. Think of one person who hurt you. You don’t have to say their name. How does it feel to think of them?” Allow silence for a minute, then, “What do you think forgiveness means? What doesn’t it mean?” Write answers.
teach: Say: “We receive mercy in order to give it. Jesus: ‘Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.’ (Luke 6:36) The Lord’s Prayer: ‘Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.’ After the prayer, Jesus adds: ‘If you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father also will forgive you; but if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.’ (Matthew 6:14-15) The parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21-35): the servant forgiven an enormous debt refused to forgive a small one. Peter asked how many times to forgive; Jesus said seventy times seven. We can’t keep God’s mercy while refusing it to others.”

Say: “What forgiveness is not. It’s not saying the wrong didn’t matter. It’s not forgetting. It’s not necessarily reconciliation: reconciliation needs the other party’s repentance and trust rebuilt, and in cases of abuse, safety comes first. It’s not a feeling. It’s not condoning. It doesn’t cancel justice or consequences. What it is: a decision to release the person from a debt of vengeance and resentment, to wish them well, and to entrust justice to God. It’s a process, often repeated. The Catechism (CCC 2843-2845): ‘It is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offense; but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion and purifies the memory in transforming the hurt into intercession.’ Practically: pray for the person, name the hurt honestly, ask for the grace, and take a step: a note, a prayer, a boundary.”

Say: “Mercy more broadly: the works of mercy, corporal (feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, bury the dead) and spiritual (instruct the ignorant, counsel the doubtful, admonish the sinner, bear wrongs patiently, forgive offenses, comfort the afflicted, pray for the living and dead). Pope Francis’s Jubilee of Mercy (2015-16) renewed this emphasis: ‘Mercy is the very foundation of the Church’s life.’ Receiving mercy changes us. A person who has been forgiven is slow to condemn. Practical step: choose a work of mercy to practice this week. If someone hurt you deeply, you might need a counselor as well as prayer; forgiveness is not a substitute for healing. Corrie’s story shows the Holy Spirit gives what we can’t manufacture.”
ask: What does Jesus say about forgiving others? (We must, as God forgives us.)
Is forgiveness a feeling? (No; it is an act of the will, helped by grace.)
Does forgiveness always mean reconciliation? (No; reconciliation also requires repentance and trust, and safety comes first.)
practice: Write the name (privately) of a person you find hard to forgive. Under it, write: What happened? What do I want? What can I hand to God?
In pairs, share (without names) one thing that makes forgiveness hard, and one thing that helps.
Pray together for those who have hurt us: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34).
Choose one corporal or spiritual work of mercy to do this week.
script.close: Pray the Our Father slowly, pausing at the line about forgiveness. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to take the step this week.

tryit: Write the name of someone you struggle to forgive.
Write what forgiveness is and what it is not.
Choose one act of mercy toward them or another.
lessons.saintStory:
Corrie ten Boom was born in 1892 in Haarlem, Netherlands, the daughter of a watchmaker. Her family was devout Dutch Reformed, and they believed it was their duty to help Jews. After the Nazi occupation, they converted part of their house into a secret hiding place. They sheltered Jews and Dutch resistance members. In February 1944, someone betrayed them and the Gestapo arrested the family. Her father died soon after. Corrie and her sister Betsie were sent to Ravensbrück concentration camp. Betsie died there in December 1944. Corrie was released a week later, due to a clerical error.
After the war, she traveled the world, preaching forgiveness. In 1947, after speaking in a church in Munich, a man came to her and held out his hand. She recognized him as one of the guards from Ravensbrück, a cruel man. He said he had become a Christian, and asked for her forgiveness. She froze. “I stood there with the coldness clutching my heart. But forgiveness is not an emotion. I knew that. Forgiveness is an act of the will… ‘Jesus, help me!’ I prayed silently. ‘I can lift my hand. I can do that much. You supply the feeling.’” She took his hand. “I forgive you, brother!” she cried.
She died in 1983 at ninety-one.

units.title: The Eucharist and the sacraments
units.eq: What happens in the sacraments, and why do they matter?

lessons.title: What is a sacrament?
lessons.idea: A sacrament is an outward sign, given by Christ, that gives the grace it signifies. The seven sacraments carry us from birth to death. They are not magic; they are encounters with Christ in the Church.
lessons.question: Which sacrament do you understand least?
lessons.activity: Make a chart of the seven sacraments with their sign (matter), words (form), minister and what they do. Fill in what you can; look up the rest. Then circle the sacrament you understand least and write two questions about it to ask a priest or catechist.
teach: A sacrament is an outward sign, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, that gives the grace it signifies (CCC 1131). The sign has matter (water, oil, bread, wine), form (words) and a minister. Jesus’ touch in the Gospels (Mark 7:31–37) continues in them (CCC 1115–1116).

There are seven, in three groups: initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), healing (Penance, Anointing of the Sick), and service of communion (Holy Orders, Matrimony) (CCC 1210–1211). Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders can be received only once because they imprint a permanent character (CCC 1121).

They work ex opere operato: by Christ’s action, not by the minister’s holiness (CCC 1127–1128). The fruit depends on our faith and disposition: a gift can be received or refused. Grace is God’s life in us (CCC 1996–2000).

Because God became flesh, he uses matter to give grace. Sacraments are not magic and not mere symbols; they are encounters. Sacramentals (blessings, holy water, medals) are different: instituted by the Church to prepare us for grace (CCC 1667–1673).
talk: Why does Christ use physical things (water, oil, bread, wine)?
Which sacrament has marked your life most?
What is the difference between a sacrament and a sign or symbol?
quiz: How many sacraments are there?|Nine|Twelve|Seven|Five|2|CCC 1113.
Ex opere operato means…|The minister’s holiness gives the effect|It works only if we feel something|It is just a symbol|The sacrament works through Christ’s action|3|CCC 1128.
Which is a sacrament of service?|Confirmation|Baptism|Reconciliation|Matrimony|3|CCC 1534.
lessons.life: Pick one sacrament and learn its words and gestures. Teach it to someone this week.
lessons.saint: The woman who touched Jesus’ cloak: she believed that a touch could heal, and it did.
lessons.mem: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
lessons.hook: Hold up water, oil, bread and a ring. Ask what each is used for and what happens when God uses them.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name the seven sacraments with their matter and form.

script.open: Hold up an object with a personal meaning (a ring, a photo, a letter) and ask the group: “Why does a physical thing carry so much meaning? What is the difference between this and a plain piece of metal?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “A sacrament, the Catechism says, is ‘an efficacious sign of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, by which divine life is dispensed to us.’ (CCC 1131) A sign: a visible thing pointing to something invisible (water for cleansing and life; bread for nourishment; oil for strength). Efficacious: it really does what it signs. Instituted by Christ: only God can attach grace to a sign. Entrusted to the Church: she celebrates it. There are seven: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist; Penance, Anointing of the Sick; Holy Orders, Matrimony.”

Say: “Why material signs? Because we are body and soul. God made matter good, and in the Incarnation, the Word became flesh. Jesus’ humanity is the primary sacrament: the visible face of the invisible God. He touched and healed (the leper, the blind man, the woman who touched him), used mud and saliva, washed feet, broke bread. After his Ascension, ‘what was visible in our Savior has passed over into his mysteries’ (Leo the Great). The Church is the sacrament of Christ in the world (LG 1). So the sacraments are the continuation of Christ’s touch. Each has matter (water, bread and wine, oil, laying on of hands) and form (the words). The minister must intend what the Church does.”

Say: “How do they work? Ex opere operato (‘by the work done’): the grace is given by Christ himself acting through the rite, not dependent on the minister’s holiness. But their fruit depends on our disposition: faith, repentance and openness. The woman with the flow of blood exercised faith. Sacraments aren’t magic. Three sacraments leave a permanent mark (the character): Baptism, Confirmation and Orders; they can’t be repeated. The sacraments give sanctifying grace (a share in God’s life) and sacramental grace specific to each. They are also signs of the Church’s unity, and we receive them within the community. Worship is not merely something we do for God but something he does for us. Practical: approach the sacraments with attention. Notice the signs (water, oil, bread, hands). Come with faith.”
ask: What is a sacrament? (An efficacious sign of grace instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church.)
Why does God use material things? (We are body and soul; the Word became flesh.)
What does ex opere operato mean? (The sacrament works by Christ’s action, not the minister’s holiness.)
practice: Read Mark 5:25-34. Notice every physical detail (touch, cloak, blood, trembling).
Make a chart of the seven sacraments: the sign (matter), the words (form), the grace.
In pairs, choose one sacrament and explain it as if to a curious friend.
Write one sign you will pay closer attention to at the next Mass, such as water, oil or bread.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, we reach out to touch you. Heal us.” Sign of the Cross. Invite everyone to make the Sign of the Cross with holy water on entering church this week.

tryit: Describe one sacrament as sign, effect and cause.
Say why Christ chose material things.
Name the signs you notice in daily life.
lessons.saintStory:
Mark and Luke both tell the story. A woman had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She had spent all she had on doctors and only grew worse. Under the Law, her condition made her ritually unclean, cut off from worship and from touching others. In a crowd pressing around Jesus, she decided: “If I touch even his garments, I shall be made well.” She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his cloak. At once her bleeding stopped.
Jesus stopped and asked, “Who touched my garments?” His disciples said, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” But he knew that power had gone out from him. The woman, trembling, came and fell at his feet and told him the whole truth. He said, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.”
He called her “daughter,” restoring her to the community. The story shows the logic of the sacraments: a material thing, touched in faith, carries the saving power of Christ. The Church has seen in this a picture of what the sacraments do.

lessons.title: The Eucharist: real presence
lessons.idea: Catholics believe that after the consecration the bread and wine are truly the Body and Blood of Christ, soul and divinity. This belief rests on John 6, the words at the Last Supper and the faith of the earliest Christians.
lessons.question: What would it mean for your Sunday if Jesus is really present on the altar?
lessons.activity: Read John 6:51–69 and notice who left and why. Read 1 Corinthians 11:27–29: what did Paul think was at stake? Then spend ten minutes in front of the Blessed Sacrament (or read the Pange Lingua / Tantum Ergo) and write what you notice about your own belief.
teach: The Church believes that after the consecration the bread and wine are truly the Body and Blood, soul and divinity of Christ (CCC 1374). The word transubstantiation names the change of substance while the appearances remain (CCC 1376). This is Christ’s own claim: “my flesh is true food” (John 6:55), and many disciples left because of it (John 6:60–66).

The words of institution (Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26) say “This is my body,” not “this represents.” Paul warns that eating unworthily brings judgment on “the body of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27–29), which only makes sense if it is more than a symbol.

The Fathers taught it from the start: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) calls the Eucharist “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ”; Justin Martyr (c. 155) says it is not common bread. Disputes about how came later; Trent defined the term in 1551.

It leads to reverence: genuflecting, preparation, the one-hour fast, Eucharistic adoration (CCC 1378–1381). Real Presence is also why Communion unites us: “we, though many, are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:16–17).
talk: Why did many disciples leave in John 6?
What does it say about Jesus that he did not soften the teaching?
How do you prepare to receive Communion?
quiz: What happens at the consecration?|The bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood|The bread symbolizes Christ|Christ is remembered|Nothing changes|0|CCC 1376.
Which passage is the “Bread of Life discourse”?|Acts 2|John 6|Luke 24|Matthew 5|1|John 6:22-71.
To receive Communion worthily one must be…|Over 18|In a state of grace|Wealthy|A member of the choir|1|CCC 1385.
lessons.life: Visit a church for ten minutes of Eucharistic adoration this week. Say nothing and let yourself be looked at.
lessons.saint: Margaret Mary Alacoque: a French Visitation nun who heard, “Behold the Heart that has so loved men.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” (John 6:68)
lessons.hook: Read John 6:60–69. Ask: “Why did many leave? Why did Peter stay?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain transubstantiation in plain words and cite two texts.

script.open: Place a piece of bread on a small plate in the center of the circle. Say, “What would you have to believe for this to be Christ’s body? What would you have to doubt?” Let a few people share.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that in the Eucharist, Jesus Christ is truly, really and substantially present: body, blood, soul and divinity, under the appearances of bread and wine (CCC 1374). This is the Real Presence. The Council of Trent used the word transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine is changed into Christ’s body and blood, while the appearances remain. Scriptural basis: John 6:51-58. Jesus said ‘the bread which I shall give for the life of the world is my flesh,’ and when the Jews objected, he insisted: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.’ He used a strong verb for ‘eat’ (trogein, chew). Many disciples left, and he didn’t call them back to explain it was a symbol.”

Say: “More evidence. The Last Supper: ‘This is my body… This is my blood of the covenant.’ (Matthew 26:26-28) Paul: ‘The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?’ (1 Corinthians 10:16) And ‘whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord.’ (11:27) Early Fathers: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) calls the Eucharist ‘the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ’; Justin Martyr (c. 155): ‘not as common bread… but the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh’; Cyril of Jerusalem and Ambrose speak of the change. For fifteen centuries, nearly all Christians held a real presence. Disagreements arose in the 16th century.”

Say: “Objections. ‘It’s a symbol.’ Reply: Jesus’ words, and the unanimous early witness. ‘It still looks like bread.’ Reply: the Church says the appearances remain; faith accepts Christ’s word. Aquinas: ‘Sight, touch and taste are deceived in thee, but hearing suffices.’ ‘Cannibalism.’ Reply: we receive Christ’s glorified body in a sacramental manner, not the flesh of a dead body. What follows? Adoration: we kneel before the Blessed Sacrament. Eucharistic hours and processions; Benediction. Reverence in reception: state of grace, one-hour fast, a bow. The devotion to the Sacred Heart: Jesus’ love for us in the Eucharist. The Eucharist makes us one: ‘Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body.’ (1 Corinthians 10:17). It sends us to the poor. Margaret Mary’s message is that this is a love story.”
ask: What does the Church mean by the Real Presence? (Christ is truly present, body, blood, soul and divinity, in the Eucharist.)
Name a Scripture text for it. (John 6:51-58; Matthew 26:26-28; 1 Corinthians 10:16 and 11:27.)
What is transubstantiation? (The substance changes; the appearances remain.)
practice: Read John 6:51-69 aloud, in turns. Mark the places where Jesus insists and where people leave.
Write the Real Presence argument in five lines for a Protestant friend.
Spend five minutes in silent adoration (before the Blessed Sacrament if possible), then write a prayer of adoration.
Plan a holy hour or a first Friday visit this month.
script.close: Pray the Tantum Ergo or: “Jesus, I adore you, truly present.” Sign of the Cross. Offer a time to visit adoration together.

tryit: Lay out the biblical case for the Real Presence.
Name the strongest objection.
Write a prayer of adoration.
lessons.saintStory:
Margaret Mary Alacoque was born in 1647 in Burgundy, France. Her father died when she was eight, and she suffered illness and family troubles. At twenty-four she entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial. She was shy and sometimes misunderstood by the other nuns.
Between 1673 and 1675, she reported a series of visions of Christ. In the most famous, while praying before the Blessed Sacrament, she saw Jesus show his heart, burning with love, and say, “Behold this Heart which has so loved men that it spared nothing, even exhausting and consuming itself, in order to testify to them its love. And in return I receive from the greater part only ingratitude.” He asked for a feast in honor of the Sacred Heart and for devotion to receive Communion on the first Friday of each month, and to spend an hour in prayer on Thursday nights.
Her superiors were skeptical, but her confessor, the Jesuit Claude la Colombière, supported her. After her death in 1690, the devotion spread. She was canonized in 1920. The Church has approved the devotion, though it doesn’t require belief in the private revelations.

lessons.title: Baptism, Confirmation and living them
lessons.idea: Baptism makes us children of God and members of the Church; Confirmation seals us with the Spirit for mission. For adults, these are not just past events but a vocation: live as the baptized.
lessons.question: Do you think of yourself as a priest, prophet and king by baptism? What would that mean?
lessons.activity: Go through the baptismal promises. Which would you find hardest to say today? Write a personal renewal of them in your own words. Then find out whether you are confirmed and, if not, what your parish offers for adults.
teach: Baptism removes original sin and all personal sin, gives new birth as a child of God, incorporates us into Christ and the Church, and imprints a permanent mark (CCC 1262–1274; Romans 6:3–11; John 3:5). Its sign is water and the Trinitarian words; anyone can baptize in an emergency.

The baptismal promises are renewed at every Easter Vigil: renouncing sin and the devil and professing the Creed. For an adult, Baptism is not only a past event but a vocation to live as a “priest, prophet and king” (CCC 897–913).

Confirmation completes Baptism: sealing with the Holy Spirit by anointing with chrism and the words “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” It deepens baptismal grace and equips for witness (CCC 1285, 1302–1305; Acts 8:14–17). The seven gifts (Isaiah 11:2) are given; the fruits (Galatians 5:22–23) are what they produce.

If you were baptized but never confirmed, you can be: ask your parish. If you were not baptized, RCIA (the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults) is the path. Either way, these sacraments are not graduations but beginnings.
talk: If you were baptized as an infant, how has that faith become your own?
What is one gift of the Holy Spirit you most need now?
What does being a “priestly people” mean for a lay person at work?
quiz: Baptism does…|Remove original and personal sins and give new life|Only mark someone as Catholic|Make no change|Give a name|0|CCC 1263.
Confirmation…|Replaces Baptism|Seals us with the Holy Spirit|Is optional for everyone|Is just a graduation|1|CCC 1303.

The seven gifts of the Spirit include…|Prudence, justice, temperance|Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord|Patience, kindness, goodness|Faith, hope, love|1|Isaiah 11:2.
lessons.life: Renew your baptismal promises this week, kneeling at home before a crucifix or holy water.
lessons.saint: Vladimir of Kyiv: a pagan prince who sent envoys to compare religions and was baptized in 988.
lessons.mem: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Romans 6:3)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would change if you took your baptism as seriously as a wedding?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name what Baptism and Confirmation do and one concrete way to live them.

script.open: Lay out any baptismal candle, certificate or photo that anyone brought. Invite each person to hold one item for a moment and say one thing it makes them remember about their own initiation.
teach: Say: “The sacraments of Christian initiation are Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist. Together they ‘lay the foundations of every Christian life.’ (CCC 1212) Baptism: the door. It forgives original sin and all personal sin, gives new birth as God’s child, makes us a member of Christ and the Church, and marks us with an indelible character. Romans 6:3-4: we are buried with Christ and rise to new life. Confirmation: the sealing with the Holy Spirit, strengthening for witness. It completes Baptism. The Eucharist: food for the journey. In the early Church, adults received all three at the Easter Vigil. The Church today does the same for adults through RCIA.”

Say: “What Baptism does in practice: You belong to God. ‘You are not your own; you were bought with a price.’ (1 Corinthians 6:19-20) You share Christ’s mission as priest, prophet and king. You are called to holiness. You have a family, the Church. Confirmation: you’ve received the Holy Spirit with his seven gifts (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord) and you are sent to witness. Many people see Confirmation as a graduation from the Church. The Church sees it as a commissioning. The question: Are you living as one baptized, confirmed and fed? What would that look like? A faith that is public, personal, and lived. Are you still in contact with your godparents or sponsor?”

Say: “Practical living. Remember your Baptism: Do you know the date? Celebrate it as a spiritual birthday. Renew your baptismal promises regularly, especially at Easter. Use holy water. Know your patron saint. Use your gifts: ask the Holy Spirit daily. Participate in parish life: join a group, serve, invite. Go to Mass weekly, Confession regularly. If you were baptized but never confirmed, talk to your parish about adult Confirmation. If you were not baptized, RCIA is available. If you know someone who left, be a bridge. Vladimir’s story shows that baptism can mark a real turning point. Don’t treat initiation as an event in the past but as a continuing process.”
ask: What are the sacraments of initiation? (Baptism, Confirmation and Eucharist.)
What does Confirmation do? (Completes Baptism; seals with the Holy Spirit for witness.)
How can you live your Baptism now? (Remember it, renew promises, use your gifts, take part in the Church.)
practice: Find your baptism and confirmation dates (or ask a family member). Write them down.
Read the baptismal promises aloud as a group, and answer ‘I do.’
Write down how you see your gifts from Confirmation at work, and one place you could use them.
Choose one concrete way to live your initiation: join a group, serve, or invite someone.
script.close: Renew baptismal promises together and bless yourselves with holy water. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to celebrate their baptismal anniversary.

tryit: Trace your own initiation.
Write what Baptism and Confirmation changed.
Choose one way to live it out this month.
lessons.saintStory:
Vladimir was prince of Kyiv, the leader of the Rus’, in the late tenth century. He came to power by war and by killing his brother. He was a pagan with a harem and built temples to the Slavic gods, even offering human sacrifice. But as ruler, he saw that his people needed a unifying faith. According to the Primary Chronicle, he sent envoys to investigate the religions of neighboring peoples: the Muslim Bulgars, the Jewish Khazars, the Latin Christians of Germany, and the Greeks of Constantinople.
The envoys were unimpressed by the first three. When they attended the liturgy at the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, they reported: “We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth. For on earth there is no such splendor or such beauty, and we are at a loss how to describe it. We only know that God dwells there among men.” In 988, Vladimir was baptized, took a Byzantine princess, Anna, as his wife, and ordered his people to be baptized in the Dnieper River.
After his baptism, he changed. He gave up his other wives, fed the poor, built churches and schools, and became known as a merciful ruler. He died in 1015. He is honored as Equal-to-the-Apostles and as the founder of Christianity among the Slavs.

units.title: Love, sexuality and chastity
units.eq: What does it mean to love?

lessons.title: Made for love
lessons.idea: God made us male and female in his image, for communion. Our bodies and sexuality are good and are meant to express self-gift. Chastity is the virtue that integrates sexuality in the person, so that love is real.
lessons.question: What messages about love and sex did you absorb growing up, and which do you now doubt?
lessons.activity: Write down what popular culture says about love and sex, then what you think the Church says. Compare. Choose one phrase from the lesson (the body is good; love is gift of self; chastity builds freedom) and write what it would change in your relationships.
teach: God made us male and female in his image (Genesis 1:27), and the body is good: it expresses the person (CCC 355–357, 2331–2336). Sexuality is for love and life; it is a language of self-giving that tells the truth only when it is total, faithful and open to life (CCC 2360–2365).

Love is willing the good of the other (CCC 1766; Aquinas). The Song of Solomon (8:6–7) shows its strength: “love is strong as death.” The Church’s teaching on chastity is not hatred of the body but a protection of persons from being used (CCC 2337–2347).

Chastity is the integration of sexuality within the whole person, and everyone is called to it according to their state: engaged, married, single or consecrated (CCC 2348–2350). It is a virtue to be built, with grace and friends, and not simply a list of prohibitions.
Be honest: many people have been hurt by sexual abuse, by shame, or by others’ choices. The Church’s teaching comes with mercy: Confession and accompaniment are always available (CCC 2352–2356).
talk: What is the difference between love and use?
How do you think the culture shapes how young adults think about relationships?
How is chastity different from repression?
quiz: Chastity is…|The same as celibacy|Hatred of the body|The successful integration of sexuality within the person|Only for single people|2|CCC 2337.
What does “image of God” mean for the body?|Persons are body and soul, and the body expresses the person|The soul is a prisoner|The body is irrelevant|Sex is bad|0|CCC 362-364.
Who is called to chastity?|Only unmarried people|Everyone, according to their state of life|Only the young|Only priests|1|CCC 2348.
lessons.life: Take a week off one media habit that shapes your view of love and sex (a feed, a show, a playlist). Notice what changes.
lessons.saint: Adam and Eve: the first man and woman, who greeted each other with a cry of joy.
misc: “The Church thinks the body is bad.”
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image… male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do films and songs say love is? What do they leave out?” Take a few answers.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to state what the Church means by love and what gift of self requires.

script.open: Say: “Everyone wants to be loved. What do you think love is? Give me one sentence, honest or cynical.” Take answers around the room. Write a few on the board. Then say, “Let’s see what the Church says that love is, and what the body has to do with it.”
teach: Say: “Genesis 1:27: ‘So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.’ The Church teaches that sexual difference is a good gift of God, and that both men and women have equal dignity as persons. We are made for communion: ‘It is not good that the man should be alone.’ The Catechism: ‘God is love and in himself he lives a mystery of personal loving communion. Creating the human race in his own image… God inscribed in the humanity of man and woman the vocation, and thus the capacity and responsibility, of love and communion.’ (CCC 2331) Love is our vocation. The body is not a shell but a part of the person. It expresses who we are. John Paul II’s Theology of the Body (talks 1979-84): the body reveals the person, and the ‘nuptial meaning of the body’ is the capacity to express love by self-gift.”

Say: “What is love? Aquinas: to love is to will the good of the other. John Paul II in Love and Responsibility: the opposite of love is not hate but use, treating a person as an object for my pleasure. Love is the affirmation of the person for their own sake. The Greek words: eros (desire), philia (friendship), agape (self-giving love). Benedict XVI’s Deus Caritas Est (2005) says that eros and agape belong together: eros must be purified and healed by agape. Love involves emotion, but isn’t reducible to it; it includes commitment. Sexuality is a profound language of the body: it speaks total self-gift, faithful, free, fruitful. The Church’s teaching on chastity and marriage comes from this. Sex outside marriage ‘lies’ with the body: it says ‘I give you everything’ without the commitment that makes it true.”

Say: “Why does the Church say sexual intimacy belongs in marriage? Because it is both unitive (it joins) and procreative (it is open to life). Marriage is a lifelong covenant that gives the safe space for total self-giving. This is demanding. Our culture says otherwise: sex as recreation, hooking up, ‘as long as it’s consensual.’ The Church doesn’t deny desire or pleasure; she insists they are goods that need a worthy context. The result of ignoring this: wounds—loneliness, regret, the sense of being used. If you’ve experienced that, mercy is available; you don’t have to be defined by your past. Chastity is for everyone: not repression but integration and freedom (CCC 2337). We’re called to love well in every state of life: single, dating, married, religious. Let’s explore what that means.”
ask: What does it mean that we are made in God’s image as male and female? (We are made for loving communion; both sexes share equal dignity.)
What did John Paul II say is the opposite of love? (Use, treating a person as an object.)
Why does the Church link sexual intimacy with marriage? (It expresses total, faithful, fruitful self-gift.)
practice: Read Genesis 2:18-25 aloud. Underline the words that express wonder, relationship and trust.
In pairs, discuss: How does our culture’s image of love differ from this? What does it get right? What does it miss?
Write your own definition of love in a sentence, using the ideas of gift and commitment.
Identify one relationship in your life where you can practice self-gift this week.
script.close: Pray Psalm 139:13-14 together: “I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Sign of the Cross. Suggest the group read the first three talks of Theology of the Body (or a summary) before next time.

tryit: Read Genesis 2:18-25 slowly.
Write what the man’s cry tells us about love.
Write one sentence on what the body says.
lessons.saintStory:
The second chapter of Genesis tells how God formed the man from the dust of the ground and put him in the garden. The man named the animals, but “for the man there was not found a helper fit for him.” God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone.” So God caused a deep sleep to fall upon him, and from his side he formed a woman, and brought her to the man.
The man’s response is the first recorded human speech in the Bible, and it is a poem: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.” It is a cry of wonder and recognition. The text goes on: “Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked, and were not ashamed.”
Before the fall, there was no shame. The two looked at each other without fear of being used. John Paul II, in his Theology of the Body, reflected on this “original nakedness” as showing what love was meant to be: complete self-gift without exploitation. Adam and Eve are the first picture of what we are made for.

lessons.title: Dating, discernment and boundaries
lessons.idea: Dating is a time to get to know someone with a view to a possible marriage, not only enjoyment. Christian dating asks for honesty, respect for the other person’s freedom and chastity, and prayer.
lessons.question: What would you want a person you date to know about your values before the relationship starts?
lessons.activity: Draft a short list of the qualities you are looking for in a spouse (or the kind of friend and partner you want to be) and a short list of boundaries you would set, with a reason for each. Share one with a trusted friend or mentor for honest feedback.
teach: Dating is a time of discernment: it is meant to help two people know whether they are called to marriage (CCC 1632, 2350). Seek character before chemistry: faith, honesty, kindness, how they treat family and strangers, how they handle conflict.

Boundaries protect love: decide beforehand, in prayer and with a friend, what physical limits fit the stage of the relationship. The Church asks engaged and dating couples to live chastity, because sexual union belongs to the covenant of marriage (CCC 2350–2351, 2390).

Healthy signs: freedom, respect for no, being known without fear, friends and family who are glad. Red flags: control, isolation, pressure, secrecy, escalating guilt. If you feel afraid, seek help; abuse is never a sign of love.

Proverbs 4:23: “Guard your heart.” Practical help: group settings, a friend who will be honest, limiting late nights alone, regular Mass and Confession, and being open about the question “Where is this going?”
talk: What makes it hard to date in a way that matches your faith?
How can you speak honestly about your values without judging?
How do you handle breakups and rejection?
quiz: What does the Church say about sex before marriage?|It is permitted when in love|It is neutral|It is required to test compatibility|It is contrary to the total self-gift of marriage|3|CCC 2353.
Why wait?|Because of fear|For no reason|Because the body’s language of total self-gift needs a total, public and permanent commitment|It is just a rule|2|CCC 2361-2362.
If someone struggles with sexual sin, the Church offers…|Exclusion|Only condemnation|Silence|Mercy and practical help|3|CCC 2359.
lessons.life: If you are dating, talk about your plans for chastity and marriage this week. If you are single, write a prayer for your future spouse or your vocation.
lessons.saint: Isaac and Rebekah: a courtship that began with prayer and ended with her free answer, “I will go.”
lessons.mem: “Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.” (Proverbs 4:23)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What makes a relationship healthy? What are red flags?” List both columns.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to draft three boundaries and one question for discernment.

script.open: Ask: “What is the hardest part of dating or discerning a relationship today? What do people get wrong? What do people do well?” Allow honest answers. Say, “The Church does not give a dating manual, but she gives principles that protect love.”
teach: Say: “Dating is the time of getting to know someone in order to discern whether marriage is God’s call. Its purpose is discernment, not just fun or companionship (though these are good). Questions to ask: Do we share faith and values? Does this person bring me closer to God? Do we respect each other? Can we communicate honestly? Does this person show good character, such as honesty, generosity, kindness, responsibility? How do they treat others? Are there warning signs: controlling behavior, disrespect, abuse, addiction? In Genesis 24, character was the test: Rebekah’s generosity. Also notice the roles of prayer, family, and her free consent. Consent is essential to a valid marriage (CCC 1626).”

Say: “Boundaries. Chastity in dating means respecting each other as persons, avoiding actions that treat the other as an object or that pull toward sex outside marriage. The Church teaches that sexual relations are reserved for marriage. That includes sexual acts short of intercourse that are directed to arousal. Practical boundaries: decide in advance; avoid situations of isolation and temptation; limit physical affection; dress modestly; keep conversations honest; pray together; have friends and community around; set time limits at night; avoid pressure; talk openly about expectations. Cohabitation: the Church teaches it is wrong and also statistically linked with higher risk of break-up. If you have already crossed lines, mercy is available: Confession, a fresh start, and decisions about boundaries going forward.”

Say: “Discerning marriage. Consider: Are we free to marry? Do we agree about children, faith, finances, family? Have we done an engagement and a marriage preparation course? Have we spoken to a priest? Do our families know and support us? Are we ready to promise for life? Break-ups are painful, but if the relationship isn’t leading to marriage, better to end it honestly, kindly. The Catechism notes that engagement (the betrothal) is a time of preparation for marriage (CCC 1632-1633): couples are called to chastity. Singleness is a valid and holy state, not a failure. Don’t settle; don’t idolize marriage. Pray for your future spouse. Pray that God will show you whether he wants you for marriage or another vocation. Like Isaac, we can wait, be quiet, and meditate.”
ask: What is the purpose of dating? (Discernment of whether marriage is God’s call.)
What does chastity mean in dating? (Respecting each other as persons, keeping sexual intimacy for marriage.)
What is essential for a valid marriage? (Free consent of both.)
practice: Make two lists: what I want in a spouse; what I bring. Mark what is essential (faith, character, commitment) and what is preference (looks, hobbies).
Write three boundaries that would protect a relationship, and one person who could hold you accountable.
In pairs, talk through: What would I do if I realized I had crossed a line? Who would I tell?
Write a short prayer for your future vocation, whatever it is.
script.close: Pray the prayer of Tobias and Sarah (Tobit 8:5-7) or the Our Father. Sign of the Cross. Encourage everyone to read Genesis 24 at home.

tryit: List what you want in a marriage partner.
Separate what is essential from what is preference.
Set one boundary you will keep.
lessons.saintStory:
In Genesis 24, Abraham, old and wanting to see his son Isaac married, sends his chief servant to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac among his relatives. The servant takes ten camels, and arrives at a well outside the city at evening, when the women come out to draw water. He prays: “O Lord, God of my master Abraham, grant me success today… Let the young woman to whom I shall say, ‘Pray let down your jar that I may drink,’ and who shall say, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels’—let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant Isaac.”
Before he finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar. She gave him water and said, “I will draw for your camels also.” She watered all ten camels, an enormous task. Her family learned the servant’s purpose and agreed. But they asked her, “Will you go with this man?” She said, “I will go.”
On the journey home, she saw a man walking in the field toward evening: Isaac, who had gone out to meditate. She veiled herself. Isaac took her into his mother’s tent, “and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.” The story shows prayer, character, family involvement, her free consent, and love.

lessons.title: Pornography, healing and freedom
lessons.idea: Pornography is widespread and harmful. The Church speaks of it plainly because it wounds the dignity of persons, but she speaks of mercy even more. Healing is possible with grace, honesty, community and professional help.
lessons.question: What do you think pornography teaches about people? About yourself?
lessons.activity: Make a written plan for freedom: one step for your phone and devices, one for community (a person you will tell), one for prayer and the sacraments, and one for care of your body and sleep. If this is not your struggle, write a plan to support a friend who is struggling, without shame.
teach: Pornography harms: it uses persons as objects, distorts desire, can become compulsive, and wounds relationships (CCC 2354). The Church calls it a grave offense because it damages the dignity of those who make and view it. Naming it clearly is part of freedom.

The way out is grace and practice. “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). There is “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). God provides “a way out” of temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13). Shame keeps people hiding; mercy brings them into the light.

Practical steps: tell a trusted person, use filters and accountability, set up your phone and room to remove easy access, go to Confession (as often as needed), pray the Our Father in temptation, find a replacement activity, and seek counseling when the habit is compulsive. Relapse is not the end.
For those harmed by others’ use (spouses, partners), the Church offers compassion and resources. Seek help from a priest or a counselor trained in this area.
talk: What small steps help you resist temptation?
Who can you tell? What stops you?
How does mercy change the way you see yourself?
quiz: The Church treats pornography as…|A harmless habit|A grave offense against dignity|A private matter|A cultural issue|1|CCC 2354.
Which response is most Christian toward someone who struggles?|Shame|Condemnation|Mercy and practical help|Silence|2|John 8:11.
What is a sign of progress?|Hiding|Never failing|Counting days|Getting up again and again with God’s help|3|The saints persevere in humility.
lessons.life: Take one practical step this week: install a filter, tell a friend or priest, or schedule a counselor.
lessons.saint: Margaret of Cortona: a young woman who lived for nine years as a nobleman’s mistress, then spent thirty years in penance and service.
misc: “Everyone does it, so it does no harm.”
“I can fix this entirely on my own.”
lessons.mem: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)
lessons.hook: Say plainly that this is a topic where shame can silence people, and that the focus is on freedom and healing, not blame.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name two practical steps toward freedom (accountability, filters, confession, counsel).

script.open: Say plainly, with warmth: “This is a topic where shame can silence people. In this room, nobody has to share anything about themselves. Our aim is freedom and mercy, not blame.” Ask: “What do you think pornography teaches about people? About ourselves?” Take a few general answers.
teach: Say: “Pornography is widespread, and most young adults have encountered it. The Church speaks clearly: ‘Pornography consists in removing real or simulated sexual acts from the intimacy of the partners, in order to display them deliberately to third parties. It offends against chastity because it perverts the conjugal act… It does grave injury to the dignity of its participants (actors, vendors, the public), since each one becomes an object of base pleasure and illicit profit for others.’ (CCC 2354) It is gravely wrong because it uses persons as objects, and because of how it affects viewers: it distorts desire, can become compulsive (neuroscience research shows addictive patterns), damages relationships and the ability to love. It often is linked to exploitation and trafficking.”

Say: “But the Church speaks mercy even more. ‘There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.’ (Romans 8:1) ‘If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.’ (John 8:36) ‘God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your strength, but with the temptation will also provide the way of escape.’ (1 Corinthians 10:13) Shame says, ‘You are disgusting; hide.’ The Gospel says, ‘You are loved; come into the light.’ Compare the woman caught in adultery: Jesus did not condemn her, and said, ‘Go, and do not sin again.’ (John 8:11) Both parts are essential. The Church recognizes that compulsion can lessen culpability, but it still harms and needs healing.”

Say: “Practical help. Grace: frequent Confession, the Eucharist, prayer, the Rosary, Scripture. Honesty: tell a trusted person: a friend, a priest, a counselor. Secrets feed addiction. Structure: filters and accountability software on phones and computers; keep devices out of the bedroom; avoid screens late at night; delete accounts or apps that trigger you. Replace: exercise, friendships, hobbies, service. Understand triggers: stress, loneliness, boredom, tiredness (HALT: hungry, angry, lonely, tired). Professional help: therapists who treat compulsive behavior; groups like Celebrate Recovery, Sexaholics Anonymous, and Catholic ministries like Integrity Restored. Progress is not linear; relapse isn’t the end. Getting up again is the fight. For those who aren’t struggling: don’t judge; help friends; avoid supporting the industry. For those who have been harmed by someone else’s use, healing is also available.”
ask: How does the Catechism describe pornography? (It offends chastity, uses persons as objects, and gravely injures dignity.)
What is the Gospel response to those who struggle? (No condemnation; freedom in Christ; grace and community.)
Name two practical steps. (Tell a trusted person; use filters; Confession; professional help.)
practice: Write a four-part plan for freedom: one step for devices, one for community (a person to tell), one for prayer and sacraments, one for body and sleep.
Share only what you choose with a partner, or write for yourself.
If it is not your struggle, write how you can support a friend without shame.
Pray together Psalm 51:10-12 and the Our Father.
script.close: Close with the prayer: “Lord, set me free and make my heart clean.” Sign of the Cross. Offer information about confession times and recovery resources, privately.

tryit: Write a plan for freedom in four parts.
Name one person you will tell.
Name one change in your phone or devices.
lessons.saintStory:
Margaret was born in 1247 in Tuscany, Italy, into a farming family. Her mother died when she was seven. Her stepmother was cold to her. At seventeen, she ran off with a young nobleman from Montepulciano, who promised marriage but never married her. For about nine years, she lived in his castle as his mistress and bore him a son. She enjoyed luxury, fine clothes and the attention of the town.
In 1273, her lover went out and did not return. His dog came back and led her to the place where his body lay, murdered. Margaret was shaken. She realized the emptiness of her life. She left the castle with her son and went back to her father’s house, but he refused to receive her, because of his wife. She was alone and poor with a child.
She turned to the Franciscans in Cortona, who accepted her. She spent years in penance, and in 1277 became a Third Order Franciscan. She cared for the sick and poor, begged for them, and founded a hospital. She was known for her hours of prayer and her gentleness. She died in 1297 and was canonized in 1728. Her life shows that no past is beyond mercy.

units.title: Vocation: what is God asking of me?
units.eq: How do I discern my life’s call?

lessons.title: Every person is called
lessons.idea: Vocation means “call.” God calls every person first to holiness and then to a particular way of living it: marriage, priesthood or consecrated life, or single life given to God. Discernment is a long conversation, not a sudden revelation.
lessons.question: What do you think you want from life? What might God want?
lessons.activity: Make three columns: gifts (what you do well), joys (what gives you life), needs (what the world around you lacks). Fill each with at least five items and look for overlap. Share with a mentor, and list two next steps in discernment (a conversation, a retreat, a trial of service).
teach: Every person is called first to holiness (CCC 825, 2013; Lumen Gentium 40) and then to a particular way of living it: marriage, priesthood and diaconate, consecrated life, or single life given to God (CCC 897–933, 1877–1879). “Vocation” comes from the Latin for “call”; God calls by name (Samuel, 1 Samuel 3; Andrew and John, John 1:35–39).

Discernment is not guessing a hidden plan. It is listening in prayer, knowing your gifts and desires, taking advice from people who know you, and watching where peace and fruit appear. Ignatius taught attention to consolation and desolation, and to testing decisions over time (CCC 2690).

God’s will for you is usually not a puzzle with one right answer to be missed. It is a call to love, and many paths can be faithful. The risk is not “choosing wrong” but never choosing, or choosing from fear.
The Church needs all vocations: parents, priests, religious, single people who serve. Pray for vocations and ask someone whose life you admire how they knew.
talk: What are your gifts? Ask a friend for their answer.
How do you tell the difference between God’s call and your fear?
What is the next faithful step?
quiz: Who is called to holiness?|Only priests|Only saints|Only monastics|Every Christian|3|CCC 2013.
Vocation means…|Education|Hobby|Career|Call|3|Latin vocare.
Discernment involves…|Prayer, gifts, advice and circumstances|Doing what is easiest|Rolling dice|Waiting for a sign in the sky|0|Ignatian discernment.
lessons.life: Ask one person who knows you well: “Where do you see God using me?” Write down the answer.
lessons.saint: Nathanael: the skeptic who was invited with the words “Come and see.”
misc: “If I choose wrong, I ruin my life.”
lessons.mem: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where have you felt most alive? Where do you feel you are most useful?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe the universal call to holiness and one step in discernment.

script.open: Hand out paper and ask, “Write the question about your future that wakes you up at night.” After two minutes, ask people to fold the papers and exchange them. Read a few anonymously to normalize the questions.
teach: Say: “The Catechism: ‘Vocation’ comes from the Latin vocare, to call. God calls every person. First, to exist and to love: ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.’ (Jeremiah 1:5) Second, to holiness through Baptism: every baptized person is called to ‘the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity’ (LG 40). Third, to a particular state of life: marriage, ordained ministry, consecrated life or single life for the Kingdom. Fourth, to particular tasks and missions in the world, work, service. The universal call to holiness was Vatican II’s emphasis: holiness isn’t only for priests and nuns.”

Say: “How does God call? Often through ordinary things: desires, gifts, circumstances, friends, needs, moments of grace, Scripture, prayer. Sometimes dramatically (Paul), usually quietly (Samuel). Ignatius of Loyola taught discernment of spirits: notice consolation (peace, joy, a sense of rightness, leading to God) and desolation (restlessness, anxiety, pulling away). Pay attention to what gives deep, lasting life over time. Discernment is a practice: pray, reflect, talk with a wise guide, test with small steps, and decide with freedom. God’s will is not a hidden riddle; it is often found in the next faithful step. The best question: ‘What is God inviting me to now?’ Discernment includes both the heart’s desires and the needs of the world.”

Say: “Obstacles. Fear: ‘What if I say yes and I am unhappy?’ God’s call is for our flourishing. The fear of missing the ‘one right answer’: God can work with many good choices. Noise: constant distraction makes it hard to listen. Pressure: from family or culture. Comparison. Postponing: ‘when life settles down.’ Unwillingness: afraid of what God might ask. Helpful practices: daily prayer and silence; Eucharist and Confession; a spiritual director; a retreat; honest conversations with friends; service. Pray the Suscipe of Ignatius: ‘Take, Lord, receive all my liberty…’ Nathanael’s story: he came with doubt and found he had been seen. You are known. Come and see.”
ask: What does ‘vocation’ mean? (A call from God.)
What are consolation and desolation? (Ignatian terms for interior movements toward or away from God.)
What is the most important question in discernment? (What is God inviting me to now?)
practice: Read John 1:43-51 aloud together.
Each person writes: What desires seem deepest in me? What gifts do I have? What do I fear? What is a next faithful step?
In pairs, share one answer, and listen without advising.
Choose one concrete step: talk to a priest, volunteer, make a retreat.
script.close: Pray the Suscipe or: “Lord, show me your will and give me the courage to follow.” Sign of the Cross. Schedule a follow-up conversation with a mentor.

tryit: Write your own “Come and see.”
List the pulls and fears about the call.
Choose one step to test it.
lessons.saintStory:
In John’s Gospel, Philip finds Nathanael and tells him: “We have found him of whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” Nathanael’s response: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” It is the cry of a skeptic, maybe even a snob. Philip doesn’t argue. He says, “Come and see.”
Nathanael goes. As he approaches, Jesus says, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!” Nathanael asks, “How do you know me?” Jesus answers, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael, overwhelmed, says, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus says, “You shall see greater things than these… you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.”
Nathanael is usually identified with Bartholomew, one of the Twelve. Tradition says he carried the Gospel to India and Armenia. The story shows that the call often comes through a friend, a question, a being known. It begins with “Come and see.”

lessons.title: Marriage and family
lessons.idea: Marriage is a covenant of love between a man and a woman, ordered to their good and to the procreation and education of children. It is a sacrament: a path to holiness and a sign of Christ’s love for the Church.
lessons.question: What do you hope for in a marriage? What worries you?
lessons.activity: Write what you hope your future home would be like: what you would pray, how you would argue, what you would give up. If you are married or engaged, write a one-page prayer for your spouse. Read Ephesians 5:21–33 and underline the verbs that apply to both husbands and wives.
teach: Marriage is a covenant between a baptized man and woman, a lifelong partnership ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children (CCC 1601; Genesis 2:18–24; Mark 10:6–9). The couple confers the sacrament on each other; the priest or deacon witnesses (CCC 1623).

Its essential properties are unity and indissolubility (CCC 1638–1640). Christ raised it to a sacrament as a sign of his love for the Church: “Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the Church” (Ephesians 5:21–33). Mutual submission “out of reverence for Christ” precedes the specific advice; love is sacrificial on both sides.

Consent makes marriage; freedom, maturity and intention to be faithful, permanent and open to children are required (CCC 1625–1632). The Church can declare that a marriage never existed, an annulment, when a defect in consent or form was present (CCC 1629); it is not Catholic divorce.

Preparation matters: marriage preparation, honest talk about money, children, faith and conflict, and a habit of prayer. Families are “domestic churches” (CCC 1655–1658). Natural Family Planning is the Church’s approved way to space births (CCC 2366–2371).
talk: What makes a marriage last, beyond feelings?
How can an unmarried person prepare for marriage now?
What does the family have to do with the Church?
quiz: The ministers of the sacrament of marriage are…|The priest|The parents|The witnesses|The couple|3|CCC 1623.
Marriage by nature is…|Permanent, faithful and open to children|Temporary and flexible|Optional|A contract only|0|CCC 1643.
An annulment declares…|The couple is free to date|The marriage failed|The children illegitimate|The marriage was never valid|3|CCC 1629.
lessons.life: Pray for the marriages you know. Offer to help a couple or a family in a concrete way (a meal, babysitting).
lessons.saint: Blessed Karl of Austria and Zita: an emperor and empress who prayed together, raised eight children and lost everything.
misc: “Marriage is a contract renewable at will.”
lessons.mem: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Mark 10:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you most want your future family to be like?” Write three words.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name the four goods of marriage and what preparing for it requires now.

script.open: Show a photo of a wedding from decades ago and one from now. Ask, “What has changed in how we imagine marriage? What has stayed the same?” Collect the two lists and compare.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that marriage is a covenant between a baptized man and woman, a lifelong partnership ordered to the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of children, raised by Christ to the dignity of a sacrament (CCC 1601). Its properties: unity (one man and one woman), indissolubility (permanent), fidelity, openness to life. The spouses are the ministers of the sacrament to each other. They exchange vows: ‘I take you to be my wife/husband, to have and to hold from this day forward, for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, until death do us part.’ Paul compares marriage to Christ’s love for the Church (Ephesians 5:25-33). The sacrament gives grace for living this love: forgiveness, patience, sacrifice, fidelity.”

Say: “What makes it work? Grace and virtue: communication, forgiveness, generosity, humility, patience, humor. Shared faith and prayer. Commitment: marriage is a decision of the will, not only feeling. Openness to children: the gift of fertility and the education of children. Sacrifice: marriage is a school of self-giving. Community: friends, family and parish. Marriage preparation: the Church requires it (often six months); it covers communication, finances, family planning, faith. NFP. Challenges: money, in-laws, infertility, illness, infidelity, boredom, stress. Resources: counselors, retreats (such as Marriage Encounter and Retrouvaille), priests. Marriage involves suffering as well as joy: Karl and Zita’s story shows that. Success is not a matter of avoiding hard times but going through them together with God.”

Say: “The family. The Church calls the family the ‘domestic church.’ Parents are the first teachers of the faith. Family life includes prayer together, meals, Sunday Mass, forgiveness, service. Couples without children: infertility is a cross; adoption, spiritual fruitfulness. Single parents, blended families, divorced and remarried: the Church ministers with care. If you hope to marry: grow in virtue now; choose wisely; live chastely; learn to listen; pray for your spouse; take preparation seriously. If you’re already married: invest in the relationship, pray together, forgive often. And if marriage isn’t your call, support married friends. Vocations need each other. Pope Francis in Amoris Laetitia describes love in family life through 1 Corinthians 13: patient, kind, not jealous, not rude, not irritable, forgives, hopes. ‘Love is the vocation of every human being.’”
ask: What are the properties of marriage? (Unity and indissolubility; fidelity and openness to life.)
Who are the ministers of the sacrament? (The spouses.)
What are some things that help a marriage last? (Grace, forgiveness, prayer, communication, commitment, community.)
practice: Write the vows in your own words as a promise you would be ready to keep.
List three habits that sustain a marriage, and a couple you admire who has them.
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7, replacing ‘love’ with your name; mark where you grow.
Write a prayer for your future marriage or for a couple you know.
script.close: Pray for married couples and for those preparing for marriage. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to interview a couple married 20 or more years.

tryit: Write the vows in your own words.
List three things that make a marriage last.
Write a prayer for your future marriage, or for a married couple you know.
lessons.saintStory:
Karl of Habsburg was born in 1887 and became emperor of Austria-Hungary in 1916, in the middle of World War I, at twenty-nine. He had married Princess Zita of Bourbon-Parma in 1911. They had a deep faith, prayed together, and tried to live their marriage as a path of holiness. Their eight children were born between 1913 and 1922.
As emperor, Karl worked for peace. He tried secretly to negotiate with the Allies. He banned the use of poison gas in his army and tried to improve social conditions. After Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918, the family was exiled. In 1921 he tried twice to regain the throne of Hungary and failed. The family was sent to the island of Madeira, in poverty, in a damp house. Karl caught pneumonia and died on April 1, 1922, at thirty-four. His last words to Zita: “I love you endlessly.”
Zita raised their children in exile, and lived to be ninety-six, dying in 1989. Karl was beatified in 2004; Zita’s cause is open. They show how marriage can be a vocation of holiness through great trials.

lessons.title: Priesthood, religious life and single life
lessons.idea: Some are called to give their whole lives to God as priests or consecrated persons; others to a single life of service. Each is a gift to the Church and a way of loving.
lessons.question: What stops you from imagining a call to priesthood or consecrated life?
lessons.activity: Read about one religious order or diocesan seminary and write three things that surprised you. Visit, call or email a vocation director if you can. If you are not considering these paths, write a note of thanks to a priest or religious who has helped you.
teach: Holy Orders configures a man to Christ the head and shepherd to serve the Church as bishop, priest or deacon (CCC 1536–1600). The ministerial priesthood is for others: to teach, sanctify and govern, and above all to celebrate the Eucharist and Confession in the person of Christ (CCC 1548–1553).

Consecrated life lives the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience (CCC 914–933). It takes many forms: monks and nuns, religious sisters and brothers, secular institutes, consecrated virgins. The Church esteems it as a special sign of the Kingdom (CCC 1619–1620) while teaching that marriage is also a sacrament and a real path to holiness; the point is not rivalry but that each state shows something of Christ’s love.

Celibacy for the Kingdom is a gift, a way of loving with an undivided heart (Matthew 19:10–12; 1 Corinthians 7:32–35). It is not a loss to be endured but a love to be lived, and it needs community, prayer and friendship to be lived well.

Single life lived in love, service and prayer is a genuine vocation, not a waiting room. Many single people serve family, parish, the poor and their work in ways that others cannot. Ask: “How can I give myself away?”
talk: Why is celibacy a gift and not a loss?
What would you do if you discovered a calling you did not expect?
How can you support priests and religious?
quiz: The evangelical counsels are…|Faith, hope, love|Wisdom, courage, justice|Poverty, chastity, obedience|Prayer, fasting, almsgiving|2|CCC 915.
Is consecrated life “higher” than marriage?|No one can say|It depends on income|It is a different vocation; both lead to holiness|Yes, always|2|CCC 1620.
Who can be ordained a priest?|Any baptized Catholic|Only the old|Anyone who studies|A baptized man called by God and the Church|3|CCC 1577.
lessons.life: Pray for vocations and ask a priest or religious how they knew their call.
lessons.saint: Saint André Bessette: a frail doorkeeper who welcomed millions to the Oratory of St. Joseph.
lessons.mem: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” (Matthew 4:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you give your life to? What would you need to let go?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe celibacy as a gift and how single people can live a vocation.

script.open: Ask: “When you hear ‘priest,’ ‘nun’ or ‘single’, what images come to mind? What are your impressions or questions?” Write them down without judging. Say, “Today we hear the Church’s account of these three paths, and give you the chance to talk with real people.”
teach: Say: “Holy Orders: men called by Christ and the Church to serve as bishops, priests and deacons. Priests celebrate the Mass and sacraments, preach, guide a parish. In the Latin Church they are normally celibate, giving their whole heart to God and his people; in Eastern Catholic Churches, married men may be ordained. Diocesan priests serve in a diocese under the bishop; religious priests belong to orders (Jesuits, Dominicans, Franciscans) with specific charisms. Deacons: transitional (on the way to priesthood) or permanent (often married). What does the priestly vocation feel like? A call to service, often confirmed by others; years of formation (usually 6-8 years); a life of prayer, availability, sacrifice, and joy. Pray for vocations: ‘The harvest is plentiful but the laborers are few.’ (Matthew 9:37)”

Say: “Consecrated life: men and women who profess the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience, in community. Forms: monks and nuns (contemplative, enclosed), friars and sisters (active, in apostolic work), members of secular institutes (living in the world), consecrated virgins, hermits, and new communities. Their life is a sign of the Kingdom: they live now what all will live in heaven. Contemplatives pray for the world; active orders teach, heal, serve. Brother André’s life: a layman in religious life, in service. Many orders welcome ‘come and see’ weekends and discernment. Religious life is not escape but total gift. The Church teaches it’s a gift to the whole Church (Vita Consecrata). Questions to ask: Am I drawn to a life centered on prayer and community? To a particular charism? Do I feel peace when I imagine it?”

Say: “Single life: people who remain unmarried, for a variety of reasons. Some choose it for the Kingdom, as lay missionaries, teachers, doctors, giving their time to the Church and the poor, sometimes making a private promise or vow. Some find themselves single without choosing it, and the Church recognizes this as a real cross and as a real vocation to live love in a different form. Single people are not second-class. The Catechism says everyone is called to chastity. Single life offers freedom for service, friendship and hospitality, but it requires community and intentional effort against loneliness. Jesus himself and Paul were single. John Paul II spoke of the ‘vocation to love,’ which includes all. It is important to discern with a spiritual director, to visit communities, and to be honest about your desires. Talk to people in each vocation.”
ask: What are the three degrees of Holy Orders? (Bishop, priest, deacon.)
What are the evangelical counsels? (Poverty, chastity and obedience.)
Is single life a vocation? (Yes, for the Kingdom or by circumstance; all are called to love.)
practice: Write three questions for a priest, a religious sister or brother, and a single adult.
If possible, invite a panel or interview people in these vocations.
Afterward, write what surprised you and what attracted or frightened you.
Pray for each vocation, and contact a vocation director if you want to learn more.
script.close: Pray: “Lord of the harvest, send laborers into your harvest.” Sign of the Cross. Offer contact information for your diocesan vocation office.

tryit: Write one question for a priest, a religious and a single adult.
Interview one of them.
Write what surprised you.
lessons.saintStory:
Alfred Bessette was born in 1845 near Montreal, the eighth of twelve children. His father died when he was nine, and his mother when he was twelve. He was frail, and had poor health his whole life. He was uneducated, worked as a farmhand, a shoemaker and a baker, and in the factories of New England. He prayed often, especially to St. Joseph.
In 1870, at twenty-five, he asked the Holy Cross Fathers at Notre Dame College in Montreal to accept him. The pastor wrote a note to the superior: “I am sending you a saint.” He was given the name Brother André and made doorkeeper of the college, a job he held for forty years. He welcomed visitors, ran errands, cleaned and cared for the sick. He prayed for them, and used oil from the lamp before St. Joseph’s statue to anoint them. Many reported healings.
Crowds came. He dreamed of building a chapel for St. Joseph, and began with a small chapel on Mount Royal in 1904, which grew into the vast Oratory. He died in 1937 at ninety-one, and a million people filed past his coffin. He was canonized in 2010. He lived the religious life in simplicity.

units.title: Work, money and the world
units.eq: How does faith shape the way I live in the world?

lessons.title: Work and calling
lessons.idea: Work is a participation in God’s creative work and a way to serve others. It also carries burdens and risks. Faith helps us ask not only “what will pay?” but “whom does this serve?”
lessons.question: What does your work give to others? What does it cost you?
lessons.activity: Write a one-paragraph description of your current or hoped-for work as service: who benefits, what skill it requires and what temptation it brings. Then list one thing you will do this week to do your work “as for the Lord,” and one boundary that protects rest and prayer.
teach: Work is part of God’s plan from the beginning: Adam is placed in the garden “to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work shares in God’s creative action and is a way we serve others and grow in virtue (CCC 2427; Laborem Exercens). Its toil came with the fall; Christ redeems it (Genesis 3:17–19).
