The dignity of work rests on the dignity of the worker: work is for the person, not the person for work (CCC 2426–2428). Workers have rights: a just wage, safe conditions, rest, and the freedom to organize (CCC 2433–2436). Employers and employees have duties of justice and honesty.

Jesus worked as a carpenter for thirty years (Mark 6:3). Paul tells the Colossians: “Whatever your task, work heartily, as serving the Lord” (3:23–24), and he warns against idleness (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12).

Vocation includes how you spend your days. Ask: What is the good this work serves? Can I do it honestly? Does it leave time for God and family? Idolatry of work and escape from work are both temptations (CCC 2184–2188).
talk: How do you balance ambition and service?
What is a fair wage, and who decides?
How do you keep Sunday different?
quiz: Work has dignity because…|The worker is a person|The state says so|It produces money|It is hard|0|CCC 2428.
The universal destination of goods means…|No private property|God intends the earth’s goods for all|Everything belongs to the state|Everything is free|1|CCC 2402.
Sabbath rest is meant to…|Waste time|Replace prayer|Free us from the idol of work|Make us lazy|2|CCC 2184.
lessons.life: Offer your work to God each morning with the Morning Offering. Notice one way you can serve someone through it.
lessons.saint: Homobonus of Cremona: a merchant whose name means “good man,” and whose shop was his chapel.
lessons.mem: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord.” (Colossians 3:23)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is your work a job, a career or a calling? What changes if it is a calling?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to write how their work or study can serve others and glorify God.

script.open: Display a list of ten common first jobs and ask the group to rate each for ‘meaningful’ and ‘paid well.’ Notice the mismatch. Say, “Calling is a third question. What is it?”
teach: Say: “Work is part of God’s plan from the beginning. Genesis 2:15: God put the man in the garden ‘to till it and keep it.’ After the fall, work became toilsome. Jesus the carpenter sanctified human work. Paul: ‘Whatever your task, work heartily, as serving the Lord and not men.’ (Colossians 3:23) The Church teaches the dignity of work (John Paul II, Laborem Exercens, 1981): work is for the person, not the person for work; it expresses our nature as creatures made in God’s image, who create; it supports ourselves and our families; it contributes to the common good. Work that isn’t paid also has dignity: caring for children, volunteering, studying. Unemployment, exploitation and overwork are injustices.”

Say: “Calling and vocation. ‘Vocation’ includes work, but isn’t identical. A job can be a way of serving. Choosing a career: consider your gifts (what you’re good at), your passions, the needs of the world, and your commitments (family, faith). Questions: Will this let me serve others? Will it let me live my values? Will it allow time for family, prayer and Sunday? Can I do it with integrity? Parable of the talents (Matthew 25): use what you’re given. Not everyone will love their job; some work is hard or dull; it can be offered to God. Josemaría Escrivá taught that ordinary work can become a path to holiness: ‘sanctifying work, sanctifying oneself in work, sanctifying others through work.’ Saints like Homobonus show that holiness doesn’t require leaving the world.”

Say: “Practical: be excellent; be honest (no cheating, corner-cutting, stealing time); treat colleagues with respect; be a person of integrity; avoid gossip; refuse unethical demands; seek fair pay and treat others fairly; keep Sunday; be generous. Be mindful of the temptation to make work an idol, with career above family and faith, or to use people as instruments. The Church warns against workaholism and also laziness. Pray at work: offer the day in the morning; brief prayers; the Angelus at noon. Find a community of Catholic professionals. If you face a conflict between conscience and work, seek counsel. If you lack a job, the Church supports you; the parish can help. And be grateful. Work is a way of loving God and neighbor.”
ask: What does Laborem Exercens teach? (Work is for the person; it has dignity.)
What questions help discern a career? (Gifts, passions, the world’s needs, commitments, integrity.)
How can work become holy? (Offer it to God, do it well, honestly and with love.)
practice: Make a chart: My gifts / What I love / What the world needs. Look for overlaps.
Write three ways to bring integrity and charity to your current work or studies.
Write a morning offering for your work.
Share one commitment with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Morning Offering or the prayer of Josemaría: “Lord, may all my work be for your glory.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to find a Catholic professional network.

tryit: List your gifts and the world’s needs.
Note where they overlap.
Write a prayer for your work.
lessons.saintStory:
Homobonus, or Omobono, was born in Cremona, Italy, in the twelfth century, the son of a merchant. He learned the trade of a tailor and cloth merchant. He married and became known as an honest businessman. He gave generously to the poor, and was known for his fair dealing and for settling disputes.
He went to Mass every morning. Once, according to a story, a man jeered that he gave away so much he would be poor; Homobonus replied that those who give to the poor never lack. People said that his supplies of cloth and wine were mysteriously replenished.
On November 13, 1197, while at Mass in the church of St. Giles, he lay prostrate in prayer, with his arms outstretched in the form of a cross. When the Gloria ended, he did not get up. He had died. The people of Cremona recognized him as a saint, and Pope Innocent III canonized him in 1199, within two years. He is the patron of tailors, shoemakers and business people. A merchant, not a monk, was recognized as a saint.

lessons.title: Money, generosity and justice
lessons.idea: Jesus talks about money more than almost anything. The Church teaches that we are stewards, not owners, and that we have duties of justice and charity to the poor. Generosity frees us.
lessons.question: What is your relationship with money: fear, pride, control, generosity?
lessons.activity: Make a simple one-month budget and decide a percentage for giving. Choose a concrete way to give time as well as money (a soup kitchen, a tutoring program, a visit). After a week, write what you noticed about generosity and fear.
teach: The earth’s goods are meant for everyone: the universal destination of goods (CCC 2402–2406). Private property is legitimate and good but carries a social duty. Jesus warns, “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24) and tells the rich fool’s parable (Luke 12:13–21).

Giving to the poor is not only charity but justice (CCC 2446). The Church asks for a preferential love for the poor (CCC 2443–2449). Sacrificial giving is part of discipleship; tithing, almsgiving and volunteering are habits worth building (Matthew 25:31–46).

Sins against justice include theft, fraud, unjust wages, gambling that harms others, and exploitation (CCC 2408–2414). Debt, consumer culture and the pull of status are spiritual issues as well as financial ones.

Practical steps: make a budget that includes giving, avoid debt that enslaves, support organizations that help the poor with dignity, and consider how your purchases affect workers and creation (CCC 2415–2418).
talk: How much is enough?
How do you give: from the surplus, or sacrificially?
What is the difference between charity and justice?
quiz: A steward is…|A caretaker of what belongs to God|An owner|A landlord|A beggar|0|CCC 2402-2405.
Almsgiving is…|Optional|A work of mercy and a duty of justice|Irrelevant|Only for the rich|1|CCC 2447.
Jesus said we cannot serve…|God and leisure|God and money|God and family|God and wealth and prayer|1|Matthew 6:24.
lessons.life: Give away something this week that costs you: money, time, or an object you like. Do it quietly.
lessons.saint: John the Almsgiver: a patriarch who called the poor “my masters” and spent the Church’s wealth on them.
lessons.mem: “You cannot serve God and mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)
lessons.hook: Ask for a quick estimate: how much of your income would you give away if you could? Reflect on why.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe the universal destination of goods and one practice of generosity.

script.open: Pass out a blank sheet and ask each person to write the three largest categories of their spending last month, from memory. Compare with a partner. Say, “Memory shows what we notice. The bank statement shows what we value.”
teach: Say: “Jesus talked about money more than almost any other subject apart from the Kingdom. ‘You cannot serve God and mammon.’ (Matthew 6:24) ‘Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.’ (Matthew 6:21) The rich young man went away sad because he had great possessions (Mark 10:17-22). Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor. But Jesus did not condemn wealth as such; he warned about its dangers: it can choke the word (Mark 4:19), foster anxiety, and harden the heart. Paul: ‘The love of money is the root of all evils.’ (1 Timothy 6:10) The Church teaches the right of private property but also the universal destination of goods: God made the earth for all (CCC 2402-2406).”

Say: “Generosity. Almsgiving is a duty of justice and charity (CCC 2447). ‘Give to everyone who begs from you.’ (Luke 6:30) Tobit 4:7-11: ‘Give alms from your possessions.’ The Church’s tradition of the tithe (10 percent) is a guide, not a legal requirement. St. John Chrysostom: ‘Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them. The goods we possess are not ours, but theirs.’ How to give: first to the Church and parish; then to the poor, with attention to effectiveness; also give time and skills. Give cheerfully, regularly, proportionally, and sacrificially (2 Corinthians 9:7). Jesus praised the widow’s mite (Mark 12:41-44). Give quietly (Matthew 6:3-4). Practical: set up automatic giving; choose causes; review your budget through prayer.”

Say: “Justice. Charity gives to the person in need; justice asks why they are in need. The Church teaches about just wages, fair prices, debt, usury, consumerism and the global economy. Be a conscientious consumer: ask where products come from; avoid waste; resist advertising’s message that you need more. Simplicity of life. Personal finances: avoid debt, save, plan, do not gamble away money. Student debt and the cost of living are real; the Church recognizes this. Vocational decisions: don’t let money be the only factor. For work: seek just pay; for employers: pay just wages. John the Almsgiver’s approach: he saw the poor as Christ himself (Matthew 25:40). The question to ask each month: Where did my money go? Does it reflect what I say I value? Giving frees us from greed.”
ask: What did Jesus say about serving God and mammon? (We cannot serve both.)
What is the universal destination of goods? (God made the earth for everyone.)
How should we give? (Regularly, proportionally, cheerfully, sacrificially, often quietly.)
practice: Review last month’s spending by category. Mark in green what reflects your values and in red what doesn’t.
Set a giving goal, as a percentage or an amount, and choose where it goes.
Plan one act of time-giving with the poor this month.
Share one change you will make with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, free me from the love of money and make me generous.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to make a monthly giving plan.

tryit: Track your spending for a week.
Mark what reflects your values.
Set a giving goal.
lessons.saintStory:
John was born around 560 in Cyprus, to a wealthy family. He married and had children, but his wife and children died, and he gave himself to charity. In 606, he was named patriarch of Alexandria, the second most important see in the Eastern Church. He was reluctant, but he accepted.
He began by ordering an inventory of the poor of the city: he found about 7,500 people who needed help. He called them “my masters and helpers,” because they helped him gain heaven. He gave away the Church’s revenues, and also the gifts that wealthy people gave him. Once a rich man offered him a gift, and John said that if he wanted to please him, he should give it to the poor. He opened hospitals and guesthouses and offered food to refugees when the Persians invaded.
When the Persians attacked Egypt, he fled to Cyprus, where he died in 619. At the end he is said to have thanked God that he had almost nothing to leave behind.

lessons.title: Catholic social teaching: caring for our neighbor
lessons.idea: The Church’s social teaching rests on the dignity of every person, the common good, solidarity and subsidiarity. It calls Christians to work for justice in family, work, politics and the environment.
lessons.question: Which issue in your community needs attention? How could you respond?
lessons.activity: Pick one social issue in your community (housing, immigration, hunger, the environment, loneliness). Apply three principles to it and write one concrete action you can take (a call, a donation, a volunteer shift, a letter). Share it with a friend and ask them to hold you to it.
teach: Catholic social teaching is the Church’s reflection on society in light of the Gospel, from Rerum Novarum (1891) to Laudato Si’ (2015) (CCC 2419–2425). It is not partisan; it challenges every ideology.

Core principles: the dignity of the human person (CCC 1700–1709); the common good (CCC 1905–1912); subsidiarity (decisions at the lowest competent level, CCC 1883–1885); solidarity (CCC 1939–1942); the preferential option for the poor (CCC 2443–2449); care for creation (CCC 2415–2418).
Micah 6:8 summarizes: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly. Luke 4:18–19 (“good news to the poor”) and Matthew 25 (“I was hungry”) give the pattern. Faith without works is dead (James 2:14–17).

Catholics can disagree on how to apply principles but not on the principles themselves. Good citizens vote, volunteer, speak up and form their conscience with the Church’s teaching (CCC 1913–1917, 2238–2246).
talk: What are non-negotiable (life, dignity) and prudential matters (how to apply)?
How should faith shape how we vote?
What one local action can you commit to?
quiz: Subsidiarity means…|Decisions should be made at the lowest competent level|No government|Higher authorities should do everything|Everything is local|0|CCC 1883.
Which is a principle of Catholic social teaching?|Profit above all|Human dignity|Nationalism|Individualism|1|CCC 1929.
Solidarity means…|Isolation|Sharing the burdens of the whole human family|Charity only|Competition|1|CCC 1939-1940.
lessons.life: Pick one social teaching document from the Papal writings page and read the first ten paragraphs. Tell someone what you learned.
lessons.saint: Louise de Marillac: a widow and mother who organized the first sisters to serve the poor in the streets.
lessons.mem: “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8)
lessons.hook: Show a map of a local need. Ask: “Who is missing from our conversations?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name four principles of Catholic social teaching and apply one.

script.open: Ask: “What is one problem in your community that you wish someone would fix? Who is hurt by it? What do you think causes it?” Write several on a board. Say, “Catholic social teaching gives tools to think and act.”
teach: Say: “Catholic social teaching is the Church’s body of teaching about society, from Rerum Novarum (1891) to Laudato Si’ (2015). Its seven themes (US bishops): life and dignity of the human person; call to family, community and participation; rights and responsibilities; option for the poor and vulnerable; the dignity of work and the rights of workers; solidarity; care for God’s creation. Key principles: human dignity (every person is made in God’s image); the common good (the conditions allowing all to flourish); subsidiarity (decisions at the closest competent level); solidarity (we are one human family); the universal destination of goods. It is sometimes called the Church’s best-kept secret, because it is little known.”

Say: “A method: See, Judge, Act. Cardinal Joseph Cardijn, who founded the Young Christian Workers, developed it for lay people. See: look honestly at the facts. Who is affected? What are the causes? Judge: evaluate in light of the Gospel and Church teaching. What does dignity ask? What does justice require? Act: decide on specific steps. St. John XXIII’s Mater et Magistra endorsed the method. Examples. Homelessness: see (numbers, causes), judge (dignity, option for the poor), act (volunteer, advocate for housing, give). Immigration: see (stories, laws), judge (the Holy Family were refugees; nations may regulate borders but must welcome as they can), act (welcome, support legal aid, pray). Poverty, racism, human trafficking, the environment, abortion, war.”

Say: “Charity and justice. Charity meets immediate needs: soup kitchen. Justice addresses causes: policies, structures. Both are required. Louise’s approach: she combined direct service with organization. The Church warns against a purely political or purely private faith. Catholic social teaching doesn’t endorse a party; it challenges every party. How to engage: pray; learn (read the Compendium of the Social Doctrine, the US bishops’ Faithful Citizenship); join (St. Vincent de Paul Society, Catholic Charities, Catholic Relief Services, Catholic Worker, JustFaith groups); vote; volunteer; advocate by writing officials; live simply. Avoid despair: change is slow. Mother Teresa said, ‘Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.’ Choose one issue and stay with it.”
ask: Name three principles of Catholic social teaching. (Dignity, common good, solidarity, subsidiarity, option for the poor.)
What are the steps of See-Judge-Act? (Observe the facts; evaluate by the Gospel; decide on action.)
What is the difference between charity and justice? (Charity meets needs; justice addresses causes.)
practice: Choose a real issue in your community. Use See-Judge-Act on a sheet: facts, principles, action.
Name the Catholic social principles involved.
Choose one action you can do in the next month, and a person who will check in.
Find an organization in your area (St. Vincent de Paul, Catholic Charities) and contact them.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make us instruments of your peace and justice.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to join a local service group.

tryit: Apply see-judge-act to a local problem.
Name the Catholic social principles involved.
Choose one action.
lessons.saintStory:
Louise de Marillac was born in Paris in 1591, probably the daughter of a nobleman and a servant. She was never legitimized, which marked her. She was educated by Dominican nuns. She wanted to be a nun, but was told her health was too fragile. In 1613 she married Antoine Le Gras, a royal secretary, and had a son, Michel. She cared for her husband through a long illness before he died in 1625.
In 1624, she met Vincent de Paul, who became her spiritual director. He was organizing charitable groups called the Confraternities of Charity. He saw that Louise had a gift for organization. She traveled around France, setting up groups and training volunteers. In 1633, she gathered a few young peasant women in her home to train them in nursing and service of the poor. This was the beginning of the Daughters of Charity, who did not live in an enclosed convent but went out into the streets to serve the sick, the poor, orphans and prisoners. Vincent told them their convent was the home of the sick, their cell a rented room, their chapel the parish church, their cloister the streets of the city.
Louise led the Daughters until her death in 1660. She was canonized in 1934, and named patron of social workers.

units.title: Hard questions
units.eq: What about suffering, science and other faiths?

lessons.title: Why does God allow suffering?
lessons.idea: Suffering is a mystery. Christians do not claim to have a complete explanation, but they have a Person: God entered suffering in Jesus. Faith offers meaning, presence and hope.
lessons.question: What suffering in your life or the world is hardest for you to square with a good God?
lessons.activity: Write a letter you could give to someone who is suffering (a friend or a past self). Do not explain. Name the pain, say you are with them, offer one practical help, and include a line of Scripture. Then reflect on what the letter shows about what you believe about God.
teach: The Catechism asks the question plainly (CCC 309): if God is good and almighty, why is there evil? No single answer satisfies; “the whole of the Christian faith is the answer” (CCC 309). God is not the author of evil and permits it only to bring a greater good (CCC 311–312).

Some suffering comes from human freedom and sin; some from a creation still “on the way” to its perfection (CCC 310). Job does not receive an explanation; he receives God’s presence (Job 38–42). The right first response to a sufferer is presence, not argument.

Christ does not explain suffering away; he enters it. On the Cross he takes our pain into God (CCC 1521). Paul writes that sufferings are “not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed” (Romans 8:18) and that God works in all things for good (8:28).

Suffering offered with Christ can be redemptive (Colossians 1:24; CCC 1505, 1521), but we never go looking for it, and it must not be used to excuse injustice or abuse. Christians are called to relieve suffering (works of mercy) and to protest evil.
talk: When have you been helped by someone’s presence in suffering?
What are the dangers of easy answers?
How can the Church accompany those who suffer?
quiz: The Church teaches that God permits evil…|And can bring a greater good from it|Because he enjoys it|Because he does not care|Because he is weak|0|CCC 311.
Jesus in suffering…|Enters it and redeems it|Explains it|Avoids it|Is silent|0|CCC 1505.
Redemptive suffering means…|Ignoring pain|Looking for pain|Suffering is good in itself|Suffering united to Christ’s can be offered for others|3|CCC 1521.
lessons.life: Visit or call someone who is suffering this week. Listen more than you speak.
lessons.saint: Job: a righteous man who lost everything and kept asking God to explain.
misc: “A good God would prevent all evil.”
lessons.mem: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.” (Romans 8:18)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that real suffering lives in the room. Invite quiet before beginning. Offer to step out.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to state what the Church does and does not say about why God allows suffering.

script.open: Say gently, “Many of us have suffered, or watched someone suffer. Tonight we ask the question honestly: why does a good God allow suffering? You don’t have to share personal details.” Ask the group to write a single word describing what suffering has done to them or someone close. Collect them without comment.
teach: Say: “This is the most serious objection to faith, and the Church does not pretend it is easy. The Catechism (CCC 309): ‘There is not a single aspect of the Christian message that is not in part an answer to the question of evil.’ The elements of the answer, taken together. One: God made the world good and did not create evil. Two: He gave creatures freedom, and love requires freedom; evil entered through the misuse of freedom (the fall). Many sufferings come from human sin: war, cruelty, injustice. Three: Some suffering comes from natural causes (disease, earthquakes), which the tradition links to a world not yet complete and wounded by the fall. Four: God permits evil but draws good from it, as Joseph told his brothers: ‘You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good.’ (Genesis 50:20)”

Say: “Five: The most important: God has entered our suffering. In Jesus, God wept at the tomb of Lazarus, was hungry, was betrayed, was tortured and died. On the cross he cried, ‘My God, why have you forsaken me?’ We do not have a God who is distant from pain. Six: Suffering is not the last word. The Resurrection shows that evil and death are defeated; Revelation 21:4: ‘He will wipe away every tear.’ Seven: Suffering can be redemptive when united with Christ (Colossians 1:24). It does not mean God sends suffering to teach lessons, but that in his hands it can bear fruit: compassion, humility, trust, solidarity. The Church never says suffering is good; it says we must relieve it. Job: God does not explain, but he appears. Sometimes the answer to suffering is presence.”

Say: “What not to say. ‘Everything happens for a reason.’ ‘God needed another angel.’ ‘It could have been worse.’ ‘You just need more faith.’ Job’s friends did harm by explaining. What helps: presence, listening, practical help, prayer, and honesty. The Psalms of lament teach us to pray our anger and grief to God. The problem of evil remains a mystery; the Church admits we don’t know all God’s reasons. Faith doesn’t take away the question; it gives a person to trust within it. For those suffering: it’s OK to be angry; keep praying; ask for help; counseling and medical care are good; don’t suffer alone. For others: show up, as the friends did in the first seven days. Josephine Bakhita, Maximilian Kolbe, Edith Stein and Mother Teresa found God in the darkness.”
ask: Did God create evil? (No; he created a good world and gave freedom.)
What is the Christian answer at the center? (God entered our suffering in Jesus and defeated death.)
What helps someone who suffers? (Presence, listening, practical help, prayer, honesty.)
practice: Read Psalm 13 or 22 aloud. Notice how it moves from complaint to trust.
Write your own lament to God in a few honest lines, with no need to resolve it.
In pairs, share how you want people to respond when you suffer.
Choose one person who is suffering and plan one act of presence this week.
script.close: Pray Psalm 13 together and end with the Our Father. Sign of the Cross. If any member is in serious distress, offer to connect them with a priest or counselor after the session.

tryit: Write an honest lament.
List what the Church says and does not say about suffering.
Plan how to be present to someone in pain.
lessons.saintStory:
Job lived in the land of Uz, a blameless and upright man who feared God, with seven sons and three daughters, and large flocks. One day, messengers came with news, one after another: raiders had taken his oxen and donkeys, fire from heaven had burned his sheep, enemies had seized his camels, and a great wind had collapsed the house where his children were feasting, killing them all. Job tore his robe, shaved his head and fell to the ground and worshiped: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return; the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.”
Then he was struck with painful sores from head to foot. His wife said, “Curse God, and die.” Three friends came to comfort him. At first they sat with him in silence for seven days, and that was the best thing they did. Then they began to argue that he must have sinned. Job insisted he was innocent and demanded that God answer.
God did answer, out of the whirlwind, not with explanations but with questions about creation: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?” Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” God rebuked the friends and restored Job. The book doesn’t solve the problem of suffering, but shows a man who stays in conversation with God.

lessons.title: Faith and science
lessons.idea: The Church holds that faith and reason cannot contradict each other, since God is the author of both. She welcomes sound science and warns against both treating Genesis as a science textbook and treating science as the only way to truth.
lessons.question: What science do you love? What conflicts have you felt between science and faith?
lessons.activity: Make two columns: questions science answers best, and questions only philosophy and theology can approach. Put at least five in each. Then read Psalm 19:1–4 and Job 38:4–7 and write how these passages treat creation as a source of wonder rather than a rival explanation.
teach: Faith and science are two ways of seeking truth, and “there can never be any real discrepancy between faith and reason” (CCC 159). Genesis 1 teaches who made the world, why, and its goodness, in the form of liturgical poetry; it does not compete with cosmology (CCC 282–289, 337).

The Church has no teaching against the big bang or biological evolution as scientific theories. The priest Georges Lemaître proposed the big bang; Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics. What the Church insists on is that creation is good and from God, that each human soul is directly created, and that humans are made in God’s image (CCC 366, 355).

The Galileo case was a failure of judgment on both sides, not a war of religion against science (see Grade 8). Scientism, the claim that only empirical science yields truth, is a philosophical position, not a scientific result.

Questions to hold: What can science tell us? What can it not? Where might theology learn from science (the age of the universe, the interconnectedness of life)? Where does science depend on assumptions it cannot prove (order, intelligibility)?
talk: What can science not answer?
What is the difference between a gap-filling God and the Creator of all?
How could you speak with a skeptic friend?
quiz: Can a Catholic accept evolution?|Only for animals|Never|Yes, as a scientific theory, holding that God creates each soul|Only if it is false|2|CCC 283, 366.
Who proposed the Big Bang theory?|An atheist|A pope|A Catholic priest|A bishop|2|Georges Lemaître.
Genesis 1 teaches…|Detailed science|Nothing|Mythology only|Truths about God and creation in poetic form|3|CCC 289.
lessons.life: Read a short article by a scientist who is a person of faith and note what you learn.
lessons.saint: Georges Lemaître: a Belgian priest and physicist who proposed that the universe began in a “primeval atom.”
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where did you first hear that faith and science disagree? Who said it?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain how Genesis 1 and science answer different questions.

script.open: Read two headlines, ‘Pope says evolution is real’ and ‘Scientists confirm universe had a beginning.’ Ask the group which they had heard, and what they thought it meant. List the reactions.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that faith and reason can’t be in real conflict because God is the author of both (CCC 159). John Paul II: ‘Science can purify religion from error and superstition; religion can purify science from idolatry and false absolutes.’ Science asks how and what, using observation and experiment. Faith asks why and who, using revelation and reason. Each has its own methods. Problems arise when one oversteps: scientism (the idea that only what science can measure is real) is a philosophy, not a scientific result; and a literalism that reads Genesis as a science textbook misreads a text whose purpose is theological.”

Say: “Key issues. Creation and the Big Bang: the Church teaches creation out of nothing and God’s continual sustaining of the universe. This is a metaphysical claim about dependence, not a cosmology. The Big Bang is a scientific theory of the universe’s expansion from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago; it fits creation but doesn’t prove it. Evolution: the Church doesn’t oppose evolution as a scientific theory. Pius XII (Humani Generis, 1950) allowed that the human body may have evolved; John Paul II (1996) said evolution is ‘more than a hypothesis’; but each human soul is directly created by God, and humans are not accidents. The Church rejects materialist ideologies that deny purpose. Adam and Eve: the Catechism affirms the original human couple and the fall as ‘a primeval event’ in history, while recognizing symbolic language in Genesis 3 (CCC 390). How to reconcile this with science is debated.”

Say: “Myths and cases. Galileo (1633): a real mistake in prudential judgment about interpreting Scripture and weighing evidence; the pope and Church were not against science; he was not tortured or burned; many Church figures were supporters. The ‘warfare thesis’ (Draper, White, 19th century) is rejected by historians of science. The Church patronized science: universities, Copernicus (a cleric), Mendel (friar), Lemaître (priest), Steno, Secchi. The Vatican Observatory is one of the oldest. Today many scientists are believers. Bioethics raises new issues. Approach: be curious and humble; study both; don’t be defensive; separate scientific claims from philosophical ones; keep the theological meaning of Genesis (creation is good, God is the source, humans are made in God’s image, there is a purpose). Lemaître’s approach: do real science and don’t use it as apologetics. Psalm 19:1: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God.’”
ask: Can faith and science truly conflict? (No; the same God is author of both.)
What does the Church say about evolution? (The body may have evolved; each soul is directly created.)
What was Lemaître’s concern with Pius XII’s 1951 address? (He wanted to keep science and theology from being confused.)
practice: Sort statements into myth, partly true, and real question: ‘The Church burned scientists,’ ‘Genesis is a science text,’ ‘Evolution disproves God,’ ‘Science proves there is no soul.’
Choose one real question and write how a thoughtful Catholic might approach it.
Look up one Catholic scientist and share one fact.
Write your own guideline for discussing faith and science with a friend.
script.close: Pray Psalm 8 or 19. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to read a short article from the Vatican Observatory or a book by a Catholic scientist.

tryit: Sort claims about science and faith.
Mark real conflicts and myths.
Write your own approach.
lessons.saintStory:
Georges Lemaître was born in 1894 in Charleroi, Belgium. He served in the Belgian army in World War I, then studied mathematics and physics. He felt a call to the priesthood and was ordained in 1923, a Catholic priest who was also a professional scientist. He studied at Cambridge and at Harvard and MIT in the United States.
In 1927, he published a paper showing that Einstein’s equations implied an expanding universe, and he proposed that the recession of distant galaxies could be explained by it. Two years later Edwin Hubble’s observations supported it. In 1931 he suggested that if the universe is expanding, it must have started from a very small, dense state, which he called the “primeval atom,” or “cosmic egg.” This became the Big Bang theory, though the term came later, from a critic.
In 1951, Pope Pius XII gave an address saying that the Big Bang seemed to confirm the Genesis creation. Lemaître was uneasy: he believed that science and faith should not be mixed in that way, and he spoke to the pope’s staff, who got the pope to stop making such claims. Lemaître believed there were two paths to truth. He became president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences in 1960, and died in 1966.

lessons.title: Other religions, other Christians
lessons.idea: The Church respects what is true and holy in other religions and works for the unity of all Christians. She also proclaims that Jesus Christ is the one Savior of all. Dialogue and mission belong together.
lessons.question: What religions or churches do your friends belong to? What do you share and where do you differ?
lessons.activity: Choose one tradition (Orthodox, Lutheran, Jewish, Muslim, Buddhist, nonbeliever). Read a short, fair description by its own members, then write three things you admire, three differences and one question you would like to ask a friend from that tradition. If possible, invite one to coffee.
teach: The Church holds that Christ is the unique Savior and that the fullness of the means of salvation subsists in the Catholic Church (CCC 816, 846). Yet she “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2; CCC 843), and God can lead those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel to salvation (CCC 847).

Other Christians are in real, if imperfect, communion with the Church through Baptism (CCC 818–819). The Orthodox have valid sacraments and apostolic succession; Protestants share Scripture and Baptism. Unity is Christ’s prayer (John 17:20–23) and the Church works for it through prayer, dialogue and service (CCC 820–822).
Judaism has a unique place: “the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839–840). Anti-Semitism is a sin against the Gospel. Muslims worship the one merciful God (CCC 841).
Dialogue is not relativism: it listens deeply and speaks honestly. Paul in Athens (Acts 17:22–31) begins with what the Athenians already believe, quotes their poets, and then proclaims Christ.
talk: How do you hold conviction and respect together?
What would a Protestant friend find strange about Catholic faith?
What is the difference between dialogue and evangelization?
quiz: Nostra Aetate is about…|Non-Christian religions|Priests|The Bible|The Eucharist|0|Vatican II.
Can non-Christians be saved?|Only baptized|God wills all to be saved; the Church teaches salvation through Christ even for those who sincerely seek him|Only Catholics|Never|1|CCC 847.
Ecumenism seeks…|The end of the Church|Uniformity|Unity of all Christians|Conversion by force|2|CCC 820.
lessons.life: Pray the Our Father this week for Christian unity, and invite a friend of another denomination for coffee.
lessons.saint: Francis of Assisi at Damietta: a friar who crossed a battle line in 1219 to speak to the Sultan.
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Ask about a friend of another faith or none. What do you admire? What do you not understand?
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain how the Church can say Christ is the only Savior and still respect other religions.

script.open: Play a short audio clip of a call to prayer, then a Jewish Shema or a Gregorian chant. Ask, “What do you hear? What do you feel? What do these have in common?” Take reactions.
teach: Say: “Vatican II’s Nostra Aetate (1965) is the foundation. It begins by looking at what humans share: the questions about the meaning of life. It says: ‘The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions. She regards with sincere reverence those ways of conduct and of life, those precepts and teachings which, though differing in many particulars from what she holds and sets forth, nonetheless often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all men.’ At the same time, the Church ‘proclaims, and is duty bound to proclaim without fail, Christ, who is ‘the way, the truth, and the life’ (John 14:6).’ So dialogue and proclamation go together. Dialogue is not relativism; it’s listening with respect while holding our convictions.”

Say: “Judaism. Our roots: the Old Testament is our Scripture; Jesus, Mary, the apostles were Jews. Paul: ‘The gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.’ (Romans 11:29) The Church condemns antisemitism and recognizes that the Jewish people are not guilty of Jesus’ death. John Paul II called Jews our ‘elder brothers.’ We differ on Jesus as Messiah. Islam: Muslims worship the one God, honor Jesus as prophet and Mary as virgin mother, pray, fast and give alms. We differ on the Trinity, the Incarnation, the crucifixion, and the status of the Qur’an and Muhammad. Hinduism and Buddhism: they seek answers about suffering, liberation; the Church looks for ‘seeds of the Word’; we differ on God, the person, salvation. Other Christians: Orthodox (very close; differ on the papacy), Protestants (differ on authority, sacraments, Mary). All baptized are brothers and sisters in Christ.”

Say: “How to engage. The Church describes four forms of dialogue: of life (living as good neighbors), of action (working together for justice), of theological exchange (scholars), and of religious experience (sharing prayer and spirituality, carefully). Practical: learn from sources they would recognize; ask rather than assume; listen to their story; share your own; don’t caricature; avoid arguing to win; know your faith; pray for them. Avoid indifferentism (all religions the same) and syncretism (mixing). Avoid arrogance and also timidity. Francis of Assisi neither compromised nor attacked. Evangelization: respects freedom; invites by witness. The Church teaches that salvation is possible for those who sincerely seek God (LG 16). Why are we still Catholic? Because we believe the fullness of truth is in Christ and his Church, and this fullness is a gift. Charity and truth together.”
ask: What does Nostra Aetate say about other religions? (The Church rejects nothing true and holy in them.)
How does the Church view the Jewish people? (As elder brothers; the covenant is irrevocable; antisemitism is condemned.)
What is the difference between dialogue and syncretism? (Dialogue listens and respects; syncretism mixes beliefs.)
practice: Make a chart with Judaism, Islam, Hinduism/Buddhism, Orthodoxy and Protestantism: what we share, where we differ, how to engage.
Pick one friend or neighbor of another faith and plan a respectful question to ask.
Write a short statement of what you would want a friend to know about your faith.
Pray for them by name.
script.close: Pray the Prayer of Saint Francis: “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to visit a different house of worship by invitation.

tryit: Write what we share with Jews, Muslims and other Christians.
Write where we truly differ.
Plan a respectful conversation.
lessons.saintStory:
In 1219, during the Fifth Crusade, Christian armies besieged the Egyptian city of Damietta. Francis of Assisi had come to the camp, troubled by the violence on both sides. He asked permission to go and speak to the Sultan, al-Malik al-Kamil, a Muslim ruler. The papal legate reluctantly agreed. Francis, with one companion, Brother Illuminatus, crossed the lines unarmed.
They were seized by the Sultan’s soldiers, beaten and chained, and brought before al-Kamil. The Sultan, a man of culture and courtesy, received them and listened to Francis preach the Gospel. Medieval accounts say Francis offered to walk through fire to show the truth of Christ, which the Sultan’s scholars refused. The Sultan was impressed by Francis’s sincerity. He offered gifts, which Francis declined, and allowed him to return safely to the Christian camp.
We don’t know exactly what was said. But Francis’s approach became a model. In his Rule of 1221, he wrote that friars who go among Muslims may live peacefully, without arguing, “subject to every human creature for God’s sake,” and, when it pleases God, announce the Word. In 2019, Pope Francis marked the 800th anniversary of the meeting by signing a Document on Human Fraternity with the Grand Imam of al-Azhar in Abu Dhabi.
