lessons.title: Friendship, community and accountability
lessons.idea: Faith is not meant to be lived alone. Friends, a parish, a small group and a spiritual director help us stay faithful. Real community requires time, honesty and forgiveness.
lessons.question: Who in your life makes it easier to follow Jesus? Who makes it harder?
lessons.activity: Map your current community: who knows you, who challenges you, who you serve. Choose one gap and one concrete step to fill it this month (join a group, ask someone to pray weekly, start a study). Then write a note of thanks to a friend who has helped your faith.
teach: We are made for communion; Genesis 2:18 says “it is not good that the man should be alone.” The Church is the community through which we grow in faith (Acts 2:42–47; Hebrews 10:24–25). Friendship, accountability and shared mission are not extras.

Good Christian friendship helps each other toward God (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12; Proverbs 27:17). It includes honesty, forgiveness, prayer together, and challenge when needed (Matthew 18:15–17). Aelred of Rievaulx wrote that “God is friendship.”

Practical forms: a small group or Bible study, a prayer partner, a mentor or spiritual director, volunteer teams, parish or campus ministry. Find one place where you are known, one where you serve and one where you are challenged.

Watch for unhealthy community: control, secrecy, cult-like pressure, and groups that discourage questions or contact with family. The Church offers a rule: authority serves, and the fruits are freedom, truth and charity.
talk: What keeps you from joining a community?
What does your parish offer for people your age?
How can you be a good friend to someone who is struggling?
quiz: Spiritual direction is…|Optional for no one|A sacrament|Ongoing guidance in the spiritual life|A therapy|2|CCC 2690.
Who strengthens our faith in community?|Friends, family, parish|Only books|Only priests|No one|0|Hebrews 10:24-25.
The communion of saints includes…|Only monks|Only canonized saints|Only the dead|The faithful on earth, in purgatory and in heaven|3|CCC 954-955.
lessons.life: Join or start something: a Bible study, a prayer group, a service night. Invite one friend.
lessons.saint: Pier Giorgio Frassati and the Society of the Shady Characters: friends who climbed mountains and prayed the Rosary on the way.
lessons.mem: “Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works.” (Hebrews 10:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who is one person who would tell you the truth if you were off track?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name a community, an accountability partner and one commitment.

script.open: Ask: “Who are the three people you spend the most time with? What do they bring out in you? Do they help you grow in faith or pull away from it?” Allow silence, then take a few answers.
teach: Say: “We are made for communion. ‘It is not good that the man should be alone.’ (Genesis 2:18) Christianity is not a private matter. Jesus formed a community: the Twelve, and a larger circle of disciples. The early Church ‘devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.’ (Acts 2:42) The Catechism speaks of the Church as communion. Friendship is a gift and a path to holiness. Aelred of Rievaulx wrote Spiritual Friendship; Aquinas said friendship is the highest form of love; Jesus calls us friends (John 15:15). A friend shares your journey and helps you toward God. Proverbs 27:17: ‘Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.’”

Say: “Community. Where do we find it? The parish: regular Mass, small groups, service. Campus ministry, young adult groups, Bible studies, prayer groups, retreats, sports leagues and service projects. Movements: Catholic Charismatic Renewal, Focolare, Communion and Liberation, FOCUS, Theology on Tap. Families. Small groups matter because we need people who know us. In our culture, loneliness is rising. Social media gives connections but not always community. What makes community healthy: shared purpose, regular meetings, honesty, hospitality, forgiveness, mutual care, openness to newcomers. What harms it: gossip, cliques, judgment, perfectionism, abuse of authority. If a Church community has hurt you, seek another, and speak with leaders.”

Say: “Accountability. Hebrews 10:24-25: ‘Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together.’ James 5:16: ‘Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.’ Accountability means having people who ask hard questions out of love: Are you praying? Are you going to Mass? How are you living chastity? How are you using money? It works best when mutual, voluntary, specific, and gentle. Form a small group of two to four people who meet weekly or monthly, with a simple pattern: check-in, Scripture, prayer, commitments. Be careful about the difference between accountability and control. A spiritual director or a confessor is another form of accountability. Pier Giorgio’s friends: they stayed in each other’s lives. Choose friends who raise you toward the heights.”
ask: Why is Christianity communal? (Jesus formed a community; we are made for communion.)
Name two forms of community. (Parish, small groups, movements, campus ministry.)
What makes accountability healthy? (Mutual, voluntary, specific, gentle, rooted in love.)
practice: Draw a circle of your relationships: closest friends, mentors, community. Mark who helps you toward God.
Identify one gap: a mentor, a group, an accountability partner.
Write an invitation to someone to start a weekly or monthly check-in.
Plan one community event for the coming month.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give us friends who lead us to you.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to make a plan for a regular small group.

tryit: List the friends who help you grow.
Name one place of accountability.
Plan one act of community this month.
lessons.saintStory:
Pier Giorgio Frassati was born in 1901 in Turin, Italy, to a wealthy family. His father owned the newspaper La Stampa and was an ambassador. Pier Giorgio was a handsome, athletic young man who loved skiing, climbing, and practical jokes. He was also deeply devout, going to Mass daily, praying the Rosary and adoring the Eucharist. He took part in Catholic student groups and served the poor with the St. Vincent de Paul Society, often giving away his money and even his coat.
He gathered a group of friends, who called themselves the Società dei Tipi Loschi, the “Society of Shady Characters.” They played pranks, took mountain trips, ate together and prayed together. They sang, climbed peaks, and said the Rosary on the trail. His motto was Verso l’alto, “To the heights.” The friendships lasted beyond his life, and the friends supported each other in faith.
He contracted polio, probably from the sick he tended, and died at twenty-four in 1925. His funeral was filled with the poor of Turin, whom his family had not known he helped. He was beatified in 1990, and canonized in 2025. His friends wrote letters about him for years.

lessons.title: Sharing the faith
lessons.idea: Evangelization means sharing the Good News in word and witness. It begins with friendship, listening and a life that raises questions, and it is always an invitation, never a trap. Every baptized person is a missionary disciple.
lessons.question: Whom has God put in your life who needs to hear about him?
lessons.activity: Write a 60-second story of how God has been present in your life (before, encounter, after). Practice it with a partner. Then write the names of three people you will pray for and one simple invitation (coffee, Mass, an event) you can offer each.
teach: Every baptized person shares in the Church’s mission (CCC 849–856, 900, 905). “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence” (1 Peter 3:15–16). Witness comes first; words follow.
Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–39) is a model: listen, start from where the person is (Isaiah), ask questions, explain Scripture, invite to Baptism. The Spirit leads; you are available.

Evangelization includes witness, proclamation, dialogue and charity (Evangelii Nuntiandi). It respects freedom: faith cannot be forced (CCC 160). Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium calls for joyful, missionary disciples who go to the margins.

Practical help: know your own story (how God has been present), learn a few basics of the faith, invite friends to Mass or an event, and pray for them by name. You do not need to be an expert; you need to be a friend.
talk: What fears do you have about sharing faith?
What is the difference between being invited and being pressured?
Who invited you into faith?
quiz: What is evangelization?|Convincing by arguments|Sharing the Good News in word and witness|Condemning others|Giving money|1|CCC 849-852.
1 Peter 3:15 says be ready to…|Give a reason for the hope that is in you with gentleness|Avoid questions|Silence others|Argue|0|1 Peter 3:15.
Who is called to evangelize?|Missionaries only|Teachers only|Every baptized person|Clergy only|2|CCC 905.
lessons.life: Invite someone to Mass, a Bible study or a service project this week.
lessons.saint: The Samaritan woman: she left her water jar at the well and told her whole town.
misc: “I need to be an expert first.”
lessons.mem: “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you.” (1 Peter 3:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When did someone share their faith with you in a way you appreciated?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to write a 60-second story of faith and one invitation to offer.

script.open: Hand out cards and ask each person to write the last time someone invited them to something that changed their life. Share a few stories. Say, “That is how most conversions begin: with an invitation.”
teach: Say: “The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) applies to every baptized person. Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium: ‘Every Christian is a missionary to the extent that he or she has encountered the love of God in Christ Jesus.’ (EG 120) Evangelization is the Church’s deepest identity (Paul VI). It has many forms: witness of life, proclamation, invitation, service, and sharing community. The new evangelization, as John Paul II said, is new in ardor, methods and expression. Most people come to faith through relationships. The Samaritan woman didn’t have a theology degree. She told her story and invited others to ‘come and see.’ Philip said the same to Nathanael.”

Say: “How to share. Start by listening: Jesus asked for a drink, then listened. Share your story: a simple three-part testimony: my life before, how I encountered Christ, and how my life is now. Be honest, including struggles. Invite: to Mass, a Bible study, a retreat, an event. Pray for the person first. Be ready to answer: 1 Peter 3:15: ‘Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.’ Know the basics: the kerygma (God loves you, Jesus died and rose for your sins, you are invited to follow him), and a few apologetics answers. Don’t argue to win. Live the faith with joy and integrity. Serve. Use social media wisely: positive, charitable. Respect freedom: the Spirit converts.”

Say: “Common difficulties. Fear of rejection: Jesus said the world would reject us, but we are sent anyway. Fear of ignorance: say ‘I don’t know, but I’ll find out.’ Wanting to be liked: the Gospel will sometimes be countercultural. Sharing with family: patience; witness first. Sharing with friends: invite them to join a group. A culture of ‘nones’ (the religiously unaffiliated): many are open but hurt. Evangelize those who left: listen to their reasons. Evangelization and service go together: Catholic Relief Services, soup kitchens. Pray: ‘Lord, send me.’ The woman left her jar: she dropped her ordinary task for the sake of the news. What jar do you need to put down? Francis Xavier traveled the world; you may be called to your dorm hall or your workplace.”
ask: Who is called to evangelize? (Every baptized Christian.)
What are the three parts of a testimony? (Before, encounter with Christ, now.)
What did the Samaritan woman say? (“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did.”)
practice: Read John 4:5-30, 39-42 aloud in parts.
Write your faith story in three short paragraphs: before, encounter, now.
Practice telling it to a partner in two minutes; the partner gives encouragement and one question.
Name one person you will invite to something this month, and pray for them by name.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, send me, and give me words and love.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to share their story with one person this week.

tryit: Write your story in three parts.
Practice telling it for two minutes.
Name one person you will invite.
lessons.saintStory:
In John 4, Jesus, tired from his journey, sat down by Jacob’s well in Samaria at noon. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, probably at noon to avoid the other women. Jews and Samaritans did not associate. Jesus asked her, “Give me a drink.” She was surprised. Jesus spoke of “living water.” She asked for it. Then he said, “Go, call your husband.” She said she had none. Jesus said, “You are right… you have had five husbands, and he whom you now have is not your husband.” She said, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.”
She raised a theological question about where to worship, and Jesus said, “The hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” She said, “I know that Messiah is coming.” Jesus answered, “I who speak to you am he.”
The woman left her water jar and went into the town, saying, “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?” Many Samaritans believed because of her testimony, and then they asked Jesus to stay two days. They said, “It is no longer because of your words that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves.” In Orthodox tradition, she is called Photina, “the enlightened one,” and honored as an evangelist.

lessons.title: A rule of life
lessons.idea: A rule of life is a simple, realistic plan for prayer, sacraments, learning, service and rest. It helps turn good intentions into habits. Start small and adjust.
lessons.question: What would you commit to for the next three months?
lessons.activity: Draft a rule of life with daily, weekly, monthly and yearly practices that you can actually keep. Share it with a friend or mentor. After two weeks, review it: what stayed, what failed, what to adjust.
teach: A rule of life is a realistic plan of daily and weekly practices that keep you close to God (CCC 2030, 2044–2045). Monastic rules (Benedict) taught that order frees us for love; “prayer and work” give a rhythm. Lay people can have a rule too.

Core practices: Sunday Mass and, if possible, more; regular Confession; daily prayer (morning offering, Scripture, evening examen); fasting and almsgiving; service; rest. “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17) starts with fixed times (Luke 18:1; CCC 2742–2745).

Start small and specific: a few minutes at the same time each day. Add one habit at a time. Review it monthly with a friend or director. If you fail, begin again without drama. The goal is love, not perfection.
Avoid two errors: legalism (the rule becomes the goal) and vagueness (no plan, so nothing happens). Grace comes first; the rule is a trellis for it.
talk: Which practice is easiest? Hardest?
What would make it sustainable?
Who will hold you to it?
quiz: A rule of life is…|A plan for habits of prayer, sacraments and service|A vow|A contract|A list of prohibitions|0|Spiritual tradition.
Start with…|Small realistic steps|A pilgrimage|Everything at once|A year of silence|0|Wisdom of the saints.
Who can help you keep a rule?|Only yourself|No one|A friend, spiritual director or small group|A website|2|Accountability.
lessons.life: Write your rule, put it where you will see it, and tell one person. Review it in a month.
lessons.saint: Pachomius: an Egyptian soldier who wrote the first rule for monks living together.
misc: “If I miss a day, I have failed.”
lessons.mem: “Pray without ceasing.” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What is one practice that would change your week if you kept it?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to present a rule with daily, weekly and monthly practices.

script.open: Display a weekly calendar template. Ask everyone to fill in one typical week quickly, with colors for work, rest, relationships and prayer. Compare patterns. Say, “A rule of life begins by seeing the week as it is.”
teach: Say: “A rule of life is a set of practices that you commit to, to keep God at the center. The word ‘rule’ comes from the Latin regula, a pattern or trellis, not a cage. A trellis supports growth. The great rules: St. Pachomius, St. Basil, St. Augustine, St. Benedict (the most influential, with ‘pray and work,’ stability, obedience), St. Francis, St. Ignatius. Lay people can have a rule, too: St. Francis de Sales’s Introduction to the Devout Life; the Third Orders; Opus Dei’s ‘plan of life.’ Jesus himself had a rhythm: he withdrew to pray, attended the synagogue, observed feasts, spent time with friends and the crowds.”

Say: “Elements. Prayer: daily (morning offering, a time of Scripture or silence, evening examination), Angelus or Rosary. Sacraments: Mass every Sunday, perhaps weekdays; Confession monthly. Study: spiritual reading, Scripture, the Catechism. Service: regular works of mercy. Community: small group, family, parish. Rest: Sabbath, sleep, leisure. Sacrifice: fasting on Fridays, giving. Work: done well. Relationships: time for family and friends. Guidance: a spiritual director. Principles: Be realistic (start small); be specific (what, when, where); be flexible but faithful; include rest; review regularly with someone. A rule for a student differs from that of a young professional or a parent. Some start with a simple Fruits-of-the-Spirit checklist.”

Say: “How to make one. Step 1: Reflect on your life now. Where does time go? Step 2: Name your goals. What do I want my life to look like in a year? Step 3: Choose a few key practices. Four or five. Example: Daily: ten minutes of prayer with Scripture; evening Examen. Weekly: Sunday Mass, one holy hour or weekday Mass, a small group, a work of mercy. Monthly: Confession, a day of reflection. Yearly: a retreat. Step 4: Tell someone. Step 5: Try it for a month, then adjust. Step 6: Be gentle with failure; start again. Pope John XXIII’s spiritual journal, Journal of a Soul, shows a lifetime of such rules. The rule is a servant, not a master. As Benedict wrote, we run the path of God’s commandments with hearts overflowing with the inexpressible sweetness of love. The Church’s liturgical year provides a rhythm too. Christ calls disciples to follow him daily (Luke 9:23).”
ask: What is a rule of life? (A set of practices that keeps God at the center and supports growth.)
Name three elements of a rule. (Prayer, sacraments, study, service, community, rest.)
How long should you try it before adjusting? (About a month.)
practice: Review how your week actually goes: where does time go?
Draft a rule of life with four or five practices: daily, weekly, monthly, yearly.
Share it with a partner who will check in at the end of the month.
Put the first practice on your calendar.
script.close: Pray the Suscipe of Benedict, “Receive me, Lord, according to your word.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to review their rules together in a month.

tryit: Draft your rule of life.
Include prayer, sacraments, study, service, rest and relationships.
Choose a first month trial.
lessons.saintStory:
Pachomius was born around 292 in Upper Egypt to pagan parents. At twenty, he was conscripted into the Roman army. While his unit was being taken down the Nile, the soldiers were locked up in a prison in Thebes. Local Christians brought them food and water, kindness that astonished Pachomius. He asked who these people were, and was told they were Christians, who loved all humans. He vowed that if he was released, he would become a Christian and serve people.
After his discharge, he was baptized and went to live with an elderly hermit named Palamon. But then he felt that God was calling him to something else: a community. Around 320 he founded a monastery at Tabennese, on the Nile. Monks lived together, with a common rule: a time for prayer, work, meals, silence, and obedience to an abbot. Before this, hermits had lived alone. Pachomius organized them in a system of communities, eventually thousands of monks, and also communities of women.
His rule was translated by Jerome into Latin and influenced Basil, Benedict and others. He died in 348 in a plague. His idea: ordinary people, in community, with a rule, can live the Gospel.

units.title: Hard questions about the Church
units.eq: Can I trust the Church’s authority and its story?

lessons.title: Infallibility and the development of doctrine
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that the Holy Spirit protects the Church’s teaching from error on faith and morals under certain conditions. Doctrine develops in understanding without changing in meaning.
lessons.question: Does the pope never make mistakes?
lessons.activity: Take three teachings (the Trinity, the Assumption, a pastoral decision such as a diocesan policy) and decide for each what level of authority it carries and how it developed. Look up one development (the doctrine of Mary as Theotokos, or the teaching on religious liberty) and trace how the Church came to state it.
teach: Infallibility is the Church’s gift of being preserved from error when she teaches definitively on faith and morals (CCC 889–892). It belongs to the Pope speaking ex cathedra, to the college of bishops teaching in union with him (especially in council), and to the whole Church in believing (CCC 91–93).

It is narrow. It is not impeccability (the Pope can sin), nor omniscience, nor does it cover every statement. Only a handful of ex cathedra definitions exist (the Immaculate Conception in 1854, the Assumption in 1950). Most Church teaching is authoritative but not defined.

Doctrine develops: understanding grows while the deposit remains the same. John Henry Newman compared it to an idea that grows without losing its identity (CCC 66, 94). The Council of Nicaea clarified, not invented, what the Church had always believed about Christ.

Distinguish dogma (revealed truths defined by the Church), settled doctrine, authoritative teaching and prudential judgments. Respond with the right level of assent (CCC 891–892), and with honest questions where you struggle.
talk: What is the difference between a pope’s opinion and a definition?
Why would God protect the Church’s teaching at all?
How can a teaching “develop” without being changed?
quiz: Which of these was defined ex cathedra?|The use of Latin|The Assumption of Mary (1950)|The date of Easter|The papal states|1|Munificentissimus Deus.
Infallibility means that the pope is…|Never to be questioned in anything|Always right on politics|Sinless|Protected from error when teaching definitively on faith or morals|3|CCC 891.

Which best describes authentic development of doctrine?|Replacing teaching with its opposite|Inventing new revelation|Deeper understanding of what was always taught|Dropping what is unpopular|2|CCC 66, 94.
lessons.life: Read a short account of how the Church came to define the Trinity or the divinity of Christ.
lessons.saint: Blessed Pius IX: the pope of the Immaculate Conception and the First Vatican Council, whose long reign is still argued over.
lessons.mem: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” (John 16:13)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does it mean for a teaching to ‘develop’ without changing?” Take answers.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain infallibility and development of doctrine with one example.

script.open: Ask: “Has the Church ever changed her mind? Can you think of an example? Is that a sign of weakness or of honesty?” Write answers. Say, “Tonight we see how the Church understands infallibility, and how doctrine can develop without being corrupted.”
teach: Say: “Infallibility: the Church teaches that Christ protects her from error when she teaches definitively on faith and morals. It is exercised in three ways: the Pope speaking ex cathedra; the bishops together with the Pope in a council; and the universal ordinary Magisterium. Vatican I (1870), under Pius IX, defined: when the Roman Pontiff ‘speaks ex cathedra, that is, when in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole Church,’ he has the infallibility which Christ gave the Church. The conditions: as pastor of all, on faith or morals, definitively, to be held by all. Ex cathedra definitions are very rare: the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption (1950). It doesn’t mean the Pope is sinless, inspired, or right about everything.”

Say: “Development of doctrine. Newman’s Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845): ‘To live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.’ The Church’s teaching doesn’t change in substance but is understood more deeply, as an acorn becomes an oak. Vincent of Lérins: progress, not alteration. Newman’s seven notes of authentic development: preservation of type, continuity of principles, power of assimilation, logical sequence, anticipation of its future, conservative action on its past, chronic vigor. A corruption contradicts the earlier teaching; a development draws out what was implicit. Examples: the Trinity (from Scripture to Nicaea), Christ’s two natures (Chalcedon), the canon, Mary’s Immaculate Conception and Assumption, religious freedom (Vatican II), slavery (always against dignity but slow to be condemned clearly), the death penalty (CCC 2267, 2018).”

Say: “Hard cases. ‘Outside the Church no salvation’: developed through the idea of baptism of desire and invincible ignorance to Vatican II’s statement. Usury: the medieval ban on interest was revised with the understanding of money and risk. Religious freedom: Pius IX’s Syllabus condemned the idea that everyone has a right to religious freedom in some senses; Dignitatis Humanae (1965) taught a civil right to religious freedom based on dignity. Critics say this is a reversal; the Church says it is a development: the earlier teaching was about error having no rights, the later about persons having rights. How do we respond? Humility: not everything is yet understood; honesty: the Church has made prudential errors and sometimes expressed truths in inadequate ways; distinguish dogmas from disciplines and prudential judgments; read documents in context. The test: is it consistent with Scripture and Tradition? Not every change is a development, and not every continuity is rigidity.”
ask: What are the three ways infallibility is exercised? (The Pope ex cathedra; the bishops with the Pope in council; the universal ordinary Magisterium.)
What is development of doctrine? (Deeper understanding of the same truth, not a change in substance.)
What is the difference between development and corruption? (Development draws out what was implicit; corruption contradicts.)
practice: Choose one doctrine (the Immaculate Conception, the Trinity, religious freedom). Trace it from Scripture to today in a timeline.
Test it against two of Newman’s notes.
Write a short reply to someone who says, ‘The Church changed its teaching.’
Share and critique with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Creed. Sign of the Cross. Suggest the group read a section of Newman’s Essay on Development or a summary.

tryit: Test a doctrine against Newman’s notes.
Distinguish development from change.
Write a reply to “the Church changed its mind.”
lessons.saintStory:
Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti was born in 1792 in Senigallia, Italy, and became pope in 1846 as Pius IX. He began as a hopeful reformer, who freed political prisoners and allowed a free press in the Papal States. But after the revolutions of 1848 and the assassination of his minister, he fled Rome. He returned under French protection and turned conservative, resisting liberalism and nationalism.
His reign, the longest in history at over 31 years, saw dramatic events. In 1854, he defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, after consulting the bishops of the world. In 1864 he issued the Syllabus of Errors, condemning a list of modern ideas, in a way that is still debated. In 1869-70 he convened the First Vatican Council, which defined papal infallibility and primacy of jurisdiction. In September 1870, the army of the new Kingdom of Italy took Rome, and he declared himself a “prisoner in the Vatican.”
He also made mistakes: the 1858 Mortara case, in which a Jewish boy secretly baptized by a servant was taken from his family by papal police, damaged Catholic-Jewish relations. He died in 1878 and was beatified in 2000 alongside John XXIII. His case shows the tension in dealing with a changing world.

lessons.title: The Church’s history: slavery, colonialism and anti-Judaism
lessons.idea: Members of the Church have sometimes sinned gravely, including by supporting slavery, colonialism and hatred of the Jewish people, while popes and saints also spoke against these wrongs. The Church teaches that Jews are not collectively guilty of Christ’s death.
lessons.question: How should Catholics tell the truth about the Church’s past?
lessons.activity: Read a primary source: a papal statement (for example, John Paul II’s Day of Pardon prayer on March 12, 2000, or Nostra Aetate 4). Write what it admits, what it does not, and what repair looks like. Then choose a concrete way to learn more about a community harmed in this history.
teach: The Church’s history includes real sin by Catholics: participation in or toleration of slavery, harm to indigenous peoples, anti-Jewish teaching and violence, and failures to protect the vulnerable. The Church is holy in Christ and “always in need of purification” (CCC 827).

Popes and councils have spoken: Paul III (1537) and Gregory XVI (1839) condemned the enslavement of indigenous peoples and the slave trade; John Paul II in 2000 asked forgiveness for sins of the Church’s children, including against Jews (CCC 597–598, 839). Vatican II’s Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected hatred of Jews and the charge of collective guilt for the Crucifixion.

Telling the truth includes the good: missionaries who defended native peoples (Bartolomé de las Casas), Catholics who hid Jews, abolitionists. Neither “the Church has always been right” nor “the Church has only done harm” is true.
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). The measure is Christ, and repentance is part of the Gospel.
talk: Why is it harder to apologize for what the Church has done than for what I have done?
What does an honest examination of the Church’s history ask of people today?
Why do both Church leaders and ordinary Catholics appear in both the good and the bad of this story?
quiz: Nostra Aetate (1965) teaches that…|The Jews are rejected by God|All religions are equal|Jews as a people are not guilty of Christ’s death|Only Catholics can be saved|2|CCC 597–598.
In 1537 Pope Paul III declared that…|The Americas belong to Europeans|Native peoples are truly human and cannot be enslaved|Conversion by force is allowed|Slavery is a good|1|Sublimis Deus.
CCC 2414 says the enslavement of human beings is…|A sin|Permitted in war|A matter of custom|Not discussed|0|CCC 2414.
lessons.life: Learn about Katharine Drexel or Peter Claver and one act of justice in your own community.
lessons.saint: Blessed Bernhard Lichtenberg: a Berlin priest who prayed publicly for the Jews after Kristallnacht.
misc: “The Church is only a history of wrongs.”
lessons.mem: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” (Galatians 3:28)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that history includes real harm done by Catholics. Commit to honesty and humility.
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name one historical wrong, what the Church has said and what repair requires.

script.open: Say: “We’re going to look honestly at some of the worst chapters of Church history. Some members of the group may feel defensive, and others angry. Both are welcome. The aim is truth.” Ask: “What have you heard about the Church and slavery, colonialism or anti-Jewish prejudice? How do you feel about it?” Allow honest answers.
teach: Say: “The Church is holy because of Christ, but her members are sinners. John Paul II, in the Jubilee of 2000, led a liturgy of repentance, asking forgiveness for sins of Christians in the past: ‘We forgive and we ask forgiveness.’ Naming the sins is part of faithfulness. Anti-Judaism: for centuries, many Christians blamed Jews collectively for the death of Jesus, the ‘deicide’ charge. This fed discrimination, expulsions, forced conversions, pogroms, ghettos, the Inquisition’s targeting of conversos, and set the stage for modern antisemitism, which contributed to the Holocaust, though Nazi ideology was racial and anti-Christian. Nostra Aetate (1965) repudiated antisemitism and the collective blame. The Catechism: Jesus’ death cannot be blamed on Jews as a people (CCC 597). Popes have visited synagogues; John Paul II prayed at the Western Wall in 2000.”

Say: “Slavery. The Church condemned slavery in principle over time: Gregory of Nyssa spoke against it in the 4th century; Pope Paul III’s Sublimis Deus (1537) said the indigenous peoples of the Americas should not be enslaved; Urban VIII (1639) and Benedict XIV; Gregory XVI condemned the slave trade (1839); Leo XIII (1888) called for abolition. But Catholics also owned slaves, Church institutions benefited from slavery, and some theologians defended it, and the Church did not condemn slavery as intrinsically evil clearly until the late 19th and 20th century (Vatican II lists slavery among infamies, GS 27). Saints like Peter Claver and Bartolomé de las Casas fought it. Colonialism: missionaries brought the Gospel, built schools and hospitals, and defended natives (Las Casas, the Jesuit reductions). The Church also benefited from empire, and some missionaries accepted colonial attitudes, suppressing cultures. Residential schools in Canada and elsewhere: abuse and cultural destruction; Pope Francis apologized in 2022. Crusades, Inquisition: see Grade 8.”

Say: “How to respond. First, honesty: don’t deny or minimize. Second, context: history is complex; avoid caricature, but context doesn’t excuse. Third, distinguish sin from teaching: the Church’s members sinned, and sometimes theologians erred; but her doctrine in its core (the dignity of every person) is what condemned these evils. Fourth, remember the heroes: Lichtenberg, Claver, Las Casas, Bakhita, Righteous Among the Nations who were Catholics. Fifth, repentance and reform: the Church has apologized, changed, and sought reconciliation, and work continues with indigenous communities, Jewish partners and Black Catholic communities. Sixth, solidarity: how can we address injustice now? Practical: learn the history; listen to descendants; support reconciliation efforts. Read ‘Memory and Reconciliation’ (International Theological Commission, 2000). Don’t use history as a weapon or a shield. And pray. Lichtenberg shows what faithful Catholics did.”
ask: What did John Paul II do in the Jubilee of 2000? (Led the Church in asking forgiveness for past sins of Christians.)
What does the Catechism say about blame for Jesus’ death? (It can’t be placed on the Jewish people as a whole.)
How should we respond to hard history? (Honestly, with context, repentance and action.)
practice: Divide a sheet into three columns: failures, repentance, heroes. Fill in at least three items each for anti-Judaism, slavery and colonialism.
In pairs, role-play a conversation with a friend who says, ‘The Church is hypocritical because of her history.’
Look up the work of one organization for reconciliation (e.g., Catholic-Jewish dialogue, indigenous healing).
Write a prayer of repentance and hope.
script.close: Pray Lichtenberg’s prayer for the persecuted: “Lord, have mercy on those who suffer, and on us all.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to read the Jubilee liturgy of 2000.

tryit: Make a list of the Church’s historical failures and good deeds.
Describe how the Church has repented.
Write a response to a friend who raises one.
lessons.saintStory:
Bernhard Lichtenberg was born in 1875 in Silesia. He became a priest and in 1932 provost of St. Hedwig’s Cathedral in Berlin. A critic of Nazism from early on, he preached against the regime’s anti-Christian ideology and defended the rights of the persecuted. 
After the night of November 9-10, 1938 (Kristallnacht), when synagogues were burned across Germany and Jewish shops were smashed, Lichtenberg decided to act. That evening, at the end of the regular evening prayers, he told the congregation that from then on they would pray publicly “for the Jews and for the poor prisoners in the concentration camps.” He did so every evening for three years.
He protested to the authorities about the killing of the mentally ill, and the persecution of Jews. In October 1941, he was denounced by two young women who had heard him pray. He was arrested and sentenced to two years in prison. He asked to be sent to the ghetto at Łódź to minister to the Jews there. After he completed the sentence, the Gestapo rearrested him. Weak with heart disease, he died on November 5, 1943, while being transported to Dachau, in the city of Hof. He was beatified in 1996.

lessons.title: Mary: why do Catholics honor her?
lessons.idea: Catholics honor Mary as Mother of God and the first disciple, and ask her to pray for us as we ask any friend. We do not worship her. The Immaculate Conception and Assumption show what God’s grace can do.
lessons.question: Do Catholics worship Mary?
lessons.activity: Read Luke 1:26–56. List every title or action given to Mary by Gabriel, Elizabeth and herself. Then pray one decade of the Rosary slowly (see the Devotions page) and write what changed in how you view Mary. Prepare a short answer to a friend who asks, “Why do you pray to Mary?”
teach: Catholics honor Mary because of her Son: she is the Mother of God (Theotokos; Luke 1:43; CCC 495), the model of faith (Luke 1:38, 45), and the first disciple (CCC 967). Honor (hyperdulia) is different from the worship (latria) due to God alone (CCC 971, 2096).

Four Marian dogmas: Mother of God (Ephesus 431), perpetual virginity (CCC 499–507), Immaculate Conception (1854; CCC 490–493), Assumption (1950; CCC 966). Each is grounded in the Church’s ancient belief and points to Christ, not away from him.

The Rosary and other devotions are ways of meditating on the life of Christ with Mary (CCC 2678, 2708). At Cana she says “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5); at the Cross Jesus gives her to the beloved disciple (John 19:26–27; CCC 501, 964).

Protestant objections deserve a respectful hearing: the silence of Scripture on some points, the sole mediation of Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). The Catholic reply is that Mary’s intercession shares in, not rivals, his mediation, as all Christians pray for one another.
talk: What is the difference between worship and veneration?
Why do many Christians find the Marian dogmas hard to accept?
How does Mary lead us to Jesus in your own experience?
quiz: The Immaculate Conception is the teaching that…|Jesus was conceived without a father|Mary never died|Mary was preserved from original sin from her conception|Mary is divine|2|CCC 491.
The Council of Ephesus (431) defined Mary as…|A prophet only|A goddess|An angel|Theotokos, Mother of God|3|It protected faith in Jesus’ divinity.
Catholics give adoration to…|The Church|Mary and the saints|God alone|God and Mary|2|CCC 2096.
lessons.life: Pray the Rosary slowly with the Gospel scenes, and notice where Mary points.
lessons.saint: Saints Francisco and Jacinta Marto: two Portuguese shepherd children who prayed the Rosary for sinners.
lessons.mem: “Blessed are you among women.” (Luke 1:42)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you could ask Jesus’ mother for anything, what would it be?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to describe four Marian dogmas and what honor differs from worship.

script.open: Place an image of Mary on the table, any artwork or icon, and invite each person to say one word that comes to mind. Write the words on the board. Say, “These are our starting points.”
teach: Say: “The Church has four Marian dogmas. Mother of God (Theotokos): Mary is truly the mother of Jesus, who is God (Council of Ephesus, 431). Luke 1:43: Elizabeth calls her ‘the mother of my Lord.’ Perpetual virginity: Mary was a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus (Lateran Council, 649). Isaiah 7:14, Luke 1:34. Immaculate Conception: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception, in view of Christ’s merits (Pius IX, 1854). Luke 1:28: ‘full of grace’ (kecharitomene) means she was already graced. Assumption: at the end of her life, Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (Pius XII, 1950). Revelation 12; ancient feast, from the 5th-6th centuries. Each dogma is about Christ and about us: Mary is the first and perfect disciple, what the Church will be.”

Say: “Why honor Mary? Because Jesus did: he obeyed her, and from the cross gave her to John: ‘Behold, your mother!’ (John 19:27) Because God chose her: ‘all generations will call me blessed.’ (Luke 1:48) Because she leads to Jesus: ‘Do whatever he tells you.’ (John 2:5) Because she is our model of faith and prayer. The Church distinguishes veneration (hyperdulia, special honor) from adoration (latria, for God alone). Catholics do not worship Mary. We ask her to pray for us, as we ask fellow Christians. Practices: the Rosary, Angelus, Hail Mary, Memorare, Marian feasts, scapular. The Rosary: twenty mysteries, from the Gospel. Marian apparitions (Guadalupe, Lourdes, Fátima): private revelations approved by the Church as worthy of belief, but they don’t add to the faith.”

Say: “Common objections. ‘Brothers and sisters of Jesus’ in the Gospels: the words (adelphoi) can mean relatives; Hebrew ach is broader; the Gospels never call them Mary’s sons. ‘Mary needed a Savior’ (Luke 1:47): yes, and was saved by anticipation, preserved from sin. ‘Not in Scripture’: the Assumption is in Tradition; the Church sees hints in Revelation 12 and Psalm 132:8; the Immaculate Conception in ‘full of grace.’ ‘Isn’t this too much?’ The Church warns against both excess and neglect; Vatican II’s Lumen Gentium chapter 8 is balanced. Mary’s place is in the mystery of Christ and the Church. Fátima children: they show that devotion to Mary is about prayer, sacrifice and love for sinners. Mary is also the mother of the Church. If you find devotion hard, start with the Hail Mary slowly, or the Magnificat. Ask her: ‘Show me your Son.’”
ask: Name the four Marian dogmas. (Mother of God, perpetual virginity, Immaculate Conception, Assumption.)
What is the difference between veneration and adoration? (Veneration is honor; adoration is for God alone.)
Are Marian apparitions required to be believed? (No; they are private revelations.)
practice: Make a chart of the four dogmas: statement, Scripture, date, what it says about Christ.
Pray one decade of the Rosary, with a Gospel scene, in silence and aloud.
Write a short reply to a friend who says Catholics worship Mary.
Choose one Marian prayer to pray daily this month.
script.close: Pray the Memorare together. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to read the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55) each day for a week.

tryit: Lay out the Marian dogmas with their roots.
Say what each says about Christ.
Write why Catholics honor Mary.
lessons.saintStory:
In 1917, in the village of Fátima, Portugal, three shepherd children—Lúcia dos Santos (10), and her cousins Francisco (9) and Jacinta Marto (7)—reported seeing a lady “brighter than the sun” on the thirteenth of each month from May to October. She asked them to pray the Rosary every day for peace and the conversion of sinners, and to offer sacrifices. On October 13, a crowd of some 70,000 people gathered, and many reported seeing the sun appear to spin and dance in the sky.
The children took her request seriously. They gave their lunch to the poor, endured thirst, wore a rough rope around their waists, and spent hours in prayer. Francisco liked to “console Jesus” by praying alone before the tabernacle. Jacinta, deeply moved by a vision of sinners suffering, offered many sacrifices.
Both fell ill in the 1918 influenza epidemic. Francisco died on April 4, 1919, at ten. Jacinta died on February 20, 1920, at nine, after painful treatment, alone in a hospital in Lisbon. They were canonized by Pope Francis in 2017, the youngest non-martyr saints in the Church. The Church approved the Fátima apparitions as worthy of belief, but no Catholic is required to believe them.

units.title: Hard questions about living the faith
units.eq: How do I hold the faith in a world that disagrees?

lessons.title: When I disagree: conscience and obedience
lessons.idea: Conscience is the voice of God in the heart, but it must be formed. Catholics are bound to follow a well-formed conscience and to give religious assent to the Church’s teaching.
lessons.question: What should I do if I cannot accept a teaching?
lessons.activity: Choose one Church teaching you find hard. Write the strongest reason the Church gives for it (use the Catechism), the strongest objection you have, and one step you will take to understand it better (a book, a priest, a friend, prayer). Share with someone you trust.
teach: Conscience is the inner judgment about right and wrong, and “a human being must always obey the certain judgment of his conscience” (CCC 1778, 1790). But it must be formed, and one is responsible for forming it (CCC 1783–1785). It is not a feeling and not an excuse to do what I want.

Formation uses Scripture, the Church’s teaching, prayer, honest examination, good counsel and the lived experience of virtue (CCC 1783–1785, 2039). When a Catholic finds a teaching difficult, the right response is to study it, pray, ask a wise guide, and not to dismiss it quickly or to hide.

Acts 5:29 (“We must obey God rather than men”) is the limit case: no authority can command what is evil. Newman’s “toast to conscience first” always presumes a conscience formed by truth. Conscientious objection to unjust laws is a duty (CCC 2242).

Disagreement is not the same as dissent. Honest questions, respectful dialogue and the patience of the saints (Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Ávila) show how to challenge from within. Public opposition that undermines the faith is different (CCC 2037–2040).
talk: What is the difference between “my feelings” and “my conscience”?
How do we know when we are being honest about a hard teaching?
Who can help someone with a hard question?
quiz: An informed conscience is one that…|Follows whatever feels right|Has been formed by truth, Scripture and the Church’s teaching|Never changes|Ignores authority|1|CCC 1783–1785.
Must we always obey a certain judgment of conscience?|No, never|Only in religious matters|Yes, but we must form it well|Only when others agree|2|CCC 1790.
Who said “I die the king’s good servant, but God’s first”?|Thomas More|Augustine|Francis|Ignatius|0|He refused to violate conscience.
lessons.life: Pick one teaching you struggle with. Read the Catechism passage and talk to a priest or mentor this month.
lessons.saint: Padre Pio: a Capuchin who obeyed when the Church forbade him to say Mass in public.
lessons.mem: “We must obey God rather than men.” (Acts 5:29)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When have you disagreed with someone you respect? How did you handle it?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to explain how to form a conscience and what it means to follow it.

script.open: Present a short case: a Catholic doctor is asked to do a procedure she believes is wrong. Ask, “What are her options? What should she consider first?” Take ideas before opening the lesson.
teach: Say: “Conscience. The Catechism: ‘Moral conscience is a judgment of reason by which the human person recognizes the moral quality of a concrete act.’ (CCC 1778) We must always follow a certain conscience. ‘Man has the right to act in conscience and in freedom.’ But conscience must be formed: it’s not just a feeling or preference. Newman: ‘Conscience has rights because it has duties.’ He also said that if he were to toast religion, he would toast conscience first and the Pope afterwards, meaning conscience rightly understood is the voice of God. A well-formed conscience will listen to Scripture, the Church’s teaching, and wise counsel. It’s a mistake to see conscience and Church teaching as opposed. The Church’s moral teaching is meant to inform conscience, not replace it.”

Say: “Obedience. In Catholic life, obedience is not blind. It’s a virtue rooted in trust that the Church has Christ’s authority (Luke 10:16). The levels of assent: for dogmas, the assent of faith; for definitive teachings, firm acceptance; for non-definitive authoritative teaching, ‘religious submission of will and intellect.’ (LG 25) That means a presumption in favor of the teaching and a willingness to study. Disagreement with prudential judgments or disciplines, such as how to organize a diocese or what the Pope says about economic policy, is legitimate. Disagreement with defined teaching is a problem. What do you do if you struggle? (1) Study: do I understand the teaching and its reasons? (2) Pray. (3) Seek counsel: a priest, a teacher. (4) Distinguish the doctrine from how it was presented or lived. (5) Remain in communion; keep the sacraments. (6) Avoid public dissent that confuses others. (7) Be patient: many saints and theologians had difficulties for years.”

Say: “Examples of faithful disagreement. Catherine of Siena urged the pope to return to Rome. Thomas More refused to sign an oath. Teresa of Avila and John of the Cross endured suspicion. Yves Congar and Henri de Lubac were silenced in the 1950s but later helped shape Vatican II. Padre Pio. Mary Ward. These people criticized or were criticized, but they remained loyal and loved the Church. The test: do I act with humility? Do I listen? Do I love the Church? Do I seek truth? When conscience and the law conflict, as for Franz Jägerstätter or the martyrs, follow conscience, accepting the cost. For most of us, the issue is smaller: a hard teaching on sexuality or authority. Don’t leave when it’s hard; ask, wrestle, wait. The Church is a family, and families argue. Obedience, rightly understood, is listening (ob-audire). Padre Pio’s humility won more than argument could.”
ask: Must we always follow our conscience? (Yes, but it must be well formed.)
What does ‘religious submission of mind and will’ mean? (A presumption in favor of authoritative teaching, with willingness to study.)
How did Padre Pio respond to unjust restrictions? (He obeyed without public protest.)
practice: Work through a case: a Catholic believes the Church is wrong about a teaching. List steps they should take.
Write your own questions about a teaching you find difficult, and who you can ask.
Write a statement of what faithful disagreement looks like and doesn’t.
Commit to finding one answer this month.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give me a humble heart and a well-formed conscience.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to speak with a priest about a hard question.

tryit: Work through a conscience-versus-teaching case.
Identify the questions to ask first.
Write what faithful disagreement looks like.
lessons.saintStory:
Padre Pio of Pietrelcina became a household name in the 1920s, when thousands flocked to the friary at San Giovanni Rotondo to see the priest with the stigmata and to confess to him. Some Church officials were suspicious. In 1923, the Holy Office, which investigated these matters, imposed restrictions on him; in 1931, he was forbidden to celebrate Mass publicly or hear confessions, and was almost confined to his room. He was suspected of fraud and self-inflicted wounds, among other things.
Padre Pio believed the accusations were false and hurtful. He could have resisted or caused a stir. He had a huge following of supporters who would have defended him. Instead, he said, “I will obey.” He said Mass privately in the friary chapel, accepted the restrictions without public complaint, and told his followers to be calm. After two years, in 1933, Pope Pius XI quietly restored his faculties.
Later, in the 1960s, new restrictions were imposed again, and he accepted them again. His obedience is one reason the Church sees his holiness as authentic. He died in 1968 and was canonized in 2002.

lessons.title: Faith, politics and the common good
lessons.idea: Faith should shape how we take part in public life. The Church teaches principles on life, justice and the common good, but no party perfectly embodies them, so Catholics must form their conscience and take part with charity.
lessons.question: How can a Catholic vote and take part in public life?
lessons.activity: Choose a current civic issue. Write how three principles (dignity, common good, subsidiarity, solidarity) apply, what questions of fact you need answered, and how you will talk about it with someone who disagrees, charitably. Then decide one local action.
teach: Jesus did not escape politics: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:15–22). The state has a legitimate sphere, and God has the final claim. Christians are called to be good citizens (CCC 2238–2243).

The common good guides civic life (CCC 1905–1912, 1913–1917). Participation, voting, public service and informed engagement are duties of citizenship (CCC 2240). The Church teaches principles but does not endorse a party; Catholics apply them prudently and disagree in good faith on means.

Some issues touch fundamental dignity (the life of the unborn and the dying, the poor, migrants, religious liberty, marriage and family, war and peace, care for creation). The bishops’ Faithful Citizenship urges forming conscience on all of them and not treating one as a trump card for the rest.
Practical habits: read widely and fairly, pray before voting, avoid contempt (CCC 2477, 2479), and serve locally. Political friendship across lines is a witness (Luke 6:27–36).
talk: What do I do when no party fits Catholic teaching?
Which issues are non-negotiable and which are matters of prudence?
How do I talk about politics with family without damaging relationships?
quiz: According to Catholic teaching, citizens should…|Stay out of politics|Take part in public life and form their conscience|Always vote for one party|Obey every law without question|1|CCC 2240.
The “common good” is…|Private interest|Whatever the government says|The conditions that allow everyone to flourish|The good of the majority only|2|CCC 1906.
Which Church document by Pope Francis addresses care for creation?|Humanae Vitae|Rerum Novarum|Evangelium Vitae|Laudato Si’|3|2015.
lessons.life: Read the U.S. bishops’ voting guide and discuss it with someone who sees things differently.
lessons.saint: Venerable Robert Schuman: a French foreign minister who rebuilt Europe with reconciliation and daily Mass.
lessons.mem: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” (Matthew 22:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What is one issue where your faith shapes how you vote or act?”
lessons.assess: Ask each person to apply three principles of Catholic social teaching to a civic issue.

script.open: Ask: “Can a person of faith be involved in politics? Should they? What are the risks of faith in politics? The risks of leaving it out?” Take answers. Say, “Tonight we find a Catholic way of thinking.”
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that political participation is a duty: ‘It is necessary that all participate, each according to his position and role, in promoting the common good.’ (CCC 1913-1915) Faithful Citizenship, the US bishops’ document, says conscience should guide Catholic voters. Vatican II: Christians shouldn’t flee their duties in the world (GS 43). Politics is a ‘demanding form of charity’ (Paul VI). The Church doesn’t endorse parties or candidates, but she forms consciences with principles: the dignity of every person from conception to natural death; the common good; subsidiarity; solidarity; the option for the poor; the family as the basic unit; religious freedom; care for creation. These principles don’t map neatly onto party platforms. A Catholic may find herself pulled in different directions.”

Say: “The hard part: weighing priorities. The bishops teach that some issues involve ‘intrinsically evil’ acts that can never be supported, like abortion and euthanasia, and these have a special seriousness; other issues, like how to reduce poverty or care for immigrants, involve prudential judgment about the best means, though the goal is fixed. Catholics can disagree on the means. Pope Francis and the bishops warn against reducing Catholic teaching to a single issue, and against ignoring any. A voter must form conscience, study the facts, pray, and weigh. Voting for a candidate because of a position one disagrees with, for proportionate reasons, can be acceptable, but never to support an intrinsic evil as such. Practical: read primary sources, not just partisan media; talk with people who disagree; avoid contempt; pay attention to local issues; vote; run for office; join a civic group.”

Say: “The Church and the state. The Church’s traditional teaching: Church and state are distinct; each has its own sphere (Jesus: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s,’ Mark 12:17). Religious freedom. Catholic social teaching also warns against both the secular state that excludes religion and the confessional state that coerces faith. Lay Catholics have the primary role in politics; clergy should form consciences, not lead parties. Be careful of idolatry of party or ideology, tribal politics and hatred. Remember Christians in all parties. Pray for leaders (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Schuman’s approach: reconciliation, patience, humility, service. Practical: choose one issue to learn about; contact your representatives; vote with a formed conscience; speak charitably online. Faith is not private, but it is not partisan.”
ask: Is political participation a Catholic duty? (Yes, according to one’s role.)
Does the Church endorse parties? (No; she forms consciences with principles.)
What is the difference between an intrinsic evil and a prudential judgment? (Intrinsic evils are always wrong; prudential issues involve judging the best means.)
practice: Choose a current policy issue. Apply Catholic principles (dignity, common good, subsidiarity, solidarity) and list how they pull.
Write what facts you need to learn before deciding.
Write a respectful way to discuss it with someone who disagrees.
Choose one civic action for this semester: register, volunteer, contact an official.
script.close: Pray for leaders: “Lord, guide those who govern, and make us faithful citizens.” Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to read Faithful Citizenship.

tryit: Apply Catholic principles to a policy issue.
Name two goods that compete.
Write what a faithful citizen does.
lessons.saintStory:
Robert Schuman was born in 1886 in Luxembourg, to a family from Lorraine, the region disputed between France and Germany. He studied law and became a politician. His region was German when he was born, French after World War I. He served in the French Parliament, was imprisoned by the Gestapo in World War II, escaped, and hid in monasteries.
After the war, as France’s foreign minister, he faced the question of how to prevent another war between France and Germany. On May 9, 1950, he announced a plan to place the coal and steel industries of both countries under a common authority, so that war between them would become “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” This became the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951, the seed of the European Union.
Schuman never married. He went to Mass daily and was known for personal modesty. He said that democracy owes its existence to Christianity, and that politics is a service. He died in 1963. In 2021, Pope Francis declared him Venerable.

lessons.title: Doubt, dryness and the dark night
lessons.idea: Doubt is part of many people’s journey. The Church distinguishes honest questions from willful rejection, and teaches that trust and prayer can carry us through seasons when God feels distant.
lessons.question: What do I do when I do not feel God?
lessons.activity: Read Psalm 88 aloud. Write your own lament in five lines: address God, say what hurts, say what you wish. Then list three people or practices that keep you steady in dry times, and tell one of them about this lesson.
teach: Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief is. Doubts can be honest questions (Thomas, John 20:24–29; the father in Mark 9:24, “I believe; help my unbelief”) or avoidance. The Church distinguishes involuntary doubt (a difficulty) from voluntary doubt (CCC 2088). Seek answers with prayer and study.

Dryness is common: God seems absent, prayer feels empty (CCC 2726–2728). Psalm 88 gives voice to this and ends in darkness, a sign that God can be addressed in despair. John of the Cross called such seasons the dark night, a purification that leads to deeper love.
Teresa of Calcutta experienced decades of spiritual dryness while serving the poor. Her letters show faith as fidelity, not feeling. The Eucharist and Confession are given for weak days.

Distinguish dryness from depression. If you feel hopeless, persistently sad or unsafe, seek a doctor or counselor as well as a priest; if you are in danger, contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately. Faith and healthcare are partners.
talk: What is the difference between a question and a rejection?
What does Psalm 88 teach about honest prayer?
What helps you when you feel nothing in prayer?
quiz: What does the Catechism say about involuntary doubt?|It means you were never a believer|It is the same as unbelief|It does not destroy faith|It is always a mortal sin|2|CCC 2088.
Who wrote about “the dark night of the soul”?|Augustine|Francis|Benedict|John of the Cross|3|He wrote of spiritual dryness.
Which psalm ends in darkness yet is part of Scripture?|Psalm 100|Psalm 150|Psalm 88|Psalm 23|2|It shows honest prayer.
lessons.life: Speak honestly to God for five minutes each day this week, in your own words.
lessons.saint: Mother Teresa of Calcutta: she served for decades in the dark, without the felt presence of God, and said she had come to love the darkness.
misc: “If I feel nothing, God is gone.”
lessons.mem: “O Lord, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.” (Psalm 88:1)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 88 aloud. Ask: “What do you notice? How does it end?” (In darkness.)
lessons.assess: Ask each person to name signs of dryness, doubt and depression, and who they could talk to.

script.open: Say: “Be honest about your inner life. On a scale of 1 to 10, how close does God feel right now? Write a number on a slip of paper. You don’t need to share it.” Allow silence. Then: “If it’s low, you are in good company.”
teach: Say: “Doubt and dryness are common. The Catechism distinguishes: involuntary doubt (difficulty in believing, which is not a sin) and voluntary doubt (deliberately fostering uncertainty). The father in Mark 9:24 says, ‘I believe; help my unbelief!’ Thomas doubted and was answered. Dryness in prayer is when we feel nothing, or find prayer boring. Reasons include fatigue, stress, sin, or God’s way of purifying our love. The ‘dark night of the soul,’ described by John of the Cross, is a stage when God withdraws consolations to draw us to a purer faith, hope and love. It differs from depression, though they can overlap; if sadness, hopelessness or loss of interest in everything persist, seek medical or psychological help, as well as spiritual guidance. Don’t assume it’s only a spiritual problem.”

Say: “What to do. One: persevere. The measure of prayer is faithfulness, not feeling. Pray even briefly; keep your time. Two: simplify. Use short prayers: ‘Jesus, I trust in you.’ The Psalms give words; the lament psalms speak to feelings of abandonment (Psalm 22, 88). Three: keep the sacraments. The Eucharist and Confession don’t depend on feelings. Four: keep serving: love is shown in deeds. Five: seek a spiritual director or a wise friend; don’t isolate. Six: examine your life: is there unconfessed sin, neglected duty, unforgiveness, overwork? Seven: take care of the body: sleep, exercise, nutrition. Eight: read the saints who went through it: Teresa of Calcutta, Thérèse of Lisieux, Jane de Chantal, John of the Cross. Nine: trust. Even Jesus on the cross prayed, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ Faith is not a feeling; it’s a decision to trust.”

Say: “Doubts about the faith itself. Honest intellectual doubts deserve honest engagement: read serious authors, talk to someone knowledgeable, and keep praying while you search. Doubts often come with life changes (college, loss, hurt). Doubts due to scandal or suffering: speak to a pastor. Doubts about whether God loves you: talk to someone. Don’t make major decisions in desolation, Ignatius advised; wait for consolation. Remember what you knew in light. Encourage others in their dryness: don’t say ‘just pray more’ but ‘I’m with you.’ Mother Teresa’s experience shows that holiness is not a constant feeling of closeness, and that God can be working deeply when we feel nothing. The course ends here; the road continues. ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ (2 Corinthians 12:9)”
ask: Is involuntary doubt a sin? (No.)
What is the dark night of the soul? (A stage where God withdraws consolations to purify faith and love.)
What should you do in a dry season? (Persevere in prayer and sacraments, keep serving, seek guidance, care for body and mind.)
practice: Write about a dry season you have had: what it felt like, what helped.
Write a short plan for the next one: one short prayer, one sacrament habit, one person to tell, one self-care practice.
Read Psalm 88 or 22 slowly. Notice that the psalm is honest.
Share one line of your plan with a partner.
script.close: Pray Mother Teresa’s prayer: “Jesus, I trust in you,” and end with the Our Father. Sign of the Cross. Encourage the group to keep meeting, to continue the journey together.

tryit: Describe your own dry season in prayer.
List what has helped in the past.
Write a plan for the next one.
lessons.saintStory:
In 1946, on a train to Darjeeling, Mother Teresa received what she called a call within her vocation: to serve Jesus in the poorest of the poor. She founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta in 1950. In the early years, she experienced visions and consolation. But beginning in 1948-49 and lasting, with brief breaks, until her death in 1997, she experienced a deep spiritual darkness: a sense of God’s absence, emptiness and abandonment.
She did not reveal this publicly. After her death, her letters were published in Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light (2007). In a letter to a priest friend, she wrote: “Jesus has a very special love for you. As for me, the silence and the emptiness is so great that I look and do not see, listen and do not hear.” She wrote that she was in “terrible darkness,” and doubted God. Some people took this as a sign she lost faith. But she continued to pray, serve and go to Mass daily. She came to see the darkness as a share in the thirst of Jesus on the cross, and wrote that she had “come to love the darkness,” because she believed it was a part of his suffering.
She was canonized in 2016. Her story is a witness to fidelity without feeling.
